Chapter 1

Milnor §§1–2, pp. 1–12: critical points, the Hessian and the index, the Morse lemma, flows

V1.1

The torus of §1

narrower
(2)–(4) not identifiedno cell attachmentsa torus of revolution, $0 < \rho < R$(1) read as $a < 0 = f(p)$

Milnor §1, pp. 1–3

A torus $M$ stands on a plane $V$ to which it is tangent (Diagram 1), $f : M \to \mathbb R$ is the height above $V$, and $M^a = \{x \in M : f(x) \le a\}$. Milnor lists five stages as $a$ increases: $M^a$ is vacuous below $f(p)$, homeomorphic to a 2-cell for $f(p) < a < f(q)$, to a cylinder for $f(q) < a < f(r)$, to a compact genus-one surface bounded by a circle for $f(r) < a < f(s)$, and is the full torus above $f(s)$. Up to homotopy type, passing $f(p)$, $f(q)$, $f(r)$, $f(s)$ attaches a 0-cell, a 1-cell, a 1-cell and a 2-cell. The four points are the critical points of $f$, and in suitable coordinates $f = x^2 + y^2$ at $p$, $f = \text{const} + x^2 - y^2$ at $q$ and $r$, and $f = \text{const} - x^2 - y^2$ at $s$: the number of minus signs is the dimension of the cell attached.

No equations are given and nothing is checked: the example is offered as an illustration of the theorems to come.

Proved in Lean

For $0 < \rho < R$ let $T \subseteq \mathbb R^3$ be the torus $(\sqrt{x_1^2 + x_2^2} - R)^2 + x_3^2 = \rho^2$, a compact surface (V3.22), and $f(x) = x_1 + R + \rho$ its height above the plane $x_1 = -(R + \rho)$, which touches $T$ at $p = (-(R + \rho), 0, 0)$. Then $f|T$ has exactly four critical points, $p$, $q = (-(R - \rho), 0, 0)$, $r = (R - \rho, 0, 0)$ and $s = (R + \rho, 0, 0)$, at the heights $0$, $2\rho$, $2R$ and $2R + 2\rho$; all four are non-degenerate, of indices $0, 1, 1, 2$. $T^a = \emptyset$ for $a < 0$ and $T^a = T$ for $a \ge 2R + 2\rho$. If $a \le b$ and $[a, b]$ contains none of the four heights, a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism of $T$ carries $T^a$ onto $T^b$, $T^a$ is a strong deformation retract of $T^b$, and the inclusion $T^a \to T^b$ is a homotopy equivalence.

What differs

  • Of the five stages only (1) and (5) are proved. That the intermediate sublevel sets are a disk, a cylinder and a torus with a disk removed is not, and neither are the cell attachments of p. 2; between critical heights only Theorem 3.1 is applied.
  • The torus is fixed: the torus of revolution with $0 < \rho < R$, standing upright on its tangent plane. Lying flat, its height function would have two circles of degenerate critical points.
  • The critical points, their indices and the four critical values are proved, where Milnor asserts them; the normal forms are not restated, but follow from the lemma of Morse (V1.8) and the indices.
  • Case (1) is printed $a < 0 < f(p)$ in the scan, whereas $f(p) = 0$; the hypothesis is $a < 0$. The details, whose Lean files sit with Chapter 3, are V3.22–V3.25.
V1.2

Attaching a cell

as in the book

Milnor §1, pp. 2–3

With $e^k$ the $k$-cell of vectors of length at most $1$ in $\mathbb R^k$, $\dot e^k$ its boundary sphere $S^{k-1}$, and $g : S^{k-1} \to Y$ continuous, the space $Y \cup_g e^k$, $Y$ with a $k$-cell attached by $g$, is obtained from the topological sum of $Y$ and $e^k$ by identifying each $x \in S^{k-1}$ with $g(x) \in Y$. For $k = 0$, $e^0$ is a point and $\dot e^0 = S^{-1}$ is empty, so that attaching a 0-cell adds a disjoint point.

Proved in Lean

For a topological space $X$, an integer $n \ge 0$ and a continuous map $\varphi : S^{n-1} \to X$, the space $X \cup_\varphi e^n$ is the pushout, in the category of topological spaces, of $\varphi$ and the inclusion of the unit sphere $S^{n-1}$ in the closed unit ball $D^n$ of $\mathbb R^n$: the quotient of $X \sqcup D^n$ by the identification of each $u \in S^{n-1}$ with $\varphi(u)$, so that a map out of it is a pair of maps on $X$ and on $D^n$ which agree along $\varphi$. For $n = 0$ the sphere is empty and $D^0$ is a point. The disk and the sphere are Mathlib's, those of its CW complexes.

V1.3

Critical points, the Hessian, index and nullity in coordinates

restated
index: the negative index of inertianon-degenerate: null space $0$Milnor's definitions become theorems

Milnor §2, pp. 4–5

A point $p$ is a critical point of a smooth $f : M \to \mathbb R$ when the induced map $f_* : TM_p \to T\mathbb R_{f(p)}$ is zero, which in local coordinates means that the first partial derivatives vanish at $p$; $f(p)$ is then a critical value. A critical point is non-degenerate when the matrix $(\partial^2 f/\partial x^i \partial x^j(p))$ is non-singular, a condition which can be checked directly not to depend on the coordinates. The index of a bilinear functional $H$ on a vector space is the maximal dimension of a subspace on which $H$ is negative definite, and its nullity is the dimension of the null space $\{v : H(v, w) = 0 \text{ for all } w\}$; a critical point is non-degenerate exactly when $f_{**}$ has nullity $0$.

The coordinate condition for a critical point is displayed in the book, but the display is lost in the scan.

Proved in Lean

Let $E$ be a real normed space and $f : E \to \mathbb R$. A point $p$ is a critical point of $f$ if $f$ is differentiable at $p$ with derivative $0$. The Hessian of $f$ at $p$ is the second derivative $d^2 f_p$, a continuous bilinear form on $E$, symmetric when $f$ is $C^2$ at $p$; it is defined at every point but only used at critical points. For a continuous bilinear form $H$ on $E$ the null space is $\{v : H(v, w) = 0 \text{ for all } w\}$, the nullity is its dimension, $H$ is non-degenerate if its null space is $0$, and the index of $H$ is the negative index of inertia of $v \mapsto H(v, v)$. For finite-dimensional $E$ the index is the largest dimension of a subspace on which $H(v, v) < 0$ for all $v \ne 0$, and non-degenerate means nullity $0$; for $E = \mathbb R^n$ and $f$ of class $C^2$ at $p$, it means that the matrix $(\partial^2 f/\partial x^i\partial x^j(p))$ is non-singular.

What differs

  • The index is defined as Mathlib's negative index of inertia, and Milnor's definition, the maximal dimension of a negative definite subspace, is a theorem.
  • Non-degeneracy is defined by a zero null space; Milnor's definition by a non-singular matrix of second partial derivatives is a theorem, for $f$ of class $C^2$ at $p$.
  • The nullity is a dimension in Mathlib's sense, which is $0$ for an infinite-dimensional null space; the counts are meaningful in finite dimension, where they are used.
V1.4

The same notions on a manifold; Morse functions

restated
the Hessian read in the preferred chartno vector-field extensionsno Hausdorff hypothesis

Milnor §2, pp. 4–5

At a critical point $p$ of $f$ on a manifold $M$, the Hessian is the symmetric bilinear functional $f_{**}$ on $TM_p$ given by $f_{**}(v, w) = \tilde v_p(\tilde w(f))$, where $\tilde v$ and $\tilde w$ are vector fields extending $v$ and $w$; it is symmetric because the Poisson bracket term $[\tilde v, \tilde w]_p(f)$ vanishes at a critical point, and hence independent of both extensions. In local coordinates its matrix in the basis $\partial/\partial x^i|_p$ is $(\partial^2 f/\partial x^i\partial x^j(p))$. The index of $f$ at $p$ is the index of $f_{**}$. Differentiable functions with no degenerate critical points are the subject of Theorem 3.5 (p. 20).

Proved in Lean

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a real normed space $E$, with no Hausdorff or countability hypothesis, $f : M \to \mathbb R$ and $p \in M$. The point $p$ is a critical point of $f$ if $df_p : T_pM \to \mathbb R$ is $0$; equivalently, $df_p$ is not surjective, which is the companion project's definition. The Hessian $f_{**}$ at $p$ is the second derivative at $\kappa(p)$ of $f \circ \kappa^{-1}$, $\kappa$ the preferred chart at $p$: a bilinear form on $E$, which Mathlib identifies with $T_pM$ through the same chart. The index and the nullity of $f$ at $p$ are those of $f_{**}$, and $p$ is a non-degenerate critical point if it is critical and $f_{**}$ is non-degenerate. A Morse function is a $C^\infty$ function on $M$ all of whose critical points are non-degenerate.

V1.5

Independence of the coordinate system

stronger
$f$ only $C^2$ at $p$coordinates in any normed spacecriticality used exactly once

Milnor §2, pp. 4–5

Milnor remarks that non-degeneracy does not depend on the coordinate system, which can be checked directly and will also follow from the intrinsic definition of the Hessian; on p. 5 he computes that the matrix $(\partial^2 f/\partial x^i\partial x^j(p))$ represents $f_{**}$ with respect to the basis $\partial/\partial x^1|_p, \dots, \partial/\partial x^n|_p$.

Proved in Lean

On normed spaces: if $\psi$ is $C^2$ at $q$, $f$ is $C^2$ at $\psi(q)$ and $df_{\psi(q)} = 0$, then $d^2(f\circ\psi)_q(v, w) = d^2 f_{\psi(q)}(d\psi_q v, d\psi_q w)$. On a manifold $M$ as in V1.4, a smooth coordinate system is a homeomorphism $y$ of an open subset of $M$ onto an open subset of a real normed space $E'$, $C^\infty$ with $C^\infty$ inverse (for $E' = E$ these are exactly the charts of the maximal atlas); let $p$ lie in its domain. If $f$ is differentiable at $p$, then $p$ is critical iff $y(p)$ is a critical point of $f \circ y^{-1}$, that is, for $E' = \mathbb R^n$, iff all the $\partial f/\partial y^i(p)$ vanish. If $f$ is $C^2$ at $p$ and $p$ is critical, the Hessian of $f \circ y^{-1}$ at $y(p)$ is $f_{**}$ composed in both arguments with the derivative of $y^{-1}$ at $y(p)$; hence non-degeneracy, index and nullity are those of $f \circ y^{-1}$ at $y(p)$, and for $E' = \mathbb R^n$, $p$ is non-degenerate iff $\det(\partial^2 f/\partial y^i\partial y^j(p)) \ne 0$.

V1.6

Functions on a slice submanifold

not in the book
the setting of Chapters 2–4Hessian of $F \circ x$, not of $F$Milnor's formulas of pp. 35–36 proved

Milnor §6, pp. 35–36

The book has no separate setting for functions on a submanifold. §2 is written for an abstract manifold, and from §6 on Milnor computes on $M \subset \mathbb R^n$ in local coordinates $u \mapsto \vec x(u)$ without comment. For $L_{\vec p}(\vec q) = \|\vec q - \vec p\|^2$ he notes that $\vec q$ is critical iff $\vec q - \vec p$ is normal to $M$ at $\vec q$ (p. 35), and that at a critical point the second partial derivatives are $2(\partial\vec x/\partial u^i \cdot \partial\vec x/\partial u^j + \partial^2\vec x/\partial u^i\partial u^j \cdot (\vec x - \vec p))$ (p. 36).

Proved in Lean

Let $V$ be a real normed space and $N \subseteq V$ a slice submanifold modelled on $Z$ in the sense of the companion project: every point of $N$ lies in the domain of a slice chart $\sigma$, a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism of an open subset of $V$ onto an open subset of $Z \times W$ carrying the points of $N$ in its domain exactly onto $Z \times \{0\}$. $N$ need not be closed; it is a smooth manifold modelled on $Z$, with the parametrizations $x(z) = \sigma^{-1}(z, 0)$. Let $T_qN \subseteq V$ be the range of the derivative of the inclusion, $F : V \to \mathbb R$, and $q \in N$ in the domain of $\sigma$. If $F$ is differentiable at $q$, then $q$ is a critical point of $F|N$ iff $\sigma(q)_1$ is a critical point of $F \circ x$, iff $dF_q$ vanishes on $T_qN$, and, for a complete inner product space $V$, iff $\nabla F(q) \perp T_qN$. If $F$ is $C^2$ at a critical point $q$ of $f = F|N$, the Hessian of $F \circ x$ at $\sigma(q)_1$ is the Hessian $f_{**}$ of V1.4 composed with the derivative of the parametrization, so non-degeneracy, index and nullity of $F|N$ at $q$ are those of $F \circ x$. For $V$ an inner product space and $L_p(y) = \|y - p\|^2$: $q$ is a critical point of $L_p|N$ iff $q - p \perp T_qN$; for any $x$ of class $C^2$ at $u$, the second derivative of $L_p \circ x$ at $u$ is $2(\langle \partial x/\partial v, \partial x/\partial w\rangle + \langle \partial^2 x/\partial v\,\partial w, x(u) - p\rangle)$; and at a critical point the index and the nullity of $L_p|N$ are those of this form.

Lemma 2.1 (Hadamard)

stronger
star-shaped, not convexany normed source, complete target$B(0) = \frac12 d^2f_0$ proved$V$ open

Milnor §2, Lemma 2.1 · p. 5

A $C^\infty$ function $f$ on a convex neighbourhood $V$ of $0$ in $\mathbb R^n$ with $f(0) = 0$ can be written $f(x) = \sum_i x_i g_i(x)$, the $g_i$ being $C^\infty$ on $V$ with $g_i(0) = \partial f/\partial x_i(0)$. The proof writes $f(x)$ as $\int_0^1 \frac{d}{dt} f(tx)\,dt$ and takes $g_i(x) = \int_0^1 \partial f/\partial x_i(tx)\,dt$.

Proved in Lean

Let $V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and convex with $0 \in V$, and $f$ smooth on $V$ with $f(0) = 0$. Then $f(x) = \sum_i x_i g_i(x)$ on $V$ for functions $g_i$ smooth on $V$ with $g_i(0) = \partial f/\partial x_i(0)$. More generally, let $V$ be open and star-shaped about $0$ in a real normed space $E$ and $f$ smooth on $V$, with values in a complete normed space and $f(0) = 0$. Then $f(x) = L(x)\,x$ on $V$ for a family of linear maps $L$ smooth on $V$ with $L(0) = df_0$; and if moreover $df_0 = 0$, then $f(x) = B(x)(x, x)$ on $V$ for a family of bilinear maps $B$ smooth on $V$, with $B(x)$ symmetric for each $x \in V$ and $B(0) = \frac12 d^2 f_0$. Along the way: if $h$ is $C^n$ on an open $U \subseteq E \times \mathbb R$ containing $V \times [0, 1]$, $V$ open, then $x \mapsto \int_0^1 h(x, t)\,dt$ is $C^n$ on $V$.

Lemma 2.2 (the lemma of Morse)

stronger
$f$ smooth only near $p$any manifold, no Hausdorff hypothesisone inverse-function step

Milnor §2, Lemma 2.2 · p. 6

Near a non-degenerate critical point $p$ of $f$ there are local coordinates $(y^1, \dots, y^n)$, all vanishing at $p$, on a neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, in which $f = f(p) - (y^1)^2 - \dots - (y^\lambda)^2 + (y^{\lambda+1})^2 + \dots + (y^n)^2$ on all of $U$, $\lambda$ being the index of $f$ at $p$. The proof writes $f = \sum x_ix_jh_{ij}$ by Lemma 2.1 and completes one square at a time by induction, after a linear change of the last $n - r + 1$ coordinates making $H_{rr}(0) \ne 0$.

Proved in Lean

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $n = \dim E$, $f$ smooth on an open set $U \ni p$, and $p$ a critical point at which $d^2 f_p$ is non-degenerate, of index $\lambda$. Then there is a homeomorphism $y$ of an open neighbourhood $U' \subseteq U$ of $p$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$, $C^\infty$ with $C^\infty$ inverse, such that $y(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) - (y^1)^2 - \dots - (y^\lambda)^2 + (y^{\lambda+1})^2 + \dots + (y^n)^2$ throughout $U'$. In coordinate-free form, there is such a $\varphi$ onto an open subset of $E$ with $\varphi(p) = 0$, $d\varphi_p = \mathrm{id}$ and $f = f(p) + \frac12 d^2 f_p(\varphi, \varphi)$ on its domain. On a smooth manifold without boundary modelled on $E$, with no Hausdorff hypothesis, for $f$ smooth on an open $U \ni p$ and $p$ a non-degenerate critical point of index $\lambda$: there is a smooth coordinate system $y$ with values in $\mathbb R^n$, domain an open neighbourhood of $p$ inside $U$, $y(p) = 0$ and the same normal form on its domain; and there is a chart $\varphi$ of the maximal atlas with domain inside $U$, $\varphi(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) + \frac12 f_{**}(\varphi, \varphi)$.

The index is forced by the normal form

stronger
criticality concluded, not assumednon-degeneracy concluded

Milnor §2, proof of Lemma 2.2 · p. 6

The proof of Lemma 2.2 begins by showing that if $f(q) = f(p) - (z^1(q))^2 - \dots - (z^\lambda(q))^2 + (z^{\lambda+1}(q))^2 + \dots + (z^n(q))^2$ in some coordinate system $z$ around $p$, then $\lambda$ must be the index of $f$ at $p$: the matrix of $f_{**}$ in the basis $\partial/\partial z^i|_p$ is diagonal with $\lambda$ entries $-2$ and $n - \lambda$ entries $2$, so $f_{**}$ is negative definite on a subspace of dimension $\lambda$ and positive definite on one of dimension $n - \lambda$, and no larger negative definite subspace exists.

Proved in Lean

On a real normed space $E$ with $n = \dim E$: if $f$ is $C^2$ at a critical point $p$ and $z$ is a homeomorphism of an open neighbourhood of $p$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb R^n$, $C^\infty$ with $C^\infty$ inverse, with $z(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) - \sum_{i \le k}(z^i)^2 + \sum_{i > k}(z^i)^2$ on its domain, $k \le n$, then $k$ is the index of $f$ at $p$. On a manifold as in V1.4, with no hypothesis on $f$: if $z$ is a smooth coordinate system around $p$ with values in $\mathbb R^n$, $z(p) = 0$, $k \le n$, and $f$ has this form on its domain, then $p$ is a non-degenerate critical point of $f$ of index $k$.

Milnor §2, Corollary 2.3 · p. 8

A non-degenerate critical point is isolated: no other critical point comes arbitrarily close to it. The corollary is stated directly after the proof of Lemma 2.2, with no proof of its own.

Let $E$ be finite-dimensional. If $f : E \to \mathbb R$ is $C^2$ at $p$ and $p$ is a non-degenerate critical point, then $p$ has a neighbourhood in which it is the only critical point of $f$. The same holds on a manifold without boundary modelled on $E$, for $f$ of class $C^2$ at $p$.

Examples of degenerate critical points

value differs
(d): the $y$ axis, not the $x$ axis(a), (c): the only critical point(b) not formalized

Milnor §2, pp. 8–9

Milnor pictures five degenerate critical points: (a) $f(x) = x^3$ at the origin; (b) $e^{-1/x^2}\sin^2(1/x)$, whose origin is a degenerate and non-isolated critical point; (c) the monkey saddle $x^3 - 3xy^2$, the real part of $(x + iy)^3$, at $(0, 0)$; (d) $f(x, y) = x^2$, whose critical points, all degenerate, form the $x$ axis, a submanifold of $\mathbb R^2$; (e) $x^2y^2$, whose degenerate critical points fill the union of the $x$ and $y$ axes, not even a submanifold of $\mathbb R^2$.

Proved in Lean

(a) The only critical point of $x^3$ on $\mathbb R$ is $0$, where the Hessian is $0$, so it is degenerate. (c) The only critical point of $x^3 - 3xy^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$ is the origin, where the Hessian is $0$. (d) The critical points of $x^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$ are the points of the line $x = 0$, and all are degenerate. (e) The critical points of $x^2y^2$ are the points of the two coordinate axes, and all are degenerate. In (d) and (e) degeneracy is the contrapositive of Corollary 2.3: a critical point that is a limit of other critical points, of a function $C^2$ there, is degenerate.

V1.13

One-parameter groups of diffeomorphisms

narrower
$M$ a vector space $E$$\varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}$ proved

Milnor §2, pp. 9–10

Milnor's 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms of $M$ is a $C^\infty$ map $\varphi : \mathbb R \times M \to M$ whose maps $\varphi_t$ are diffeomorphisms of $M$ with $\varphi_{t+s} = \varphi_t \circ \varphi_s$. It determines the vector field $X_q(f) = \lim_{h \to 0} (f(\varphi_h(q)) - f(q))/h$, which is said to generate $\varphi$, and each orbit $t \mapsto \varphi_t(q)$ solves $d\varphi_t(q)/dt = X_{\varphi_t(q)}$ with $\varphi_0(q) = q$.

Proved in Lean

On a real normed space $E$, a one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms is a map $\varphi : \mathbb R \times E \to E$, $C^\infty$ in $(t, x)$, such that each $\varphi_t$ is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism of $E$ and $\varphi_{t+s} = \varphi_t\circ\varphi_s$ for all $t$, $s$. A vector field $X : E \to E$ generates $\varphi$ if for every $x$ the curve $h \mapsto \varphi_h(x)$ has derivative $X(x)$ at $h = 0$. Then $\varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}$, and if $X$ generates $\varphi$, every orbit $t \mapsto \varphi_t(x)$ is an integral curve of $X$.

Global flows, and smooth dependence on the initial point

global, not local and iteratedsmooth dependence proved, not quotedvector spaces only

Milnor §2, pp. 10–11

In the proof of Lemma 2.4 Milnor quotes as well known, citing Graves, that the equation $d\varphi_t(q)/dt = X_{\varphi_t(q)}$, $\varphi_0(q) = q$, has locally a unique solution which depends smoothly on the initial conditions. Covering the compact support $K$ by finitely many such neighbourhoods gives $\epsilon_0 > 0$ and solutions for $|t| < \epsilon_0$, smooth in both variables; for larger $t$ he iterates $\varphi_{\epsilon_0/2}$, and says it is not difficult to verify that the result is well defined, smooth, and satisfies $\varphi_{t+s} = \varphi_t\circ\varphi_s$.

Proved in Lean

Let $E$ be a complete real normed space and $X : E \to E$ bounded and globally Lipschitz, for instance $C^1$ with compact support. Through every point there is an integral curve of $X$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$, every integral curve is a flow line, and the flow satisfies $\varphi_0 = \mathrm{id}$ and $\varphi_{s+t} = \varphi_s\circ\varphi_t$, is jointly continuous in $(t, x)$, and each $\varphi_t$ is a homeomorphism with inverse $\varphi_{-t}$. If $X$ is $C^n$, $1 \le n \le \infty$, with compact support, then $(t, x) \mapsto \varphi_t(x)$ is $C^n$ on $\mathbb R \times E$ and each $\varphi_t$ is a $C^n$ diffeomorphism.

If a smooth vector field on $M$ vanishes outside some compact set $K \subset M$, then it generates exactly one 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms of $M$.

V2.1

Sublevel sets and strong deformation retracts

stronger
the strong form, fixing $A$ throughoutMilnor gives no definition

Milnor §3, pp. 12–13

Throughout §3, $M^a = f^{-1}(-\infty, a] = \{p \in M : f(p) \le a\}$. Milnor uses “deformation retract” without a definition: in the proof of Theorem 3.1 he builds a 1-parameter family of maps $r_t : M^b \to M^b$ with $r_0$ the identity and $r_1$ a retraction onto $M^a$, concludes that $M^a$ is a deformation retract of $M^b$, and so that the inclusion is a homotopy equivalence.

Proved in Lean

For a real function $f$ on a set and $c \in \mathbb R$, $M^c = \{x : f(x) \le c\}$. A subset $A$ of a topological space $X$ is a strong deformation retract of $X$ if there are a continuous map $r : X \to X$ with values in $A$ and a homotopy $r_t$, $0 \le t \le 1$, from $r_0 = \mathrm{id}_X$ to $r_1 = r$ with $r_t(a) = a$ for all $t$ and all $a \in A$. If $A \subseteq B$ are subsets of a space and $A$ is a strong deformation retract of $B$, the inclusion $A \to B$ is a homotopy equivalence, with $r_1$ as homotopy inverse.

Theorem 3.1 on a Euclidean space

$M = \mathbb R^n$ with an inner producta diffeomorphism of $E$ onto itself$a = b$ allowed

Milnor §3, Theorem 3.1 · p. 12

For a smooth real function $f$ on a manifold $M$ and $a < b$, if the set $f^{-1}[a, b]$ of points where $a \le f \le b$ is compact and free of critical points of $f$, then $M^a$ and $M^b$ are diffeomorphic; moreover $M^a$ is a deformation retract of $M^b$, so the inclusion $M^a \to M^b$ is a homotopy equivalence. The proof chooses a Riemannian metric, takes $\rho$ equal to $1/\langle \mathrm{grad} f, \mathrm{grad} f\rangle$ on $f^{-1}[a, b]$ and vanishing outside a compact neighbourhood of it, and pushes $M^b$ down to $M^a$ along the flow $\varphi_t$ of $\rho\,\mathrm{grad} f$; then $\varphi_{b-a}$ carries $M^a$ diffeomorphically onto $M^b$.

Proved in Lean

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, $f : E \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$, $a \le b$, and suppose that $f^{-1}[a, b]$ is compact and contains no critical point of $f$. Then there is a $C^\infty$ diffeomorphism $\Phi$ of $E$ with $\Phi(M^a) = M^b$; $M^a$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^b$; the inclusion $M^a \to M^b$ is a homotopy equivalence; and $M^a$ and $M^b$ are homeomorphic.

Theorem 3.2 on a Euclidean space

narrower
$M = \mathbb R^n$ with an inner productretraction onto an embedded cellMilnor's $\mu$ constructed$\partial F/\partial\eta \ge 1$, not $> 1$

Milnor §3, Theorem 3.2 · p. 14

Take a smooth $f : M \to \mathbb R$ and a non-degenerate critical point $p$ of index $\lambda$, with $c = f(p)$, and assume that for some $\epsilon > 0$ the set $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon, c + \epsilon]$ is compact with $p$ its only critical point. Then, once $\epsilon$ is small enough, $M^{c+\epsilon}$ is homotopy equivalent to $M^{c-\epsilon}$ with a $\lambda$-cell attached. In the proof a function $\mu$ modifies $f$ near $p$ to a smooth $F$ with $F^{-1}(-\infty, c - \epsilon] = M^{c-\epsilon} \cup H$, and four Assertions show that $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e^\lambda$ is a deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$.

The scan prints “a k-cell” and renders the index as “A”; both are read as $\lambda$, as the proof requires.

Proved in Lean

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space, $f : E \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$, $p$ a critical point at which $d^2 f_p$ is non-degenerate, $\lambda$ its index and $c = f(p)$, and suppose that for some $\epsilon_0 > 0$ the set $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon_0, c + \epsilon_0]$ is compact and contains no critical point other than $p$. Then there is $\epsilon_1 > 0$ such that for every $\epsilon$ with $0 < \epsilon \le \epsilon_1$ there is a map $\chi$ from the closed unit ball $D^\lambda$ of $\mathbb R^\lambda$ to $E$, continuous and injective on $D^\lambda$, with $\chi(z) \in M^{c-\epsilon}$ exactly when $|z| = 1$ and $\chi(D^\lambda) \subseteq M^{c+\epsilon}$, such that $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup \chi(D^\lambda)$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$. Hence the inclusion of $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup \chi(D^\lambda)$ in $M^{c+\epsilon}$ is a homotopy equivalence, and there is an injective continuous $\varphi : S^{\lambda-1} \to M^{c-\epsilon}$ such that $M^{c+\epsilon}$ is homotopy equivalent to $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup_\varphi e^\lambda$.

Assertion 2 uses $\partial F/\partial\eta \ge 1$; the scan shows $> 1$, which fails where $\mu' = 0$.

V2.7

A cell meeting a closed set in its boundary is attached to it

hypotheses explicit
$M$ Hausdorff, $A$ closedthe subspace is the adjunction space

Milnor §3, proof of Theorem 3.2 · p. 16

With $e^\lambda$ the set of points of the coordinate patch with $(u^1)^2 + \dots + (u^\lambda)^2 \le \epsilon$ and $u^{\lambda+1} = \dots = u^n = 0$, Milnor notes that $e^\lambda \cap M^{c-\epsilon}$ is precisely the boundary $\dot e^\lambda$, so that $e^\lambda$ is attached to $M^{c-\epsilon}$ as required. That the subspace $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e^\lambda$ is then the space $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup_\varphi e^\lambda$ defined in §1 is not argued.

Proved in Lean

Let $A$ be a closed subset of a Hausdorff space $M$ and $\chi : \mathbb R^n \to M$ continuous and injective on $D^n$, with $\chi(z) \in A$ exactly when $|z| = 1$, for $z \in D^n$. Then the subspace $A \cup \chi(D^n)$ of $M$ is the pushout of $\varphi = \chi|S^{n-1} : S^{n-1} \to A$ and the inclusion $S^{n-1} \to D^n$, that is, $A \cup_\varphi e^n$ (V1.2), and $\varphi$ is injective. Consequently, if $f : M \to \mathbb R$ is continuous, $a \le b$, $\chi$ is as above for $A = M^a$, $\chi(D^n) \subseteq M^b$, and $M^a \cup \chi(D^n)$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^b$, then $M^b$ is homotopy equivalent to $M^a \cup_\varphi e^n$.

Theorem 3.2 in a Morse patch, and on a submanifold

narrower
$N \subseteq V$, $f = F|N$Hausdorff usedthe patch half in any Hausdorff space

Milnor §3, Theorem 3.2 · p. 14

For a non-degenerate critical point $p$ of index $\lambda$, $c = f(p)$, with $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon, c + \epsilon]$ compact and free of other critical points, $M^{c+\epsilon}$ has the homotopy type of $M^{c-\epsilon}$ with a $\lambda$-cell attached, for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$. The proof works in a coordinate neighbourhood $U$ of $p$ in which $f = c - \xi + \eta$; Assertion 3, that $F^{-1}(-\infty, c - \epsilon]$ is a deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$, is Theorem 3.1 applied to $F$, and the rest of the argument takes place in the patch.

Proved in Lean

(i) The topological half, in any Hausdorff space $M$. Let $X$, $Y$ be finite-dimensional real inner product spaces with $\dim X = \lambda$, $f : M \to \mathbb R$, $p \in M$, and $\varphi$ a homeomorphism of an open neighbourhood of $p$ onto an open subset of $X \times Y$ with $\varphi(p) = 0$, $f = f(p) - |x|^2 + |y|^2$ on its domain, and image containing the ball $|x|^2 + |y|^2 \le 2\epsilon$, $\epsilon > 0$. Let $\mu$ satisfy Milnor's four conditions, and let $F = f - \mu(|x|^2 + 2|y|^2)$ on the domain of $\varphi$ and $F = f$ elsewhere. If $F^{-1}(-\infty, f(p) - \epsilon]$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^{f(p)+\epsilon}$, the conclusion of V2.6 about the cell holds in $M$ for this $\epsilon$. (ii) Let $V$, $Z$ be finite-dimensional, $N \subseteq V$ a slice submanifold modelled on $Z$, $F : V \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$, $f = F|N$, $p \in N$ a non-degenerate critical point of $f$ of index $\lambda$, $c = f(p)$, and suppose that for some $\epsilon_0 > 0$ the set $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon_0, c + \epsilon_0]$ is compact and contains no critical point of $f$ other than $p$. Then there is $\epsilon_1 > 0$ such that for every $\epsilon \in (0, \epsilon_1]$ there is a cell $\chi(D^\lambda) \subseteq N^{c+\epsilon}$, $\chi$ continuous and injective on $D^\lambda$, meeting $N^{c-\epsilon}$ exactly in $\chi(S^{\lambda-1})$, with $N^{c-\epsilon} \cup \chi(D^\lambda)$ a strong deformation retract of $N^{c+\epsilon}$; and $N^{c+\epsilon}$ is homotopy equivalent to $N^{c-\epsilon} \cup_\varphi e^\lambda$ for an injective $\varphi$.

Remark 3.3: several critical points on one level

narrower
submanifolds of $V$ onlydisjoint Morse chartscells attached one at a time

Milnor §3, Remark 3.3 · p. 19

When the level $f^{-1}(c)$ contains $k$ non-degenerate critical points $p_1, \dots, p_k$, of indices $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k$, the same kind of proof gives that $M^{c+\epsilon}$ is homotopy equivalent to $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e^{\lambda_1} \cup \dots \cup e^{\lambda_k}$.

Proved in Lean

Let $N \subseteq V$, $F$ and $f = F|N$ be as in V2.8 (ii), $S$ a finite set of non-degenerate critical points of $f$, all with value $c$, and suppose that for some $\epsilon_0 > 0$ the set $f^{-1}[c - \epsilon_0, c + \epsilon_0]$ is compact and all its critical points lie in $S$. Then there is $\epsilon_1 > 0$ such that for every $\epsilon \in (0, \epsilon_1]$ there are cells $e_p = \chi_p(D^{\lambda_p})$, $p \in S$, $\lambda_p$ the index of $p$, each $\chi_p$ continuous and injective on $D^{\lambda_p}$, meeting $N^{c-\epsilon}$ exactly in $\chi_p(S^{\lambda_p - 1})$, contained in $N^{c+\epsilon}$ and pairwise disjoint, such that $N^{c-\epsilon} \cup \bigcup_{p \in S} e_p$ is a strong deformation retract of $N^{c+\epsilon}$.

Milnor §3, Remark 3.4 · p. 20

With a small change in the proof of 3.2, $M^c$ too is a deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$, being one of $F^{-1}(-\infty, c]$, which is one of $M^{c+\epsilon}$ (Diagram 8). Together with 3.2, Milnor says, one sees easily that $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e^\lambda$ is a deformation retract of $M^c$.

The scan prints it as “Remark 2.4”; p. 24 cites it as Remark 3.4.

Proved in Lean

Under the hypotheses of V2.6, $E$ a finite-dimensional real inner product space, there is $\epsilon_1 > 0$ such that for every $\epsilon \in (0, \epsilon_1]$: $M^c$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$; and there is a map $\chi$ from $D^\lambda$ to $E$, continuous and injective on $D^\lambda$, with $\chi(z) \in M^{c-\epsilon}$ exactly when $|z| = 1$, such that the part of $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup \chi(D^\lambda)$ lying in $M^c$ is a strong deformation retract of $M^c$.

Iterated adjunction spaces in place of CW-complexes

narrower
attaching maps not cellularcells in the listed orderno cellular approximation

Milnor §3, Theorem 3.5 · p. 20

Theorem 3.5 asserts the homotopy type of a CW-complex, for whose definition Milnor refers to J. H. C. Whitehead. In the proof (p. 23) each attaching map is replaced, by cellular approximation, by a map into the $(\lambda_j - 1)$-skeleton, so that attaching the new cells to a CW-complex gives a CW-complex again.

Proved in Lean

A space $K$ is an iterated adjunction space with cells $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ if it is obtained from the empty space by attaching a $\lambda_1$-cell, then a $\lambda_2$-cell, and so on, each along an arbitrary continuous map of its boundary sphere into the space built so far (V1.2). A space $X$ has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ if it is homotopy equivalent to such a $K$.

Theorem 3.5 for a compact submanifold of Euclidean space

narrower
compact $N \subseteq V$, $f = F|N$iterated adjunction space, not CWnon-compact case not done

Milnor §3, Theorem 3.5 · p. 20

A manifold $M$ carrying a differentiable function without degenerate critical points, all of whose sublevel sets $M^a$ are compact, is homotopy equivalent to a CW-complex with one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each critical point of index $\lambda$. The proof (pp. 23–24) lists the critical values $c_1 < c_2 < \dots$, notes that $M^a$ is vacuous for $a < c_1$, passes each critical level by Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 and Remark 3.3, and carries the cells along homotopy equivalences by Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7; the non-compact case uses a direct limit and Whitehead's theorem.

Proved in Lean

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $N \subseteq V$ a compact slice submanifold modelled on a finite-dimensional $Z$, $F : V \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^\infty$, and suppose that every critical point of $f = F|N$ is non-degenerate. Then the critical points of $f$ can be listed without repetition as $p_1, \dots, p_k$, with $f(p_1) \le \dots \le f(p_k)$, so that $N$ has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells $(\lambda(p_1), \dots, \lambda(p_k))$ in the sense of V2.11, $\lambda(p)$ the index of $p$. In particular $N$ has the homotopy type of such a complex whose number of cells of dimension $\lambda$ is, for every $\lambda$, the number $C_\lambda$ of critical points of index $\lambda$. If the critical values are distinct, the list is strictly increasing.

Lemma 3.6 (Whitehead)

as in the book

Milnor §3, Lemma 3.6 · p. 20

If two maps $\varphi_0$, $\varphi_1$ of the sphere $\dot e^\lambda$ into $X$ are homotopic, the identity of $X$ extends to a homotopy equivalence $k$ from $X \cup_{\varphi_0} e^\lambda$ to $X \cup_{\varphi_1} e^\lambda$. The proof gives explicit formulas for $k$ and for a map $\ell$ the other way, and says it is not difficult to verify that $k\ell$ and $\ell k$ are homotopic to the identities.

Proved in Lean

Let $X$ be a topological space, $n \ge 0$, and $\varphi_0, \varphi_1 : S^{n-1} \to X$ homotopic maps. Then there is a homotopy equivalence $k : X \cup_{\varphi_0} e^n \to X \cup_{\varphi_1} e^n$ which is the identity on $X$. The proof uses Milnor's formulas for $k$ and $\ell$; the homotopies he leaves to the reader are written down, built through the exponential law for the locally compact $[0, 1]$, which is the fact, used silently, that $[0, 1] \times$ (a quotient map) is a quotient map.

Lemma 3.7, and the Assertion of p. 22

stronger
the extension is nameduses the formula for $k$ of Lemma 3.6

Milnor §3, Lemma 3.7 · p. 21

For an attaching map $\varphi : \dot e^\lambda \to X$, every homotopy equivalence $f : X \to Y$ extends to a homotopy equivalence $F$ from $X \cup_\varphi e^\lambda$ to $Y \cup_{f\varphi} e^\lambda$. The proof, after an unpublished paper of Hilton, takes $F = f$ on $X$ and the identity on the cell, and rests on an Assertion (p. 22): if a map $F$ has a left homotopy inverse $L$ and a right homotopy inverse $R$, then $F$ is a homotopy equivalence, and $R$ (or $L$) is a two-sided homotopy inverse.

Proved in Lean

Let $X$, $Y$ be topological spaces, $\varphi : S^{n-1} \to X$ continuous and $f : X \to Y$ a homotopy equivalence. Then the map $F : X \cup_\varphi e^n \to Y \cup_{f\varphi} e^n$ equal to $f$ on $X$ and to the identity on the cell is a homotopy equivalence. And for maps $F$, $L$, $R$: if $LF \simeq \mathrm{id}$ and $FR \simeq \mathrm{id}$, then $RF \simeq \mathrm{id}$.

Milnor §§4–5, pp. 25–32: Reeb, the torus, the Morse inequalities, the Euler characteristic

V3.2

Small sublevel sets at the extrema are closed cells

restated
a ball, its sphere onto the level setcompactness and a strict minimumindex $0$ at a minimum, $n$ at a maximum

Milnor §4, proof of Theorem 4.1 · p. 25

In the proof of Reeb's theorem, with $f(p) = 0$ the minimum and $f(q) = 1$ the maximum, Milnor says that if $\epsilon$ is small enough the sets $M^\epsilon = f^{-1}[0, \epsilon]$ and $f^{-1}[1 - \epsilon, 1]$ are closed $n$-cells, by the lemma of Morse (2.2).

Proved in Lean

(i) On a manifold $M$ modelled on a real normed space $E$, a local minimum or local maximum of any $f : M \to \mathbb R$ is a critical point. If moreover $M$ is a smooth manifold without boundary, $E$ has finite dimension $n$, $f$ is smooth on an open $U \ni p$ and $p$ is a non-degenerate local minimum (maximum), then the index of $f$ at $p$ is $0$ (resp. $n$), and there are smooth coordinates $y$ on an open subset of $U$ containing $p$, with values in $\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean norm, such that $y(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) + \|y\|^2$ (resp. $f = f(p) - \|y\|^2$) on the domain of $y$. (ii) Let $X$ be a compact topological space, $f : X \to \mathbb R$ continuous with a strict global minimum at $p$ ($f(p) < f(x)$ for all $x \ne p$), and $y$ a homeomorphism from an open neighbourhood of $p$ onto an open subset of a real normed space $F$, with $y(p) = 0$ and $f = f(p) + \|y\|^2$ on its domain. Then there is $\delta > 0$ such that for every $0 < \varepsilon < \delta$ the map $v \mapsto y^{-1}(\sqrt\varepsilon\, v)$ is continuous and injective on the closed unit ball of $F$, maps it onto $\{f \le f(p) + \varepsilon\}$, and maps the unit sphere onto the level set $\{f = f(p) + \varepsilon\}$. Applied to $-f$, the same holds at a strict maximum.

Theorem 4.1 (Reeb)

narrower
$N$ a submanifold of $V$exactly two critical pointsa homeomorphism, as in Milnor

Milnor §4, Theorem 4.1 (Reeb) · p. 25

A compact manifold $M$ carrying a differentiable function with only two critical points, both non-degenerate, is homeomorphic to a sphere. The proof: the two critical points are the minimum and the maximum; small sublevel and superlevel sets are closed $n$-cells by Lemma 2.2; $M^\epsilon$ is homeomorphic to $M^{1-\epsilon}$ by Theorem 3.1; so $M$ is two closed $n$-cells matched along their boundary.

Remark 1 adds that the theorem remains true for degenerate critical points, with a more difficult proof, and Remark 2 that $M$ need not be diffeomorphic to $S^n$.

Proved in Lean

Let $N$ be a compact slice submanifold of a finite-dimensional real normed space $V$, modelled on a finite-dimensional space of dimension $n$, and $f = F|N$ with $F : V \to \mathbb R$ smooth. If $f$ has exactly two critical points, both non-degenerate, then $N$ is homeomorphic to the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$. For a compact $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$ modelled on $\mathbb R^n$, $n \ge 1$, the same holds for every smooth $f : N \to \mathbb R$, which is always the restriction of a smooth function on $\mathbb R^{K+1}$. In dimension $0$, where every point is critical, $N$ has exactly two points.

Subadditive and additive functions

restated
indices of a preorder for spacesargument order reversedevery pair $a \le b$ allowed

Milnor §5, Definition · p. 28

An integer-valued function $S$, defined on certain pairs of spaces, is subadditive if $S(X, Z) \le S(X, Y) + S(Y, Z)$ for every $X \supset Y \supset Z$, and additive if equality always holds.

Proved in Lean

Spaces are replaced by the elements of a preordered set $\iota$, $a \le b$ standing for $X_a \subseteq X_b$. A function on pairs is an integer-valued function $S(a, b)$ of two indices, used only for $a \le b$, where $S(a, b)$ stands for Milnor's $S(X_b, X_a)$, the smaller space written first. $S$ is subadditive if $S(a, c) \le S(a, b) + S(b, c)$ whenever $a \le b \le c$, and additive if equality always holds.

Milnor §5, Lemma 5.1 · p. 28

For a subadditive $S$ and spaces $X_0 \subset X_1 \subset \dots \subset X_n$, $S(X_n, X_0) \le \sum_{i=1}^n S(X_i, X_{i-1})$, with equality when $S$ is additive. The proof is by induction on $n$, and taking $X_0 = \emptyset$ gives inequality (1), $S(X_n) \le \sum_i S(X_i, X_{i-1})$.

Proved in Lean

If $S$ is subadditive and $X_0 \le X_1 \le \dots \le X_n$ with $n \ge 1$, then $S(X_0, X_n) \le \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} S(X_k, X_{k+1})$, that is, in Milnor's notation, $S(X_n, X_0) \le \sum_{i=1}^n S(X_i, X_{i-1})$; if $S$ is additive, equality holds. One form assumes subadditivity only on the triples $X_0 \le X_m \le X_{m+1}$, which is all the induction uses.

V3.9

The homology of a filtration, and its Morse numbers

restated
abstract, not singular homologyfiniteness a consequence on chains

Milnor §5, pp. 28–30

Milnor works with singular homology with coefficients in a field $F$: $R_\lambda(X, Y)$, the $\lambda$-th Betti number of $(X, Y)$, is the rank over $F$ of $H_\lambda(X, Y; F)$, for any pair for which this rank is finite. He uses the exact sequence of a triple $X \supset Y \supset Z$, with its final $\to 0$ (p. 29), and $C_\lambda$ counts the critical points of index $\lambda$.

Proved in Lean

Fix a field $F$ and a preordered set $\iota$. A homology of a filtration assigns to every degree $i \ge 0$ and indices $a$, $b$ a vector space $H_i(a, b)$ over $F$, to be read as $H_i(X_b, X_a; F)$, finite-dimensional for $a \le b$, and to every triple $a \le b \le c$ a long exact sequence of $F$-linear maps $\cdots \to H_i(a,b) \to H_i(a,c) \to H_i(b,c) \to H_{i-1}(a,b) \to \cdots \to H_0(a,b) \to H_0(a,c) \to H_0(b,c) \to 0$, exact at every term. Nothing else is assumed: no functoriality, no compatibility between the sequences of different triples, no vanishing of $H_*(a, a)$, no excision. For a chain $X_0 \le X_1 \le \dots \le X_n$ the Betti numbers are $R_i = \dim H_i(X_0, X_n)$ and the Morse numbers are $C_i = \sum_{k<n} \dim H_i(X_k, X_{k+1})$. On a chain indexed by $\mathbb N$ the structure can be built from the exact sequences and the finiteness of the steps alone, so that the finiteness of the total homology is a consequence.

For a filtration with the cell hypothesis, $R_l = 0$ if no critical point has index $l$, and, if every index is at most $N$, $\sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i R_i = \sum_{p \in P} (-1)^{\mathrm{ind}(p)}$, the left side being the whole alternating sum.

The Poincaré–Hopf integer

restated
defined by vector fields, not homology$K \ge 1$, $N$ non-emptyidentified with homology in V3.38

Milnor §5, p. 28, and §6, Application 2

Milnor's $\chi$ is the Euler characteristic $\sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda$ of singular homology over a field (p. 28). In Application 2 (pp. 36–37) he uses that the sum of the indices of any vector field on a compact $M$ is a topological invariant, citing Steenrod (§39.7), so that it equals $\chi(M)$.

Proved in Lean

Let $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$ be a compact non-empty slice submanifold modelled on $\mathbb R^{d+1}$. An integer $\chi$ is an Euler number of $N$ if every smooth tangent vector field on $N$ whose zeros are finitely many distinct points has index sum $\chi$, the index being that of the Milnor project: the index at a zero of the extension $x \mapsto v(r(x)) + (x - r(x))$ of $v$ to a tubular neighbourhood, $r$ the nearest-point retraction. For $K \ge 1$ an Euler number exists: this is the Poincaré–Hopf theorem of the Milnor project, where it is the degree of the Gauss map of the boundary of a tubular neighbourhood. It is unique, and is written $\chi(N)$.

The index of the gradient field is $(-1)^\lambda$

narrower
embedded $N$, induced metricproved, not asserted$\operatorname{sgn}\det = (-1)^\lambda$

In Application 2 Milnor asserts, without proof, that $(-1)^\lambda$ is the index of the vector field $\mathrm{grad} f$ at a point where $f$ has index $\lambda$.

Proved in Lean

Let $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$, $K \ge 1$, be a compact non-empty slice submanifold modelled on $\mathbb R^{d+1}$, $F : \mathbb R^{K+1} \to \mathbb R$ smooth and $f = F|N$. The tangential gradient $v(q) = P_q\nabla F(q)$, $P_q$ the orthogonal projection onto $T_qN$, is the gradient of $f$ for the metric induced from $\mathbb R^{K+1}$; its zeros are exactly the critical points of $f$, and it is a smooth tangent field. If $q$ is a non-degenerate critical point of $f$ of index $\lambda$, the derivative of $v$ at $q$ is an invertible endomorphism of $T_qN$ whose determinant has sign $(-1)^\lambda$, and the index of $v$ at $q$ is $(-1)^\lambda$. Along the way: for a non-degenerate symmetric form $H(v, w) = \langle Av, w\rangle$ on a finite-dimensional inner product space, $\operatorname{sgn}\det A = (-1)^{\mathrm{index}\,H}$.

Consequently the alternating count is the same for all Morse functions on $N$, and every Euler number of $N$ equals the alternating count of any one Morse function. Every smooth $f : N \to \mathbb R$ is the restriction of a smooth function on $\mathbb R^{K+1}$.

V3.23

The height function: four critical points, of indices 0, 1, 1, 2

restated
indices proved, normal forms not restatedthe upright torusexactly four critical points

Milnor §1, p. 3

The points $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$ at which the homotopy type of $M^a$ changes are the critical points of $f$: in any coordinates $(x, y)$ near them both partial derivatives of $f$ vanish, and one can choose coordinates with $f = x^2 + y^2$ at $p$, $f = \text{const} - x^2 - y^2$ at $s$, and $f = \text{const} + x^2 - y^2$ at $q$ and $r$. The number of minus signs is the dimension of the cell attached in passing the point.

Proved in Lean

Let $f = x_1 + R + \rho$ on $T$, the height above the plane $\{x_1 = -(R + \rho)\}$, which touches $T$ at $p = (-(R + \rho), 0, 0)$; the axis of revolution is parallel to the plane, so the torus stands upright. The critical points of $f$ are exactly $p$, $q = (-(R - \rho), 0, 0)$, $r = (R - \rho, 0, 0)$ and $s = (R + \rho, 0, 0)$, with critical values $0$, $2\rho$, $2R$, $2R + 2\rho$. All four are non-degenerate, of indices $0, 1, 1, 2$; $f$ is a Morse function on $T$, with $C_0 = 1$, $C_1 = 2$, $C_2 = 1$ and $C_\lambda = 0$ for $\lambda \ge 3$.

two independent proofsevery Morse function on $T$

Proved in Lean

$0$ is an Euler number of $T$ in the sense of V3.17, and every Euler number of $T$ is $0$: by V3.20 from $C_0 - C_1 + C_2 = 1 - 2 + 1$, and independently of Morse theory, because the rotation field $(-x_2, x_1, 0)$ is a smooth tangent field on $T$ without zeros. V3.26

Relative singular homology and the exact sequence of a pair

not in the book
quoted by Milnor, built hereMathlib had no relative homologyhomotopy invariance for pairs

Milnor §5, pp. 28–29

Milnor quotes the homology of pairs with coefficients in a field, and its exact sequences, as standard (p. 28); on p. 29 he replaces a pair by a homotopy equivalent one without comment.

Proved in Lean

Coefficients are an object $R$ of an abelian category with coproducts, for instance a field or any commutative ring; pairs $(X, A)$ are embeddings $A \hookrightarrow X$. The relative chain complex $C(X, A)$ is the cokernel of the chain map $C(A) \to C(X)$ of singular chains, which is injective, so that $0 \to C(A) \to C(X) \to C(X, A) \to 0$ is exact; $H_n(X, A)$ is its homology, and both are functorial in maps of pairs. The sequence $\cdots \to H_{n+1}(X, A) \to H_n(A) \to H_n(X) \to H_n(X, A) \to H_{n-1}(A) \to \cdots \to H_0(X) \to H_0(X, A) \to 0$ is exact at every place, and its boundary is natural. $H_n(X, \emptyset) \cong H_n(X)$ naturally, and $H_n(X, X) = 0$. A map of pairs inducing isomorphisms in the homology of both spaces induces isomorphisms in relative homology; maps of pairs homotopic through maps of pairs induce the same maps. If $A \subseteq B \subseteq X$ and $B$ is a strong deformation retract of $X$, then $H_n(B, A) \to H_n(X, A)$ is an isomorphism and $H_n(X, B) = 0$. With these data singular homology is a homotopy-invariant homology pretheory in the sense of Mathlib's formulation of the Eilenberg–Steenrod axioms.

quoted by Milnor, built herethe third isomorphism theorem

Milnor quotes the homology exact sequence of a triple $X \supset Y \supset Z$: its portion $H_\lambda(Y, Z) \to H_\lambda(X, Z) \to H_\lambda(X, Y)$ for subadditivity (p. 28), its final $\to 0$ (p. 29), and its boundary $H_{\lambda+1}(X, Y) \to H_\lambda(Y, Z)$ in Lemma 5.3 (p. 30).

(i) If the interiors of a family of subsets of a space $X$ cover $X$, the inclusion of the chains made of simplices each lying in one member of the family into all singular chains is a chain homotopy equivalence, for any coefficients. The homology of disks, spheres and cells

not in the book
quoted by Milnor, computed hereembedded cells and spheres too

Milnor §5, p. 29

Milnor quotes that $H_*(e^\lambda, \dot e^\lambda)$ is the coefficient group in dimension $\lambda$ and $0$ otherwise.

Proved in Lean

Coefficients in a commutative ring $R$; $D^n$ and $S^{n-1}$ are the closed unit ball and unit sphere of $\mathbb R^n$, with $S^{-1} = \emptyset$. $H_i(D^n, S^{n-1}) \cong R$ for $i = n$ and $H_i(D^n, S^{n-1}) = 0$ for $i \ne n$. For $n \ge 1$, $H_0(S^n) \cong R$, $H_n(S^n) \cong R$ and $H_i(S^n) = 0$ for $i \ne 0, n$; $H_0(S^0) \cong R \oplus R$. Over a field, $\dim H_i(D^n, S^{n-1}) = [i = n]$ and $\dim H_i(S^n) = [i = 0] + [i = n]$. More generally, if $E$ is Hausdorff and $\chi : \mathbb R^k \to E$ is continuous and injective on $D^k$, the pair $(\chi(D^k), \chi(S^{k-1}))$ has the homology of $(D^k, S^{k-1})$, and an image of $S^n$ under a map continuous and injective on it has the homology of $S^n$.

V3.31

Attaching cells to a closed set: the step “by excision”

stronger
several disjoint cells at onceany commutative ringnot literally excision

Milnor §5, p. 29

For $M^{a_i}$, which has the homotopy type of $M^{a_{i-1}} \cup e^{\lambda_i}$, Milnor writes $H_*(M^{a_{i-1}} \cup e^{\lambda_i}, M^{a_{i-1}}) = H_*(e^{\lambda_i}, \dot e^{\lambda_i})$, by excision, which is the coefficient group in dimension $\lambda_i$ and $0$ otherwise.

Proved in Lean

Let $E$ be a Hausdorff space, $Y \subseteq X \subseteq E$ with $Y$ closed, and $\chi_j : \mathbb R^{k_j} \to E$, $j = 1, \dots, m$, maps continuous and injective on the closed unit balls $D^{k_j}$, whose cells $e_j = \chi_j(D^{k_j})$ are pairwise disjoint, such that $\chi_j(z) \in Y$ exactly when $\|z\| = 1$, and $X = Y \cup e_1 \cup \dots \cup e_m$. Coefficients in a commutative ring $R$. For one cell of dimension $k$, the inclusion $(e_1, \chi_1(S^{k-1})) \to (X, Y)$ and the characteristic map $(D^k, S^{k-1}) \to (X, Y)$ induce isomorphisms in all degrees: $H_k(X, Y) \cong R$ and $H_i(X, Y) = 0$ for $i \ne k$. For several cells, $H_i(X, Y) \cong R^{c_i}$, $c_i$ the number of cells of dimension $i$; over a field $\dim H_i(X, Y) = c_i$.

  • The step is not literally excision: the closure of the set to be excised is not inside the interior of $M^{a_{i-1}}$. One first deforms $X$ minus the centre of the cell onto $Y$, pushing the punctured cell radially onto its boundary, and then excises; $Y$ must be closed.

V3.32

The Morse inequalities for any filtration of a space

restated
any filtration of any spacefiniteness of the total a consequence

Milnor §5, pp. 28–30

Milnor applies Lemma 5.1 to $R_\lambda$, to $\chi$ and to $S_\lambda$ on the chain $\emptyset = M^{a_0} \subset M^{a_1} \subset \dots \subset M^{a_k} = M$, which gives Theorem 5.2 and the inequalities $(4_\lambda)$.

Proved in Lean

Let $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ be subsets of a space and $\Bbbk$ a field. With $H_i(a, b) = H_i(X_b, X_a; \Bbbk)$ for $a \le b$ and the exact sequences of triples of V3.27, singular homology is a homology of a filtration in the sense of V3.9, provided every step $(X_{k+1}, X_k)$ has finite-dimensional homology. Consequently, for $n \ge 1$, if the steps $k < n$ have finite-dimensional homology, so has $(X_n, X_0)$, and with $b_i = \dim H_i(X_n, X_0; \Bbbk)$ and $C_i = \sum_{k < n} \dim H_i(X_{k+1}, X_k; \Bbbk)$: $b_l \le C_l$; $b_l - b_{l-1} + \dots \pm b_0 \le C_l - C_{l-1} + \dots \pm C_0$ for every $l$; and $\sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i b_i = \sum_{i \le N} (-1)^i C_i$ if no step has homology in degree $N + 1$. Under the cell hypothesis of V3.11, $C_i$ is the number of critical points of index $i$, and the alternating sum is $\sum_{p \in P} (-1)^{\mathrm{ind}\,p}$ when every index is at most $N$.

V3.33

Betti numbers, and the homology of a slab

restated
pairs need strong deformation retractsthe bottom moves by a triple

Milnor §5, pp. 28–29

$R_\lambda(X, Y)$ is the rank over $F$ of $H_\lambda(X, Y; F)$ (p. 28). On p. 29, $H_*(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}}) = H_*(M^{a_{i-1}} \cup e^{\lambda_i}, M^{a_{i-1}})$, the pair being replaced, by Theorems 3.1 and 3.2, by one in which $M^{a_i}$ becomes $M^{a_{i-1}}$ with a cell attached.

Proved in Lean

For a space $X$, $b_i(X) = \dim_\Bbbk H_i(X; \Bbbk)$, Mathlib's singular homology, is Milnor's $R_i(X)$; it is $0$ by convention if $H_i(X; \Bbbk)$ is infinite-dimensional, which never happens for the spaces below. Homeomorphic spaces have the same Betti numbers. If $A \subseteq B \subseteq D$ and $A$ is a strong deformation retract of $B$, then $H_i(D, A) \cong H_i(D, B)$, by the sequence of the triple, in which $H_*(B, A) = 0$. The slab lemma: let $A \subseteq B \subseteq X' \subseteq X$ be subsets of a Hausdorff space, $B$ closed, and $e_1, \dots, e_m$ pairwise disjoint cells attached to $B$ as in V3.31, with $B \cup e_1 \cup \dots \cup e_m \subseteq X'$; if $A$ is a strong deformation retract of $B$, $B \cup e_1 \cup \dots \cup e_m$ one of $X'$, and $X'$ one of $X$, then $H_i(X, A; \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional, of dimension the number of cells of dimension $i$.

V3.34

The Morse filtration of a compact submanifold

narrower
compact $N \subseteq V$, $f = F|N$one critical value per slabfiniteness of $H_*$ proved

Milnor §5, p. 29

For a compact $M$ and a differentiable $f$ with isolated, non-degenerate critical points, Milnor takes $a_1 < \dots < a_k$ with exactly $i$ critical points in $M^{a_i}$ and $M^{a_k} = M$, and finds $H_*(M^{a_i}, M^{a_{i-1}})$ to be the coefficient group in dimension $\lambda_i$, the index of the $i$-th critical point, and $0$ in every other dimension.

Proved in Lean

Let $N$ be a compact slice submanifold of a finite-dimensional real normed space $V$, modelled on a finite-dimensional space, and $F : V \to \mathbb R$ smooth such that every critical point of $f = F|N$ is non-degenerate. (i) If $a' \le a$ are not critical values and all critical values in $(a', a)$ are equal, then $H_i(N^a, N^{a'}; \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional, of dimension the number of critical points of index $i$ in $f^{-1}(a', a)$. (ii) There are $n \ge 1$ and non-critical values $a_0 \le a_1 \le \dots$ with $N^{a_0} = \emptyset$, $N^{a_n} = N$ and at most one critical value in each $(a_k, a_{k+1})$; by (i) each step $(N^{a_{k+1}}, N^{a_k})$ has finite-dimensional homology over every field. (iii) Hence $H_i(N; \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional for every $i$. These statements hold for every space homeomorphic to $N$, homology being carried along the homeomorphism.

Theorem 5.2 in singular homology

narrower
compact $N \subseteq V$, $f = F|N$every input of p. 29 proved$H_i = 0$ above $\dim N$

Milnor §5, Theorem 5.2 · p. 29

(The weak Morse inequalities.) On a compact manifold $M$, with $C_\lambda$ the number of critical points of index $\lambda$ and Betti numbers taken over a field $F$: $R_\lambda(M) \le C_\lambda$ and $\sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda(M) = \sum (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$.

Proved in Lean

In the setting of V3.34, with $n = \dim N$, $b_i = \dim H_i(N; \Bbbk)$ for any field $\Bbbk$, and $C_\lambda = C_\lambda(f)$: (2) $b_\lambda \le C_\lambda$ for every $\lambda$; (3) $\sum_{i=0}^n (-1)^i b_i = \sum_{\lambda=0}^n (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$; and $H_i(N; \Bbbk) = 0$ for $i > n$, so that the left side of (3) is the whole alternating sum. The same holds for every space homeomorphic to $N$.

narrower

Milnor §5, Corollary 5.4 · p. 31

If $C_{\lambda+1} = C_{\lambda-1} = 0$ then $R_\lambda = C_\lambda$ and $R_{\lambda+1} = R_{\lambda-1} = 0$. Milnor notes that the corollary finds the homology groups of complex projective space (§4) without Theorem 3.5.

Proved in Lean

In the setting of V3.35, over every field: if $\lambda \ge 1$ and $C_{\lambda+1} = C_{\lambda-1} = 0$, then $b_\lambda = C_\lambda$ and $b_{\lambda+1} = b_{\lambda-1} = 0$; if $C_1 = 0$, then $b_0 = C_0$ and $b_1 = 0$; and if no two consecutive $C_i$ are non-zero, then $b_i = C_i$ for every $i$.

V3.38

The Euler characteristic, three ways

restated
three descriptions of $\chi$ identifiedindependent of the field

Milnor §5, p. 28, and formula (3)

Milnor's Euler characteristic is $\chi(X, Y) = \sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda(X, Y)$ (p. 28); formula (3) gives $\chi(M) = C_0 - C_1 + \dots \pm C_n$ (p. 29), and in Application 2 (pp. 36–37) $\chi(M)$ is the index sum of every vector field. That $\chi(M)$ is the same over every field is never stated.

Proved in Lean

(i) Let $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$, $K \ge 1$, be a compact non-empty slice submanifold of dimension $d + 1 \ge 1$. Every Euler number $\chi$ of $N$ (V3.17, the Poincaré–Hopf integer) satisfies $\chi = \sum_{i=0}^{d+1} (-1)^i \dim H_i(N; \Bbbk)$ for every field $\Bbbk$; the same holds for every space homeomorphic to $N$. (ii) For a compact Hausdorff smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, the integer $\chi(M)$ of V4.18 ($\sum_\lambda (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$ for any Morse function) equals $\sum_{i=0}^{\dim M} (-1)^i \dim H_i(M; \Bbbk)$ for every field $\Bbbk$. In particular this alternating sum does not depend on the field.

V3.39

The Morse inequalities on a compact manifold

hypotheses explicit
Hausdorff assumedthrough a Whitney embeddingthe lacunary principle added

Milnor §5, Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 5.4 · p. 29

§5 is stated for a compact manifold $M$ and a function with isolated, non-degenerate critical points: $R_\lambda(M) \le C_\lambda$, $\sum (-1)^\lambda R_\lambda(M) = \sum (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$, the inequalities $(4_\lambda)$ and Corollary 5.4, for Betti numbers over a field.

Proved in Lean

The homology over any field of a compact $k$-dimensional slice submanifold of $\mathbb R^n$, or of a space homeomorphic to one, is finite-dimensional and vanishes above degree $k$. Let $M$ be a compact Hausdorff smooth manifold without boundary, modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space, of dimension $n$. Then $H_i(M; \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional and is $0$ for $i > n$, and for every Morse function $g$ on $M$, with $b_i = \dim H_i(M; \Bbbk)$ and $C_\lambda = C_\lambda(g)$: $b_\lambda \le C_\lambda$; $(4_\lambda)$; $\sum_{i \le n} (-1)^i b_i = \sum_{\lambda \le n} (-1)^\lambda C_\lambda$; and $b_i = C_i$ for every $i$ if no two consecutive $C_i$ are non-zero.

V3.41

$\mathbb CP^n$ and Milnor's coordinates

restated
rank-one projections $zz^*$slice charts from Milnor's coordinates

Milnor §4, p. 26

$\mathbb CP_n$ is the set of equivalence classes of $(n + 1)$-tuples $(z_0, \dots, z_n)$ of complex numbers with $\sum|z_j|^2 = 1$. On the set $U_0$ where $z_0 \neq 0$, set $|z_0|\,z_j/z_0 = x_j + iy_j$; then $x_1, y_1, \dots, x_n, y_n$ "are the required coordinate functions, mapping $U_0$ diffeomorphically onto the open unit ball in $\mathbb R^{2n}$".

Proved in Lean

Here $\mathbb CP^n$ is the set of Hermitian projections of trace $1$ in the space $M_{n+1}(\mathbb C)$ of complex matrices (the Grassmannian of V14.16 with $m = 1$). Every point of it is $P = zz^*$, that is $P_{ab} = z_a\bar z_b$, for a unit vector $z \in \mathbb C^{n+1}$. For $0 \le k \le n$ let $U_k$ be the set of $P$ with $\operatorname{Re}P_{kk} > 0$; every point of $\mathbb CP^n$ lies in some $U_k$. On $\mathbb R^{2n} = \mathbb C^n$, with coordinates $z_j = x_j + iy_j$ ($j \neq k$), put $\operatorname{param}_k(z) = vv^*$, where $v_k = \sqrt{1 - |z|^2}$ and $v_j = z_j$ for $j \neq k$; and for a matrix $P$ put $\operatorname{coord}_k(P) = (P_{jk}/\sqrt{\operatorname{Re}P_{kk}})_{j \neq k}$. Then $\operatorname{coord}_k(\operatorname{param}_k(z)) = z$ for $|z| < 1$, and for $P \in \mathbb CP^n \cap U_k$, $|\operatorname{coord}_k(P)| < 1$ and $\operatorname{param}_k(\operatorname{coord}_k(P)) = P$. $\mathbb CP^n$ is a compact slice submanifold of $M_{n+1}(\mathbb C)$ of dimension $2n$, and at every $x \in \mathbb CP^n \cap U_k$ it has a slice chart whose parametrization is $z \mapsto \operatorname{param}_k(\operatorname{coord}_k(x) + z)$ near $0$.

V3.42

Milnor's function on $\mathbb CP^n$: critical points and indices

as in the book
one critical point of each even index

Milnor §4, pp. 26–27

$f(z_0 : z_1 : \dots : z_n) = \sum c_j|z_j|^2$, with distinct real constants $c_j$. In the coordinates of $U_0$, $f = c_0 + \sum_{j=1}^n(c_j - c_0)(x_j^2 + y_j^2)$; so the only critical point within $U_0$ is the centre $p_0$, non-degenerate, of index twice the number of $j$ with $c_j < c_0$. Similarly at $p_1, \dots, p_n$. "Every possible even index between $0$ and $2n$ occurs exactly once."

The scan of p. 26 prints the definition as $f = c_j|z_j|$; the display that follows it confirms $\sum c_j|z_j|^2$.

Proved in Lean

For real numbers $c_0, \dots, c_n$ let $f(P) = \sum_j c_j\operatorname{Re}P_{jj}$ on $\mathbb CP^n$, so that $f(zz^*) = \sum_j c_j|z_j|^2$. In the coordinates of V3.41, $f(\operatorname{param}_k(z)) = c_k + \sum_{j \neq k}(c_j - c_k)(x_j^2 + y_j^2)$ for $|z| \le 1$. Suppose the $c_j$ are distinct. Then the critical points of $f$ are exactly the $n + 1$ points $p_k = \operatorname{param}_k(0)$ (the projections onto the coordinate axes); $p_k$ is non-degenerate, of index $2\,\#\{j : c_j < c_k\}$; so $f$ is a Morse function. The map $k \mapsto \#\{j : c_j < c_k\}$ is a bijection of $\{0, \dots, n\}$, and so the number $C_\lambda$ of critical points of index $\lambda$ is $1$ for $\lambda = 0, 2, \dots, 2n$ and $0$ for every other $\lambda$.

V4.1

The normal bundle and the endpoint map

stronger
$k = n$ allowed$M$ neither closed nor compactthe twisted map $E_\Gamma$

Milnor §6, p. 32

For a $k$-dimensional manifold $M$ differentiably embedded in $\mathbb R^n$, $k < n$, Milnor takes the set $N \subset M \times \mathbb R^n$ of pairs $(q, v)$ with $v$ perpendicular to $M$ at $q$, the total space of the normal vector bundle, which, he says, is not difficult to show to be an $n$-manifold differentiably embedded in $\mathbb R^{2n}$; and the endpoint map $E : N \to \mathbb R^n$, $E(q, v) = q + v$.

Proved in Lean

Throughout, $M \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ is a slice submanifold modelled on $\mathbb R^k$ with complement $\mathbb R^w$; if $M$ is non-empty, $k + w = n$. The normal bundle is $N = \{(q, v) \in M \times \mathbb R^n : v \perp T_qM\}$; when $k + w = n$ it is a slice submanifold of $\mathbb R^n \times \mathbb R^n$ of dimension $n$ (the Milnor project's construction). The endpoint map is $E(q, v) = q + v$; more generally, for a map $\Gamma : \mathbb R^n \to \mathbb R^n$, $E_\Gamma(q, v) = \Gamma(q) + v$, smooth over every open set on which $\Gamma$ is smooth, with $E_{\mathrm{id}} = E$.

V4.2

Focal points and their multiplicity

hypotheses explicit
nullity read in a chart of $N$focal set = critical values of $E$

Milnor §6, Definition · p. 32

A point $e = q + v$, $(q, v) \in N$, is a focal point of $(M, q)$, of multiplicity $\mu$, when the Jacobian of $E$ at $(q, v)$ has nullity $\mu > 0$, and a focal point of $M$ when it is one of $(M, q)$ for some $q \in M$; intuitively, focal points are where nearby normals meet. The proof of Corollary 6.2 uses that the focal points are exactly the images under $E$ of its critical points.

Proved in Lean

Assume $k + w = n$. The nullity of $E$ at $x \in N$ is the dimension of the kernel of $dE_x$, the tangent space of $N$ at $x$ being identified with $\mathbb R^n$ by the chart of $N$ at $x$. A point $e \in \mathbb R^n$ is a focal point of $(M, q)$ with multiplicity $\mu$ if $(q, e - q) \in N$ and the nullity of $E$ at $(q, e - q)$ is $\mu > 0$; a focal point of $(M, q)$ if this holds for some $\mu$; and a focal point of $M$ if it is a focal point of $(M, q)$ for some $q \in M$. The nullity is positive exactly at the critical points of $E$, the points where $dE$ is not onto; so the set of focal points of $M$ is the set of critical values of $E$.

Theorem 6.1 (Sard)

Milnor §6, Theorem 6.1 (Sard) · p. 33

For a $C^1$ map $f : M_1 \to M_2$ between differentiable manifolds of the same dimension, each with a countable basis, the critical points, where the Jacobian of $f$ is singular, have an image of measure $0$ in $M_2$. Milnor gives no proof, referring to de Rham.

Let $M$ be a second countable smooth manifold without boundary modelled on a finite-dimensional real normed space $E$, $F$ a finite-dimensional real normed space with a Haar measure $\mu$, $U \subseteq M$ open and $f : M \to F$ smooth on $U$. Then the image under $f$ of the points of $U$ where $df$ is not onto is $\mu$-null; in particular, for $f$ smooth on $M$, the set of critical values is null. $E$ and $F$ are required to lie in the same universe of Lean's type theory, a formality with no mathematical content.

V4.5

The first and second fundamental forms

restated
$\ell_v$ for every vector $v$the coordinates of a slice chart

Milnor §6, pp. 33–34

In local coordinates $u^1, \dots, u^k$ on $M \subset \mathbb R^n$, with $\vec x(u)$ the inclusion, the first fundamental form is the matrix $g_{ij} = \partial\vec x/\partial u^i \cdot \partial\vec x/\partial u^j$, and the second fundamental form is the symmetric matrix $(\vec\ell_{ij})$ of vector-valued functions, $\vec\ell_{ij}$ the normal component of $\partial^2\vec x/\partial u^i\partial u^j$. For a unit vector $\vec v$ normal to $M$ at $q$, the matrix $(\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$ is the second fundamental form of $M$ at $q$ in the direction $\vec v$. Milnor gives no invariant definition and works in a fixed coordinate system.

Proved in Lean

For $q \in M$, the coordinates $u \mapsto x(u)$ are the inverse of the slice chart of $M$ chosen at $q$, with $x(u_q) = q$; $dx$ and $d^2x$ are its first and second derivatives at $u_q$. The first fundamental form is the bilinear form $g(\xi, \eta) = \langle dx\,\xi, dx\,\eta\rangle$ on $\mathbb R^k$; the second fundamental form in a direction $v \in \mathbb R^n$ is $\ell_v(\xi, \eta) = \langle v, d^2x(\xi, \eta)\rangle$; and for a linear map $T$ of $\mathbb R^n$ the form $(\xi, \eta) \mapsto \langle T\,dx\,\xi, dx\,\eta\rangle - \ell_v(\xi, \eta)$ is the one attached to $E_\Gamma$ with $T = d\Gamma_q$, equal to $g - \ell_v$ for $T = \mathrm{id}$.

Milnor §6, p. 34

In coordinates for which $(g_{ij})$ is the identity matrix at $q$, the principal curvatures $K_1, \dots, K_n$ of $M$ at $q$ in the normal direction $\vec v$ are the eigenvalues of $(\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$; the reciprocals of those that are non-zero are the principal radii of curvature.

The shape operator $S_v$ of $M$ at $q$ in the direction $v$ is the endomorphism of the tangent space $T_qM = \operatorname{range} dx$ with $\langle S_v a, b\rangle = \ell_v(dx^{-1}a, dx^{-1}b)$; it is self-adjoint. The principal curvatures of $M$ at $q$ in the direction $v$ are its $k$ eigenvalues, with multiplicity, in decreasing order; the multiplicity of $K$ is the dimension of the eigenspace of $K$.

Lemma 6.3: focal points along a normal line

stronger
any normal $v$, not only unit ones$t = 0$ set asidemultiplicity = eigenspace dimension

Milnor §6, Lemma 6.3 · p. 34

Let $\vec v$ be a unit normal to $M$ at $\vec q$. On the normal line $\ell = \{\vec q + t\vec v\}$ the focal points of $(M, q)$ are exactly the points $\vec q + K_i^{-1}\vec v$ with $1 \le i \le k$ and $K_i \ne 0$; counted with their multiplicities, there are therefore at most $k$ of them on $\ell$.

Proved in Lean

Assume $k + w = n$, and let $\mathrm{mult}_q(e)$ be the multiplicity of $e$ as a focal point of $(M, q)$, $0$ if it is not one. For $q \in M$, $v \perp T_qM$ and $t \in \mathbb R$: $\mathrm{mult}_q(q + tv) = 0$ if $t = 0$, and otherwise it is the multiplicity of $1/t$ as an eigenvalue of $S_v$. Hence $q + tv$ is a focal point of $(M, q)$ iff $t = K^{-1}$ for a non-zero principal curvature $K$ in the direction $v$, the multiplicity of $q + K^{-1}v$ is that of $K$, and for any finitely many values of $t$ the multiplicities of the points $q + tv$ add up to at most $k$.

restated

Milnor §6, proof of Lemma 6.3 · p. 34

Milnor chooses unit normal fields $\vec w_1, \dots, \vec w_{n-k}$, orthogonal to each other, coordinates $(u, t)$ on $N$ given by $(u, t) \mapsto (\vec x(u), \sum_\alpha t^\alpha\vec w_\alpha(u))$, and takes inner products of the partial derivatives of $E$ with $\partial\vec x/\partial u^1, \dots, \partial\vec x/\partial u^k, \vec w_1, \dots, \vec w_{n-k}$. For $\Gamma$ differentiable at $q$, the derivative of $E_\Gamma$ at $(q, v)$ is $(a, b) \mapsto d\Gamma_q(a) + b$ on this tangent space, and its nullity equals the nullity of the form $(\xi, \eta) \mapsto \langle d\Gamma_q\,dx\,\xi, dx\,\eta\rangle - \langle v, d^2x(\xi, \eta)\rangle$ on $\mathbb R^k$. For $\Gamma = \mathrm{id}$: the nullity of $E$ at $(q, v)$ is the nullity of $g - \ell_v$.

Milnor §6, pp. 35–36

For fixed $\vec p \in \mathbb R^n$, $f = L_{\vec p}$ satisfies $f(\vec x(u)) = \|\vec x(u) - \vec p\|^2$ and $\partial f/\partial u^i = 2\,\partial\vec x/\partial u^i \cdot (\vec x - \vec p)$, so $f$ has a critical point at $\vec q$ iff $\vec q - \vec p$ is normal to $M$ at $\vec q$. At a critical point the second partial derivatives are $2(\partial\vec x/\partial u^i \cdot \partial\vec x/\partial u^j + \partial^2\vec x/\partial u^i\partial u^j \cdot (\vec x - \vec p))$, which on setting $\vec p = \vec x + t\vec v$ becomes $2(g_{ij} - t\,\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$.

The second display is cut off in the scan; its value is the one used on p. 38.

(iv) If $M$ is non-empty of dimension $d + 1$, it is diffeomorphic to a compact $N \subseteq \mathbb R^{K+1}$ on which every smooth tangent field with finitely many zeros has index sum $\chi(M)$.

Corollary 6.8 on a submanifold of $\mathbb R^n$

stronger
$f$ need not be bounded$M$ need not be compactderivatives in fixed coordinates

Milnor §6, Corollary 6.8 · p. 37

A bounded smooth $f : M \to \mathbb R$ is a uniform limit of smooth functions $g$ without degenerate critical points, and $g$ may be chosen so that, on a given compact set $K$, its derivatives of every order $i \le k$ are uniformly close to those of $f$.

Proved in Lean

Let $M \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be any slice submanifold, $f : M \to \mathbb R$ smooth, bounded or not, $\varepsilon > 0$, $r \in \mathbb N$, and finitely many smooth coordinate systems $y_j$ on open subsets of $M$, with values in $\mathbb R^k$, with compact sets $K_j$ inside their ranges. There is a Morse function $g$ on $M$ with $|g - f| < \varepsilon$ on all of $M$ and $\|D^i((g - f) \circ y_j^{-1})(u)\| < \varepsilon$ for every $j$, every $i \le r$ and every $u \in K_j$. One can take $g = f + \langle a, \beta(\cdot)\rangle$ with $a$ small, where $\beta(y) = y/\sqrt{1 + \|y\|^2}$ is the diffeomorphism of $\mathbb R^n$ onto its open unit ball; for compact $M$ also $g = f + \langle a, \cdot\rangle$.

Lemma 6.9: the index of $L_p$

restated
$> 1/t$, not $\ge 1/t$the direction $p - q$ not normalizedthe case $p = q$ included

Milnor §6, Lemma 6.9 · p. 37

At a non-degenerate critical point $\vec q$ of $L_{\vec p}$, the index is the number of focal points of $(M, \vec q)$ on the segment from $\vec q$ to $\vec p$, counted with multiplicity. The proof (p. 38): the index of $2(g_{ij} - t\,\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$ is its number of negative eigenvalues, which, for $(g_{ij})$ the identity, is the number of eigenvalues of $(\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$ that are $\ge 1/t$; compare Lemma 6.3.

Milnor adds that an analogous statement in Part III, the Morse index theorem, will be of fundamental importance.

Proved in Lean

(i) The index of $g - \ell_v$ is the number of principal curvatures in the direction $v$, counted with multiplicity, that are greater than $1$. (ii) At a critical point $q$ of $L_p$, the index of $L_p$ is the number of principal curvatures of $M$ at $q$ in the direction $p - q$ that are greater than $1$. (iii) If $k + w = n$ and $q$ is a non-degenerate critical point of $L_p$, the index of $L_p$ at $q$ is $\sum_{t \in [0, 1]} \mathrm{mult}_q(q + t(p - q))$, all but finitely many terms vanishing: the number of focal points of $(M, q)$ on the segment from $q$ to $p$, each counted with its multiplicity.

Chapter 5

Milnor §7, pp. 39–42: the Lefschetz theorem on hyperplane sections

V5.2

Milnor's form $Q'$, and multiplication by $i$

stronger
the sign change for the bilinear formcoordinate-free

Milnor §7, p. 39

Writing $z^h = x^h + iy^h$ in a complex quadratic form $Q(z) = \sum b_{hj}z^hz^j$ of $k$ variables and taking real parts gives a real quadratic form $Q'$ in $2k$ variables. Since $Q(iz) = -Q(z)$, an orthogonal change of variables turns $Q'$ into $-Q'$.

Proved in Lean

For a complex vector space $V$ and a continuous complex-bilinear $B : V \times V \to \mathbb C$, $\mathrm{Re}\,B$ is a real bilinear form; for $B(z, z') = \sum b_{hj}z^hz'^j$ on $\mathbb C^k$ its quadratic form is Milnor's $Q'$. Multiplication by $i$ is a real-linear isomorphism $J$ with $J^2 = -1$ (inverse $-J$), and $\mathrm{Re}\,B(iv, iw) = -\mathrm{Re}\,B(v, w)$ for all $v$, $w$. On a complex inner product space the real inner product $\mathrm{Re}\langle v, w\rangle$, the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb R^{2k}$ when $V = \mathbb C^k$, satisfies $\mathrm{Re}\langle iv, iw\rangle = \mathrm{Re}\langle v, w\rangle$: $J$ is orthogonal.

Milnor §7, Assertion 1 · p. 39

The eigenvalues of $Q'$ come in opposite pairs: with $e$, of multiplicity $\mu$, $-e$ is an eigenvalue of the same multiplicity. Milnor says this clearly follows from the orthogonal change of variables carrying $Q'$ into $-Q'$.

Proved in Lean

Let $V$ be a complex inner product space, $B$ a continuous complex-bilinear form on $V$ and $e \in \mathbb R$. Then $\mathrm{Re}\,B - e\,\mathrm{Re}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $\mathrm{Re}\,B + e\,\mathrm{Re}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ have the same nullity. If $A$ is a real-linear operator on $V$ with $\mathrm{Re}\langle Au, w\rangle = \mathrm{Re}\,B(u, w)$ for all $u$, $w$ (the matrix of $Q'$ in orthonormal real coordinates), then the $e$-eigenspace of $A$ is the null space of $\mathrm{Re}\,B - e\,\mathrm{Re}\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, and the $e$- and $(-e)$-eigenspaces of $A$ have the same dimension.

Milnor §7, proof of Assertion 2 · p. 40

With $z^1, \dots, z^k$ complex coordinates for $M$ near $q$, $w_\alpha(z)$ the coordinates of the inclusion $M \to \mathbb C^n$ and $v$ a unit normal, the real inner product $w \cdot v = \mathrm{Re}\sum_\alpha w_\alpha\bar v_\alpha$ has the real expansion $\text{const} + Q'(x, y) + \text{higher terms}$, and clearly, Milnor says, the quadratic terms $Q'$ determine the second fundamental form of $M$ at $q$ in the normal direction $v$.

Proved in Lean

Let $V$ be a complex normed space, $F$ a complex inner product space, $w : V \to F$ complex $C^2$ on a neighbourhood of $q$ (in particular holomorphic there), and $p \in F$. Then the real Hessian at $q$ of $z \mapsto \|w(z) - p\|^2$ is $(\xi, \xi') \mapsto 2(\mathrm{Re}\langle dw_q\xi, dw_q\xi'\rangle + \mathrm{Re}\langle w(q) - p, d^2w_q(\xi, \xi')\rangle)$, where $dw_q$ and $d^2w_q$ are the complex first and second derivatives. The first term is unchanged by $(\xi, \xi') \mapsto (i\xi, i\xi')$, being the first fundamental form of $w$; the second changes sign, being the real part of a complex bilinear form.

Milnor §7, p. 41

Not in Milnor's text. On p. 41 he bounds the index of $L_p$ at a critical point $q$ by counting focal points: by Lemma 6.9 it is the number of focal points of $(M, q)$ between $p$ and $q$; there are at most $2k$ on the whole normal line, distributed symmetrically about $q$ by Assertion 2, so at most $k$ between $p$ and $q$. Let $G$, $L$, $H$ be bilinear forms on a real normed space and $J$ any map of it such that, for all $v$, $H(v, v) = G(v, v) - L(v, v)$, $G(Jv, Jv) = G(v, v)$ and $L(Jv, Jv) = -L(v, v)$. Then $H(Jv, Jv) = 2G(v, v) - H(v, v)$. On a complex vector space with $J = i\cdot$ and $L = \mathrm{Re}\,B$, $B$ complex bilinear, the condition on $L$ is automatic; on a complex inner product space with $G(v, v) = \|v\|^2$ it reads $H(iv, iv) = 2\|v\|^2 - H(v, v)$.

For a complex manifold $M$ of complex dimension $k$, bianalytically embedded in $\mathbb C^n$, the index of $L_p$ at a non-degenerate critical point is $\le k$: the focal points of $(M, q)$ along a normal line come in pairs symmetric about $q$ (Assertions 1 and 2), and Lemma 6.9 counts those between $p$ and $q$.

For such an $N$, every $p \in V$ and every critical point $q$ of $L_p = \|\cdot - p\|^2$ on $N$, degenerate or not, twice the index of $L_p$ at $q$ is at most $\dim_{\mathbb R}N$; so if $\dim_{\mathbb R}N = 2k$, the index is at most $k$.

Under Hypothesis (N), for every field $\mathbb k$: $H_r(X, A; \mathbb k) = 0$ for $r < k$; hence the map $H_r(A; \mathbb k) \to H_r(X; \mathbb k)$ induced by the inclusion is bijective for $r + 1 < k$ and surjective for $r < k$. On the way: at a non-degenerate critical point of $L_p$ on $M$, the function $-L_p$ has index at least $k$.

Milnor §7, Corollary 7.3 · p. 41

Let $V$ be an algebraic variety of complex dimension $k$ in $\mathbb CP_n$ and $P$ a hyperplane containing the singular points of $V$. Then the inclusion $V \cap P \to V$ induces isomorphisms of homology groups in dimensions less than $k - 1$, and is onto in dimension $k - 1$.

Proved in Lean

Let $V \subseteq \mathbb CP^n$ (V3.41) be closed and $P$ the hyperplane $z_0 = 0$, the set of projections $Q$ with $Q_{00} = 0$. The affine part of $V$ is the set of $u \in \mathbb C^n = \mathbb R^{2n}$ for which the projection onto the line of $(1, u)$ belongs to $V$; it is homeomorphic to $V \setminus P$, and its points go to infinity as their images approach $V \cap P$. Suppose the affine part is a slice submanifold of $\mathbb R^{2n}$ of dimension $2k$, complex for multiplication by $i$, and suppose Hypothesis (N) for $V \cap P$ in $V$ (V5.17). Then for every field $\mathbb k$ the map $H_r(V \cap P; \mathbb k) \to H_r(V; \mathbb k)$ induced by the inclusion is bijective for $r < k - 1$ and surjective for $r = k - 1$.

Milnor §7, Theorem 7.4, pp. 41–42

Under the same hypotheses, the relative homotopy group $\pi_r(V, V \cap P)$ is zero for $r < k$. The proof uses $f = 0$ on $V \cap P$ and $f = 1/L_p$ elsewhere, whose critical points have index $\ge k$, and a neighbourhood of $V \cap P$ that deforms into $V \cap P$ (from the triangulability of algebraic varieties).

Proved in Lean

Under the hypotheses of V5.18: for $r < k$, every continuous map $h : I^r \to V$ is homotopic, relative to $h^{-1}(V \cap P)$, to a map into $V \cap P$; the same holds for maps from any compact space that admits a continuous injection into a real vector space of dimension $< k$, and for the abstract pair $(X, A)$ of V5.17. Consequently, for every $x \in V \cap P$, the map $\pi_i(V \cap P, x) \to \pi_i(V, x)$ induced by the inclusion is bijective for $i + 1 < k$ and surjective for $i < k$.
