V6.1

Tangent spaces, the projection $P_q$, and vector fields

narrower
$N \subseteq V$ with the induced metrictangent vectors are vectors of $V$

Milnor §8, pp. 43–44

Milnor works on an abstract smooth manifold $M$, with tangent spaces $TM_p$, vector fields $X$, and directional derivatives $X_pf$ of real functions $f$ in the direction of a tangent vector $X_p$.

Proved in Lean

In the embedded setting, $V$ is a finite-dimensional real inner product space and $N \subseteq V$ a slice submanifold, closed or not, with the induced metric. $T_qN \subseteq V$ is the range of the derivative at $q$ of the inclusion $N \to V$, and $P_q$ is the orthogonal projection of $V$ onto $T_qN$. For $F : N \to E$ into a normed space, the linear map $dN\,F\,q : V \to E$ is the derivative of $F$ at $q$ read on ambient vectors: on $v \in T_qN$ it is $dF_q(v)$, and if $F = G$ on $N$ near $q$ for some $G : V \to E$ differentiable at $q$, then $dN\,F\,q\,v = dG_q(v)$ for $v \in T_qN$. A vector field is a map $X : N \to V$ with $X(q) \in T_qN$ for every $q$, smooth if it is smooth as a map $N \to V$. The map $q \mapsto P_q$ is smooth, so every tangent vector $u$ at a point extends to the smooth vector field $q \mapsto P_qu$.

What differs

  • The substance of §§8–9 is verified for submanifolds of a Euclidean space with the induced metric. Every Riemannian manifold is isometric to such an $N$ by Nash's embedding theorem, which is neither in Mathlib nor proved here, so these are statements about embedded manifolds.

V6.3

Affine connections on an abstract manifold

restated
Mathlib's covariant derivative(2), (4) where differentiable(1) a separate class

Milnor §8, pp. 43–44

An affine connection at $p$ is a rule giving, for a tangent vector $X_p$ and a vector field $Y$, a tangent vector $X_p \vdash Y$ at $p$, the covariant derivative of $Y$ along $X_p$; it is bilinear and satisfies $X_p \vdash (fY) = (X_pf)Y_p + f(p)\,X_p \vdash Y$. A global connection is such a rule at every point subject to the smoothness condition (1); it then satisfies (2) bilinearity, (3) $(fX) \vdash Y = f(X \vdash Y)$ and (4) $X \vdash (fY) = (Xf)Y + f(X \vdash Y)$, and (1)–(4) may serve as the definition.

A footnote identifies $X \vdash Y$ with Nomizu's $\nabla_XY$.

Proved in Lean

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold in Mathlib's sense, modelled on a real normed space, and $\nabla$ a Mathlib covariant derivative on its tangent bundle, $X_p \vdash Y$ being the value at $X_p$ of the linear map $\nabla Y(p) : T_pM \to T_pM$. Then Milnor's (3), $(fX) \vdash Y = f(X \vdash Y)$, holds at every point; (2), additivity in $Y$, holds at every point where both summands are differentiable; and (4), $X \vdash (fY) = (Xf)Y + f(X \vdash Y)$, holds at every point where $f$ and $Y$ are differentiable. Dependence on $X_p$ only, and linearity in $X_p$, are part of the definition.

V6.4

The connection of the induced metric, and rules (1)–(4)

narrower
the induced connection onlyone global formula, no Christoffel(2), (4) where differentiable

Milnor §8, p. 44

A global affine connection satisfies (1) $X \vdash Y$ is smooth when $X$ and $Y$ are smooth vector fields; (2) $X \vdash Y$ is bilinear in $X$ and $Y$; (3) $(fX) \vdash Y = f(X \vdash Y)$; (4) $X \vdash (fY) = (Xf)Y + f(X \vdash Y)$. In local coordinates it is determined by its Christoffel symbols, $\partial_i \vdash \partial_j = \sum_k \Gamma^k_{ij}\partial_k$.

Proved in Lean

In the embedded setting put $v \vdash Y = P_q(dY_q(v))$ for $v \in T_qN$ and $Y : N \to V$, and $(X \vdash Y)(q) = P_q(dY_q(X(q)))$. Then $X \vdash Y$ is tangent to $N$ at every point, and: (1) $X \vdash Y$ is smooth when $X$ is a smooth vector field and $Y$ is smooth; (2) it is additive in $X$, and additive in $Y$ at every point where both summands are differentiable; (3) $(fX) \vdash Y = f(X \vdash Y)$ for every function $f$; (4) at $q$, $X \vdash (fY) = (Xf)Y + f(X \vdash Y)$ with $Xf = df_q(X(q))$, when $f$ and $Y$ are differentiable at $q$ and $X(q)$, $Y(q)$ are tangent.

V6.5

Covariant derivative along a curve

narrower
$DX/dt = P(X')$embedded $N$, induced connectiondifferentiability at $t$

Milnor §8, pp. 45–46

A vector field $V$ along a parametrized curve $c$ assigns to each $t$ a tangent vector $V_t \in TM_{c(t)}$, smoothly; the velocity field is $dc/dt = c_*(d/dt)$. Given a connection, the covariant derivative $V \mapsto DV/dt$ is characterized by three axioms: (a) $D(V + W)/dt = DV/dt + DW/dt$; (b) $D(fV)/dt = (df/dt)V + f\,DV/dt$ for a smooth real function $f$ on $\mathbb R$; (c) if $V$ is induced by a vector field $Y$, $V_t = Y_{c(t)}$, then $DV/dt$ is the covariant derivative of $Y$ in the direction of the velocity vector of $c$.

Proved in Lean

For a curve $c : \mathbb R \to N$, a vector field along $c$ is a map $X : \mathbb R \to V$ with $X(t) \in T_{c(t)}N$ for all $t$; the velocity $c'(t)$ is tangent when $c$ is smooth; and $DX/dt\,(t) = P_{c(t)}(X'(t))$. Then (a) $D(X + Y)/dt = DX/dt + DY/dt$ at $t$ when $X$, $Y$ are differentiable at $t$; (b) $D(fX)/dt = f'X + f\,DX/dt$ at $t$ when $f$, $X$ are differentiable at $t$ and $X(t)$ is tangent; (c) if $c$ is smooth and $Y : N \to V$ is differentiable at $c(t)$, then $D(Y \circ c)/dt\,(t) = c'(t) \vdash Y$.

The differential equations $dv^k/dt + \sum_{i,j} (du^i/dt)\Gamma^k_{ij}v^j = 0$ have solutions uniquely determined by their initial values; since the equations are linear, Milnor says, the solutions can be defined for all relevant values of $t$, citing Graves.

Let $A : \mathbb R \to \mathrm{End}(E)$ be continuous. (i) On a real normed space $E$, two solutions of $x' = A(t)x$ on an open interval, or on $\mathbb R$, that agree at one time agree everywhere. Milnor §6, p. 33

Milnor §8, Definition 8.5 · p. 48

A connection is symmetric when $(X \vdash Y) - (Y \vdash X) = [X, Y]$, the bracket being the Poisson bracket $[X, Y]f = X(Yf) - Y(Xf)$. For coordinate fields this says $\Gamma^k_{ij} = \Gamma^k_{ji}$, and Milnor notes the converse.

Embedded: the bracket of two maps $X, Y : N \to V$ is $[X, Y](q) = dY_q(X(q)) - dX_q(Y(q))$. For vector fields differentiable at $q$ it is tangent to $N$ at $q$; for smooth $f$ and smooth vector fields, $X(Yf) - Y(Xf) = [X, Y]f$, where $Xf = df(X)$; and the induced connection is symmetric: $X \vdash Y - Y \vdash X = [X, Y]$ at $q$ for vector fields differentiable at $q$.

Lemma 8.6: the fundamental lemma of Riemannian geometry

narrower
existence only for embedded $N$abstract uniqueness onlyKoszul, not Christoffel

Milnor §8, Lemma 8.6 · p. 48

On a Riemannian manifold there is exactly one symmetric connection compatible with the metric. Uniqueness: Corollary 8.4 applied to $\partial_i$, $\partial_j$, $\partial_k$ gives three linear equations, whose solution is the first Christoffel identity, and multiplying by $(g^{k\ell})$ gives the second. Conversely, defining $\Gamma^\ell_{ij}$ by this formula, one can verify that the connection is symmetric and compatible with the metric.

Proved in Lean

Embedded: call an operation $D$ on maps $N \to V$ symmetric and compatible if, on smooth vector fields, $D(X, Y)$ is tangent, $D(X, Y) - D(Y, X) = [X, Y]$, and $X\langle Y, Y'\rangle = \langle D(X, Y), Y'\rangle + \langle Y, D(X, Y')\rangle$. The induced connection $P(dY(X))$ is such an operation (existence); every such operation satisfies the Koszul formula $2\langle D(X, Y), Z\rangle = X\langle Y, Z\rangle + Y\langle X, Z\rangle - Z\langle X, Y\rangle + \langle [X, Y], Z\rangle - \langle [X, Z], Y\rangle - \langle [Y, Z], X\rangle$ on smooth vector fields; and every such operation agrees with $P(dY(X))$ on smooth vector fields at every point (uniqueness). Abstract: for a manifold with a Riemannian metric on its tangent bundle, two covariant derivatives that are both symmetric and compatible (V6.11, V6.13) satisfy the Koszul formula and agree on every vector field differentiable at the point; with Mathlib's predicates, two torsion-free metric connections agree on such fields, for a finite-dimensional model space and a $C^1$ metric.

The curvature tensor and its sign

as in the book

Milnor §9, p. 51

The curvature tensor of an affine connection measures how far the second covariant derivative $\partial_i \vdash (\partial_j \vdash Z)$ is from being symmetric in $i$ and $j$; it is defined by $R(X, Y)Z = -X \vdash (Y \vdash Z) + Y \vdash (X \vdash Z) + [X, Y] \vdash Z$. A footnote says that Nomizu gives $R$ the opposite sign, and that Milnor's convention makes $\langle R(\partial_h, \partial_i)\partial_j, \partial_k\rangle$ the classical symbol $R_{hijk}$.

Proved in Lean

For a covariant derivative on an abstract manifold, Milnor's curvature of vector fields is $R(X, Y)Z = -X \vdash (Y \vdash Z) + Y \vdash (X \vdash Z) + [X, Y] \vdash Z$; it is the negative of Nomizu's, and Kobayashi–Nomizu's, $\nabla_X\nabla_YZ - \nabla_Y\nabla_XZ - \nabla_{[X, Y]}Z$, and $R(Y, X)Z = -R(X, Y)Z$. In the embedded setting the same formula, with the induced connection and the bracket of V6.13, defines $R(X, Y)Z$ for maps $N \to V$. Mathlib defines no curvature, so there is no Mathlib sign to compare with.

Lemma 9.1: the curvature is a tensor

narrower
embedded $N$, induced connectionan explicit formula in $\mathrm{II}$the computation for $Z$ differs

Milnor §9, Lemma 9.1 · p. 51

$R(X, Y)Z$ at $p$ is determined by $X_p$, $Y_p$, $Z_p$ alone, whatever the fields do near $p$, and depends trilinearly on them; in short, $R$ is a tensor. The proof checks $R(fX, Y)Z = fR(X, Y)Z$ and leaves the analogous identities for $Y$ and $Z$ to similar computations, which Milnor calls easy.

Proved in Lean

In the embedded setting, for smooth vector fields $X$, $Y$, $Z$ and every $q$, $R(X, Y)Z\,(q) = \mathrm{II}_q(Y_q, \mathrm{II}_q(X_q, Z_q)) - \mathrm{II}_q(X_q, \mathrm{II}_q(Y_q, Z_q))$, that is, $R(X, Y) = D_YD_X - D_XD_Y$ on $T_qN$. Consequently $R(X, Y)Z$ at $q$ depends only on $X_q$, $Y_q$, $Z_q$, and it is the value of a trilinear map $T_qN \times T_qN \times T_qN \to T_qN$, the curvature tensor of $N$ at $q$.

The Gauss equation

not in the book
with Milnor's sign of $R$computes the curvature of the sphere

Milnor no counterpart in the book

The book has no such formula: Milnor never relates the curvature tensor of a submanifold to its second fundamental form.

Proved in Lean

For all $x, y, z, w \in V$, $\langle D_yD_xz - D_xD_yz, w\rangle = \langle \mathrm{II}(x, z), \mathrm{II}(y, w)\rangle - \langle \mathrm{II}(x, w), \mathrm{II}(y, z)\rangle$ at $q$; hence, for smooth vector fields $X$, $Y$, $Z$ and any $W : N \to V$, $\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle = \langle \mathrm{II}(X, Z), \mathrm{II}(Y, W)\rangle - \langle \mathrm{II}(X, W), \mathrm{II}(Y, Z)\rangle$ at every point, with Milnor's sign of $R$. With $Z = X$, $W = Y$ and the symmetry of $\mathrm{II}$ this gives $\langle R(X, Y)X, Y\rangle = \langle \mathrm{II}(X, X), \mathrm{II}(Y, Y)\rangle - \|\mathrm{II}(X, Y)\|^2$, Gauss's curvature for a surface in $\mathbb R^3$.

Lemma 9.3, symmetries (1)–(3)

narrower
embedded $N$, induced connectionno bracket-free extensions needed

Milnor §9, Lemma 9.3 · p. 53

The curvature tensor of a Riemannian manifold satisfies (1) $R(X, Y)Z + R(Y, X)Z = 0$, (2) $R(X, Y)Z + R(Y, Z)X + R(Z, X)Y = 0$, (3) $\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle + \langle R(X, Y)W, Z\rangle = 0$. (1) is immediate from the definition; (2) and (3) are proved for fields whose brackets vanish, which suffices since all terms are tensors, (3) being reduced to $\langle R(X, Y)Z, Z\rangle = 0$, clearly an equivalent assertion.

Proved in Lean

A trilinear map $R$ on a real inner product space is called a curvature tensor if it satisfies (1) $R(X, Y)Z + R(Y, X)Z = 0$, (2) $R(X, Y)Z + R(Y, Z)X + R(Z, X)Y = 0$ and (3) $\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle + \langle R(X, Y)W, Z\rangle = 0$. For a linear map $T$, $\langle TZ, W\rangle$ is skew in $Z$, $W$ iff $\langle TZ, Z\rangle = 0$ for all $Z$. The curvature tensor of $N$ at each point (V6.17) satisfies (1)–(3). For maps $X$, $Y$, $Z$ of $N$ into $V$, (1) holds with no hypothesis; for smooth vector fields, (2) and (3) hold at every point.

Sectional curvature

stronger
any independent pairdepends only on the planethe same in both sign conventions

Milnor §19, Remark after Lemma 19.1 · p. 100

For orthogonal unit vectors $A$, $B$ at $p$, Milnor calls $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle$ the sectional curvature determined by $A$ and $B$, and notes that it is the Gaussian curvature of the surface formed by the geodesics through $p$ whose velocities lie in the plane of $A$ and $B$.

Proved in Lean

For a trilinear map $R$ and vectors $X$, $Y$, put $K(X, Y) = \langle R(X, Y)X, Y\rangle / (\|X\|^2\|Y\|^2 - \langle X, Y\rangle^2)$, which is $0$ when $X$, $Y$ are dependent; for an orthonormal pair it is Milnor's $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle$. If $R$ satisfies (1)–(3), $K$ depends only on the plane: $K(aX + bY, cX + dY) = K(X, Y)$ whenever $ad - bc \ne 0$. With the standard sign, $-R$ also satisfies (1)–(3), and $\langle (-R)(X, Y)Y, X\rangle = \langle R(X, Y)X, Y\rangle$: the sectional curvature is the same number in both conventions.

Chapter 7

Milnor §10, pp. 55–66: geodesics and completeness

V7.1

Geodesics

narrower
submanifolds of a Euclidean spacegeodesics live on open setsNash's theorem quoted, not used

Milnor §10, p. 55

On a connected Riemannian manifold $M$, a parametrized path $\gamma : I \to M$, $I$ any interval of the real line, is called a geodesic if its acceleration field $\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt}$ is identically zero; that is, if the velocity field $\frac{d\gamma}{dt}$ is parallel along $\gamma$. Here $D/dt$ is the covariant derivative along a curve of §8, for the Levi-Civita connection of an abstract Riemannian manifold.

Proved in Lean

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space (Milnor's $\mathbb R^K$) and $N \subseteq V$ a slice submanifold with the induced metric; $N$ need not be closed, compact or connected. A curve $\gamma : \mathbb R \to V$ is a geodesic on an open set $s \subseteq \mathbb R$ if it is $C^\infty$ on $s$, $\gamma(t) \in N$ for $t \in s$, and the acceleration $\gamma''(t)$ in $V$ is orthogonal to $T_{\gamma(t)}N$ for every $t \in s$. The velocity of a curve in $N$ is tangent to $N$, so the condition reads $P_{\gamma(t)}\gamma''(t) = 0$, $P$ the orthogonal projection onto the tangent space: this is $\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt} = 0$ for the covariant derivative $D/dt = P \circ d/dt$ of Chapter 6, and for a smooth curve $c : \mathbb R \to N$ the equivalence of the two conditions is a theorem. Constant curves at points of $N$ are geodesics.

What differs

  • Milnor's $M$ is an abstract Riemannian manifold. In Chapters 7–11 of the formalization it is a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space with the induced metric, and every row of these chapters is read in that setting; the narrowing is recorded here once rather than on every row. Every Riemannian manifold is of this kind by Nash's embedding theorem, which is quoted in the Lean files but neither proved nor used.
  • Mathlib has no Levi-Civita connection, geodesics or exponential map on an abstract manifold. In the embedded setting the connection is the tangential part of the derivative in $V$, and the Hausdorff property that Milnor uses silently is automatic.
  • Geodesics live on open sets: a geodesic on a closed interval, which Milnor allows, is represented by one on a slightly larger open interval. That the two notions give the same exponential map is proved later (V7.7).
  • Milnor's standing assumption that $M$ is connected is not made; it is assumed exactly where it is needed (finiteness of the distance, Theorem 10.9 for all pairs, Corollary 10.10, the Hopf–Rinow equivalence).
V7.2

Constant speed and homogeneity

stronger
every affine change $t \mapsto at + b$length = speed times $(b - a)$

Milnor §10, pp. 55 and 57

Since $\frac{d}{dt}\langle\frac{d\gamma}{dt}, \frac{d\gamma}{dt}\rangle = 2\langle\frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\gamma}{dt}, \frac{d\gamma}{dt}\rangle = 0$, the length $\|d\gamma/dt\|$ of the velocity vector of a geodesic is constant, and the parameter $t$ is a linear function of arc length (p. 55). On p. 57 Milnor adds homogeneity: if $t \mapsto \gamma(t)$ is a geodesic, then so is $t \mapsto \gamma(ct)$ for every constant $c$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a geodesic on an open set $s \subseteq \mathbb R$. Then $\frac{d}{dt}\|\gamma'\|^2 = 2\langle\gamma'', \gamma'\rangle = 0$ on $s$. If $s$ is preconnected (an open interval), the speed $\|\gamma'\|$ is constant on $s$, and the length of $\gamma$ on every $[a, b] \subseteq s$ (V7.11) is $\|\gamma'(t_0)\|\,(b - a)$, for any $t_0 \in s$. For all real $a$ and $b$, the curve $t \mapsto \gamma(at + b)$ is a geodesic on $\{t : at + b \in s\}$.

V7.3

The geodesic equation

restated
$\gamma'' = \mathrm{II}(\gamma', \gamma')$no Christoffel symbolschart solutions are geodesics

Milnor §10, p. 55

In terms of a local coordinate system $u^1, \dots, u^n$, the condition for $\gamma$ to be a geodesic becomes the system of second-order differential equations $\frac{d^2u^k}{dt^2} + \sum_{i,j}\Gamma^k_{ij}\frac{du^i}{dt}\frac{du^j}{dt} = 0$, $k = 1, \dots, n$, with the Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^k_{ij}$ of the connection. The existence of geodesics therefore rests on the existence theorem for such systems.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be $C^\infty$ on an open set $s$, with $\gamma(s) \subseteq N$. Then $\gamma$ is a geodesic on $s$ iff $\gamma'' = \mathrm{II}_\gamma(\gamma', \gamma')$ on $s$, $\mathrm{II}$ the second fundamental form, iff the lift $t \mapsto (\gamma(t), \gamma'(t))$, which lies in $TN = \{(x, v) : x \in N,\ v \in T_xN\}$, is an integral curve of the geodesic spray $(x, v) \mapsto (v, \mathrm{II}_x(v, v))$. In a slice chart with parametrization $x$ on an open set $T$ of the model space $Z$, put $A^+ = (A^{\mathsf T}A)^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}$ for injective $A$ and $\Gamma(u)(w, w) = (dx_u)^+\big(d^2x_u(w, w)\big)$. The field $(u, w) \mapsto (w, -\Gamma(u)(w, w))$ is smooth on $T \times Z$, and if $(u, w)$ is a $C^\infty$ solution of $u' = w$, $w' = -\Gamma(u)(w, w)$ on an open set, with $u$ in $T$, then $x \circ u$ is a geodesic there.

Theorem 10.1: existence, uniqueness and smooth dependence for ODEs

stronger
proved, not quoteduniqueness on every common intervaluniqueness for $C^1$ equations

Milnor §10, Theorem 10.1 · p. 56

Given a point $(u_1, v_1) \in \mathbb R^{2n}$ and $C^\infty$ functions $F = (F^1, \dots, F^n)$ defined near it, there are a neighbourhood $W$ of $(u_1, v_1)$ and a number $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for every $(u_0, v_0) \in W$ the equation $\frac{d^2u}{dt^2} = F(u, \frac{du}{dt})$ has a unique solution $t \mapsto u(t)$, defined for $|t| < \varepsilon$, with $u(0) = u_0$ and $\frac{du}{dt}(0) = v_0$; moreover the solution is $C^\infty$ as a function of $(u_0, v_0, t)$ on $W \times (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$. Milnor passes to the first-order system $du/dt = v$, $dv/dt = F(u, v)$ and quotes Graves.

Proved in Lean

Existence and smooth dependence. Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $U \subseteq E \times E$ open, $F : E \times E \to E$ smooth on $U$, and $z_1 \in U$. There are a neighbourhood $W$ of $z_1$, an $\varepsilon > 0$ and a map $(z, t) \mapsto u_z(t)$, smooth on $W \times (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$, such that for every $z = (u_0, v_0) \in W$: $u_z(0) = u_0$, $u_z'(0) = v_0$, and $(u_z(t), u_z'(t)) \in U$ and $u_z''(t) = F(u_z(t), u_z'(t))$ for $|t| < \varepsilon$. Uniqueness. Let $E$ be any real normed space and $G$ of class $C^1$ on an open $U \subseteq E$: two solutions of $x' = G(x)$ with values in $U$, defined on a common open preconnected set and agreeing at one of its times, agree on all of it. In particular, for $F$ of class $C^1$ on $U \subseteq E \times E$, two pairs with $u_i' = v_i$, $v_i' = F(u_i, v_i)$ and $(u_i, v_i) \in U$ on an open interval, with the same position and velocity at one time, have $u_1 = u_2$ on that interval.

The exponential map

restated
geodesics near $[0, 1]$, not on $[0, 1]$the two domains agree (Ch. 9, 11)

Milnor §10, pp. 57–58

For $v \in TM_q$, suppose there is a geodesic $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ with $\gamma(0) = q$ and $\frac{d\gamma}{dt}(0) = v$; then $\exp_q(v) = \gamma(1)$, and by homogeneity $\gamma(t) = \exp_q(tv)$ (p. 57). On p. 58 Milnor notes that $\exp_q(v)$ is defined when $\|v\|$ is small enough, in general not for large $v$, but is always uniquely defined when it is defined at all.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $q, v \in V$, a geodesic from $q$ with initial velocity $v$ is a geodesic on an open interval $(-\delta, 1 + \delta)$, $\delta > 0$, with $\gamma(0) = q$ and $\gamma'(0) = v$ (then $q \in N$ and $v \in T_qN$). The domain of $\exp$ is the set of pairs $(q, v)$ for which one exists, and $\exp_q(v) = \gamma(1)$ (off the domain $\exp_q(v)$ is set to $q$, a placeholder). Any two such geodesics agree on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$, so $\exp_q(v)$ is well defined. For $q \in N$, $(q, 0)$ is in the domain and $\exp_q(0) = q$; and for such a $\gamma$, each $s \mapsto \gamma(ts)$ with $t$ near $[0, 1]$ is a geodesic from $q$ with initial velocity $tv$, so $\exp_q(tv) = \gamma(t)$.

The tangent manifold, $\exp$ near the zero section, and $d(\exp_q)_0$

stronger
one neighbourhood of the zero sectionembedded $TN \subseteq V \times V$

Milnor §10, p. 58

The tangent manifold $TM$ is given a $C^\infty$ structure by the coordinates $(u^1, \dots, u^n, t^1, \dots, t^n)$, where $t^1\partial_1 + \dots + t^n\partial_n$ is a tangent vector at a point with coordinates $u$. Lemma 10.2 says that for each $p \in M$ the map $(q, v) \mapsto \exp_q(v)$ is defined throughout a neighbourhood $V$ of $(p, 0)$ in $TM$, and is differentiable there. In the Jacobian of $F(q, v) = (q, \exp_q(v))$ at $(p, 0)$, the column $F_*(\partial/\partial t^j) = \partial/\partial u_2^j$ amounts to $d(\exp_p)_0 = \mathrm{id}$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: $TN = \{(q, v) \in V \times V : q \in N,\ v \in T_qN\}$ is a slice submanifold of $V \times V$ (the companion project). (i) For every $q_0 \in N$ there are an open $U \ni q_0$, an $\varepsilon > 0$ and $F$ smooth on $U \times \{\|v\| < \varepsilon\}$ such that, for $p \in N \cap U$ and $v \in T_pN$ with $\|v\| < \varepsilon$, $(p, v)$ is in the domain of $\exp$ and $\exp_p(v) = F(p, v)$. (ii) There is one open $O \subseteq V \times V$ containing $(q, 0)$ for every $q \in N$ such that every point of $TN \cap O$ is in the domain of $\exp$, and $\exp$ is smooth on $TN \cap O$, both as a restriction of smooth maps on open sets of $V \times V$ and as a map on the manifold $TN$. (iii) For $q \in N$, $\exp_q$, as a map on the vector space $T_qN$, has derivative at $0$ the inclusion $T_qN \to V$.

V7.9

Normal radius

restated
the name is the exposition’s“diffeomorphically” in two senses

Milnor §10, Lemma 10.3 (3) · p. 59

Part (3) of Lemma 10.3 says that, for each $q$ in the neighbourhood $W$, $\exp_q$ maps the open $\varepsilon$-ball in $TM_q$ diffeomorphically onto an open set $U_q$. The book has no name for such an $\varepsilon$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $q \in N$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, let $B_\varepsilon(q) = \{v \in T_qN : \|v\| < \varepsilon\}$. Then $\varepsilon$ is a normal radius at $q$ if there are open sets $O, U \subseteq V$ and maps $F$ smooth on $O$ and $G$ smooth on $U$ with: $B_\varepsilon(q) \subseteq O$, $B_\varepsilon(q)$ in the domain of $\exp_q$ and $\exp_q = F$ there; $\exp_q$ maps $B_\varepsilon(q)$ into $U$ with $G(\exp_q v) = v$; and $G$ maps $U_q = N \cap U$ into $B_\varepsilon(q)$ with $\exp_q(G(y)) = y$. So $\exp_q$ is a bijection of $B_\varepsilon(q)$ onto the open subset $U_q$ of $N$, and it and its inverse are restrictions of smooth maps. A normal radius yields a diffeomorphism in Mathlib's sense: $\exp_q$ restricts to a PartialDiffeomorph of the open $\varepsilon$-ball onto $U_q$.

Lemma 10.3: uniformly normal neighbourhoods

restated
unique initial vector, not geodesicinverse, not implicit, function theorem

Milnor §10, Lemma 10.3 · p. 59

For each $p \in M$ there are a neighbourhood $W$ of $p$ and a number $\varepsilon > 0$ such that: (1) any two points of $W$ are joined by a unique geodesic in $M$ of length $< \varepsilon$; (2) this geodesic depends smoothly on the two points, in that if $t \mapsto \exp_{q_1}(tv)$, $0 \le t \le 1$, is the geodesic joining $q_1$ and $q_2$, the pair $(q_1, v) \in TM$ depends differentiably on $(q_1, q_2)$; (3) for each $q \in W$, $\exp_q$ maps the open $\varepsilon$-ball in $TM_q$ diffeomorphically onto an open set $U_q \supseteq W$. Proof (pp. 58–59): $F(q, v) = (q, \exp_q v)$ has nonsingular Jacobian $\begin{pmatrix} I & I \\ 0 & I \end{pmatrix}$ at $(p, 0)$, and "the implicit function theorem" gives a local inverse.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for each $p \in N$ there are an open set $O \ni p$ of $V$ and an $\varepsilon > 0$ such that, with $W = N \cap O$: (1) for all $q_1, q_2 \in W$ there is exactly one $v \in T_{q_1}N$ with $\|v\| < \varepsilon$ and $\exp_{q_1}(v) = q_2$; and a geodesic from $q_1$ with initial velocity of norm $< \varepsilon$ ending at $q_2$ is $t \mapsto \exp_{q_1}(tv)$ for this $v$; (2) there are an open $O_2 \subseteq V \times V$ containing $W \times W$ and $G$ smooth on $O_2$ with $G(q_1, q_2)$ the vector of (1); (3) $\varepsilon$ is a normal radius (V7.9) at every $q \in W$, and $U_q \supseteq W$. In particular every point of $N$ has a normal radius, and $\exp_q$ restricts to a PartialDiffeomorph of an open ball of $T_qN$ onto an open neighbourhood of $q$ in $N$.

Right after Lemma 10.3 Milnor remarks, without proof, that with more care it would be possible to choose $W$ so that the geodesic joining any two of its points lies completely within $W$, and refers to J. H. C. Whitehead, Convex regions in the geometry of paths (1932).

V7.11

Piecewise smooth paths and their lengths

hypotheses explicit
break points as a finite setadmissible paths, a wider classadditivity and invariance proved

Milnor §11, p. 67; used from p. 59

A piecewise smooth path is a map $\omega : [0, 1] \to M$ with a subdivision $0 = t_0 < t_1 < \dots < t_k = 1$ such that each $\omega|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ is $C^\infty$ (p. 67, where the notion is first defined). From Theorem 10.4 on (p. 59) such paths on intervals $[a, b]$, and their arc lengths $\int\|d\omega/dt\|\,dt$, are used without further comment.

Proved in Lean

Let $c$ be a curve in a real normed space (complete, for the statements involving $\int c'$) and $a \le b$. The length of $c$ on $[a, b]$ is $L(c|[a, b]) = \int_a^b\|c'(t)\|\,dt$, $c'$ being $0$ where $c$ is not differentiable. $c$ is piecewise smooth on $[a, b]$ if it is continuous there and, for a finite set $B$ of break points, $C^\infty$ (one-sided derivatives at the ends) on every $[s, t] \subseteq [a, b]$, $s < t$, with no point of $B$ in $(s, t)$. $c$ is admissible on $[a, b]$ if it is continuous there, differentiable off a countable subset of $(a, b)$, and $\|c'\|$ is integrable. Piecewise smooth paths are admissible. For admissible paths $\int_a^bc' = c(b) - c(a)$, so $\|c(b) - c(a)\| \le L$; length is additive under subdivision; a path of length $0$ is constant; and speed $k$ gives length $k(b - a)$. Restriction, concatenation at a common endpoint, reversal and translation of the parameter preserve piecewise smoothness; lengths add under concatenation and are unchanged by reversal and translation.

Lemma 10.5: the Gauss lemma

stronger
the identity for every $x$, not $x \perp w$no curve $v(t)$ needed

Milnor §10, Lemma 10.5 · p. 60

In $U_q$ the geodesics through $q$ are the orthogonal trajectories of the hypersurfaces $\{\exp_q(v) : \|v\| = \text{constant}\}$. The proof considers the surface $f(r, t) = \exp_q(r\,v(t))$ for a curve $v(t)$ of unit vectors and shows that $\langle\partial f/\partial r, \partial f/\partial t\rangle$ is independent of $r$, hence zero.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\varepsilon$ be a normal radius at $q \in N$ (V7.9) and regard $\exp_q$ as a map on the vector space $T_qN$. For $w, x \in T_qN$ with $\|w\| < \varepsilon$, $$\langle d(\exp_q)_w(w),\ d(\exp_q)_w(x)\rangle = \langle w, x\rangle;$$ in particular the radial velocity $d(\exp_q)_w(w)$ is orthogonal to $d(\exp_q)_w(x)$ when $x \perp w$. Moreover $d(\exp_q)_w$ is injective on $T_qN$, and $\|d(\exp_q)_{rw}(w)\| = \|w\|$ for $0 \le r \le 1$.

Milnor §10, proof of Theorem 10.4, p. 61

In the proof of Theorem 10.4, Milnor observes that for every $\delta > 0$ a path from $q$ to a point of the shell of radius $r$ contains a segment that joins the shells of radii $\delta$ and $r$ and lies between them; by Lemma 10.6 that segment has length $\ge r - \delta$, and letting $\delta \to 0$ gives length $\ge r$.

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\varepsilon$ be a normal radius at $q$ and $0 < s < \varepsilon$. If $c$ is an admissible path in $N$ on $[a, b]$ with $c(a) = q$ and $c(b)$ outside the open normal ball of radius $s$, there are $a \le t_1 < t_2 \le b$ with $c(t_1) = q$, $c(t) \in U_q \setminus \{q\}$ for $t_1 < t \le t_2$, $c(t)$ in the open normal ball for $t_1 \le t < t_2$, $\|G(c(t_2))\| = s$, and $L(c|[t_1, t_2]) \ge s$.

Theorem 10.4: short geodesics are shortest

stronger
paths on any parameter intervalin (i), admissible paths

Milnor §10, Theorem 10.4 · p. 59

Let $W$ and $\varepsilon$ be as in Lemma 10.3, let $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ be the geodesic of length $< \varepsilon$ joining two points of $W$, and let $\omega : [0, 1] \to M$ be any other piecewise smooth path joining the same two points. Then $\int_0^1\|d\gamma/dt\|\,dt \le \int_0^1\|d\omega/dt\|\,dt$, where equality can hold only if the point sets $\omega([0, 1])$ and $\gamma([0, 1])$ coincide. Thus $\gamma$ is the shortest path joining its end points. Proof on p. 61.

stronger
extends past both endsneeds the sharp equality case

Milnor §10, Corollary 10.7 · p. 61

If a path $\omega : [0, \ell] \to M$, parametrized by arc length, has length less than or equal to the length of any other path from $\omega(0)$ to $\omega(\ell)$, then $\omega$ is a geodesic. Then $c$ is a geodesic on $(0, \ell)$ (in particular smooth there, also at its break points), and $c$ agrees on $[0, \ell]$ with a geodesic defined on an open interval $(-\delta, \ell + \delta)$. On the way: being a geodesic is a local property, and a segment of $c$ inside a set of Lemma 10.3 agrees with a geodesic on an open set containing it.

The distance $\rho$

restated
values in $[0, \infty]$positivity is not clear: shell crossing

Milnor §10, p. 62

For $p, q \in M$, $\rho(p, q)$ is the greatest lower bound of the arc lengths of the piecewise smooth paths joining $p$ and $q$, and this "clearly" makes $M$ a metric space.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $p, q \in V$, $\rho(p, q) \in [0, \infty]$ is the infimum of the lengths of the piecewise smooth paths $c$ in $N$, on any $[a, b]$, with $c(a) = p$ and $c(b) = q$ ($\infty$ if there is none, as when $q \notin N$). Then $\rho(p, q) \le L(c|[a, b])$ for every such path, $\rho(p, p) = 0$ for $p \in N$, $\rho$ is symmetric and satisfies the triangle inequality; if $\varepsilon$ is a normal radius at $p$ and $0 < s < \varepsilon$, every point outside the open normal ball of radius $s$ about $p$ is at distance $\ge s$; and for $p, q \in N$, $\rho(p, q) = 0$ implies $p = q$. So $\rho$ is a metric on $N$ with values in $[0, \infty]$.

Metric balls and the topology

restated
neighbourhood bases at each pointsmall metric balls are normal balls

Milnor §10, p. 62

The compatibility of the metric $\rho$ with the usual topology of $M$ follows "easily" from Theorem 10.4.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\varepsilon$ be a normal radius at $p \in N$. For $v \in T_pN$ with $\|v\| < \varepsilon$, $\rho(p, \exp_pv) = \|v\|$; and for $0 < r \le \varepsilon$, $\rho(p, y) < r$ iff $y$ lies in the normal ball $\exp_p\{v \in T_pN : \|v\| < r\}$. Consequently, for every $p \in N$, the metric balls $\{y : \rho(p, y) < r\}$, $r > 0$, form a basis of the neighbourhoods of $p$ in $N$ for the topology of a subspace of $V$.

Continuity and finiteness of $\rho$; the metric space $(N, \rho)$

restated
continuity of $\rho$, used, never statedconnected means preconnected

Milnor §10, p. 62

Milnor says that $\rho$ "clearly" makes $M$ a metric space, compatible with its topology by Theorem 10.4; finiteness rests on the standing assumption that $M$ is connected (p. 55). The continuity of $\rho$ is never stated, but the proof of Theorem 10.9 uses it (p. 63: a point of the compact shell $S$ at minimum distance from $q$, and an equality at the supremum $t_0$ "by continuity").

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for all $p, q \in V$, $\|q - p\| \le \rho(p, q)$. The function $(x, y) \mapsto \rho(x, y)$, with values in $[0, \infty]$, is continuous on $N \times N$ (topology of a subspace of $V \times V$). If $N$ is (pre)connected, $\rho(p, q) < \infty$ for all $p, q \in N$. Hence $\rho$ makes $N$ an extended metric space whose topology is that of $N$, and, for connected $N$, a metric space with distance $\rho$ and the topology of $N$; these structures are given by name, since $N$ already carries the metric of $V$.

Metric and geodesic completeness

restated
open intervals, not closed segmentsthe equivalence glues geodesics

Milnor §10, pp. 58, 62 and 64

$M$ is geodesically complete if $\exp_q(v)$ is defined for all $q \in M$ and all $v \in TM_q$; this is "clearly" equivalent to the requirement that every geodesic segment $\gamma_0 : [a, b] \to M$ can be extended to an infinite geodesic $\gamma : \mathbb R \to M$ (p. 58, recalled p. 62). On p. 64: a subset of $M$ is bounded if it has finite diameter, and $M$ is complete as a metric space if every Cauchy sequence converges.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: $(N, \rho)$ is complete if every sequence in $N$ that is Cauchy for $\rho$ converges for $\rho$ to some point of $N$; for connected $N$ this is the completeness of the metric space of V7.21. A set $X \subseteq V$ is bounded if $\rho(x, y) \le d$ for all $x, y \in X$ and some real $d$ (a nonempty bounded set lies in $N$). $N$ is geodesically complete if $\exp_q(v)$ is defined for every $q \in N$ and $v \in T_qN$. If $\exp_q$ is defined on all of $T_qN$, then $t \mapsto \exp_q(tv)$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$ for every $v$; and $N$ is geodesically complete iff every geodesic on a nonempty open interval (or preconnected open set) is the restriction of a geodesic on $\mathbb R$.

Milnor uses, without stating them as results: that a geodesic is $t \mapsto \exp_q(tv)$ (p. 57); that geodesics can be continued (pp. 58, 62); and, in the proof of Corollary 10.10 (p. 64), that $\exp_p$ maps the disk of radius $d$ in $TM_p$ onto a compact set, which needs $\exp_p$ continuous on the whole disk. (iii) Geodesics $t \mapsto \exp_y(tw)$ on an open interval $I \ni 0$ continue, from the position and velocity at any $s \in I$, by the geodesic with those initial data. (iv) The domain of $\exp$ is open in $TN$, and $\exp$ is continuous on it; in particular, if $\exp_p$ is defined on all of $T_pN$, it is continuous there.

restated
a geodesic near $[a, b]$, not on it

Where $\exp_q(v)$ is defined it lies in $N$. If $v \in T_pN$, $t \mapsto \exp_p(tv)$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$ and $\rho(p, \exp_pv) = \|v\|$, then $t \mapsto \exp_p(tv)$ is a minimal geodesic on $[0, 1]$, of length $\|v\|$.

There is $w \in T_pN$ with $\|w\| = \delta$ and $\rho(p, q) = \delta + \rho(\exp_pw, q)$. (ii) Let $\gamma$ be a geodesic on $\mathbb R$ with $\|\gamma'(0)\| = 1$, $0 < t_0 < t_1$, and $\sigma$ a geodesic on an open (preconnected) set containing $[t_0, t_1]$ with $\|\sigma'(t_0)\| = 1$ and $\sigma(t_0) = \gamma(t_0)$. If $\rho(\gamma(0), \sigma(t_1)) \ge t_1$, i.e. the broken path ($\gamma$ on $[0, t_0]$, then $\sigma$), of length $t_1$, is minimal, then $\sigma(t_1) = \gamma(t_1)$.

Milnor §10, Corollary 10.10 · p. 64

If $M$ is geodesically complete, then every bounded subset of $M$ has compact closure; consequently $M$ is complete as a metric space. Proof: for $X$ of diameter $d$ and $p \in X$, $\exp_p$ maps the disk of radius $d$ in $TM_p$ onto a compact set which, by Theorem 10.9, contains $X$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) if $N$ is (pre)connected and $\exp_p$ is defined on all of $T_pN$ for some $p \in N$, every bounded $X \subseteq V$ (V7.22) has compact closure, contained in $N$. (ii) If every bounded set has compact closure contained in $N$, then $(N, \rho)$ is complete. (iii) Hence, if $N$ is connected and geodesically complete, every bounded set has compact closure in $N$, and $(N, \rho)$ is complete.

V7.30′

Familiar examples of geodesics: $\mathbb R^n$ and $S^n$

narrower
only $\mathbb R^n$ and $S^n$proved in Chapter 10uniqueness, not reflections

Milnor §10, pp. 65–66

In Euclidean space $\mathbb R^n$ the equations for a geodesic become $d^2x_i/dt^2 = 0$, whose solutions are the straight lines. The geodesics on $S^n$ are precisely the great circles, the intersections of $S^n$ with the planes through its centre: reflection in such a plane is an isometry fixing the great circle, hence fixing the unique minimal geodesic between two nearby points of it, and there is a great circle through any point in any direction. Antipodal points are joined by a continuum of minimal geodesics; any other two points by a unique minimal geodesic and an infinite family of non-minimal ones. Meridians of a surface of revolution are geodesics, and on a right circular cylinder the geodesics are the generating lines, the circles and the helices, two points being joined by infinitely many.

Proved in Lean

(i) On the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n \ge 1$, with the induced metric: for unit vectors $p \perp u$ and $L \in \mathbb R$, the great circle $c(t) = \cos(Lt)\,p + \sin(Lt)\,u$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$; and for any $p, q$, every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(S^n; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with such a great circle, with $L \ge 0$. For $q \ne \pm p$ the geodesics from $p$ to $q$ are, up to their values off $[0, 1]$, the arcs $\gamma_0, \gamma_1, \dots$ of V10.23, with strictly increasing energies: infinitely many geodesics. (ii) If every tangent space of $N \subseteq V$ is $V$ (an open subset of $V$, with the flat metric) and the segment from $p$ to $q$ lies in $N$, then $t \mapsto p + t(q - p)$ is a geodesic of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ and every geodesic of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ agrees with it on $[0, 1]$: the geodesics of $V$ are the straight lines.

The path space and its “tangent spaces”

restated
$\Omega$ has no manifold structure, here toopaths are maps on $\mathbb R$break points need not match

Milnor §11, p. 67

$\Omega(M; p, q)$ is the set of piecewise smooth paths $\omega : [0, 1] \to M$ from $p$ to $q$, each $\omega|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ of class $C^\infty$ for some subdivision. Milnor thinks of $\Omega$ as "something like an infinite dimensional manifold", to be topologized only in §16, and defines its "tangent space" $T\Omega_\omega$ as the vector space of piecewise smooth vector fields $W$ along $\omega$ with $W(0) = 0$ and $W(1) = 0$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric ($P_x$ the projection onto $T_xN$, extended by $P_x = 0$ off $N$): for $p, q \in V$, $\Omega(N; p, q)$ is the set of maps $\omega : \mathbb R \to V$ that are piecewise smooth on $[0, 1]$ (V7.11), with $\omega(t) \in N$ for $t \in [0, 1]$, $\omega(0) = p$ and $\omega(1) = q$. For a map $\omega$, $T\Omega_\omega$ is the real vector space of maps $W$ that are piecewise smooth on $[0, 1]$ and tangent along $\omega$ ($P_{\omega(t)}W(t) = W(t)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$), with $W(0) = W(1) = 0$; it depends only on $\omega$ on $[0, 1]$.

V8.2

Variations and variation fields

stronger
any open parameter set, any normed space“clearly” $W \in T\Omega_\omega$ proved

Milnor §11, p. 68

A variation of $\omega$ keeping the end points fixed is a map $\bar\alpha : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \to \Omega$ with $\bar\alpha(0) = \omega$ and a subdivision $0 = t_0 < \dots < t_k = 1$ such that $\alpha(u, t) = \bar\alpha(u)(t)$ is $C^\infty$ on each strip $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [t_{i-1}, t_i]$; an $n$-parameter variation replaces $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)$ by a neighbourhood of $0$ in $\mathbb R^n$. The variation vector field is $W_t = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$, and "clearly" $W \in T\Omega_\omega$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $P$ be a real normed space (Milnor's $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb R^n$) and $U \ni 0$ open in $P$. A map $\alpha(u, t)$ is a variation with break points $B$ (a finite set) if $\alpha(u, t) \in N$ for $u \in U$, $t \in [0, 1]$; $\alpha(u, 0)$ and $\alpha(u, 1)$ do not depend on $u \in U$; and $\alpha$ is $C^\infty$ on every closed strip $U \times [s, t]$, $0 \le s < t \le 1$, with no point of $B$ in $(s, t)$. Every $\alpha(u, \cdot)$ then lies in $\Omega(N; \omega(0), \omega(1))$, $\omega = \alpha(0, \cdot)$, and composing with a smooth map into $P$ sending $0$ into $U$ gives a variation again. For $P = \mathbb R$, $W_t = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$ lies in $T\Omega_\omega$, and every $\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(u, t)$ is tangent to $N$ at $\alpha(u, t)$.

V8.3

Lemma 11.A: every family of tangent fields comes from one variation

stronger
any number of parametersno completeness: uniform $\varepsilon$

Milnor §11, pp. 68 and 74

Given $W \in T\Omega_\omega$ there is a variation with $\bar\alpha(0) = \omega$ and $\frac{d\bar\alpha}{du}(0) = W$: "in fact one can set" $\bar\alpha(u)(t) = \exp_{\omega(t)}(uW_t)$ (p. 68). On p. 74, 2-parameter variations with prescribed variation fields $W_1$, $W_2$ are chosen without comment.

There are $\varepsilon > 0$ and a finite set $B$ such that $\alpha(u, t) = \exp_{\omega(t)}(\Lambda(t)u)$ is a variation with break points $B$ on the ball $\|u\| < \varepsilon$, with $\alpha(0, t) = \omega(t)$ and derivative $\Lambda(t)$ in $u$ at $u = 0$, for $t \in [0, 1]$. In particular every $W \in T\Omega_\omega$ is the variation field of $\exp_{\omega(t)}(uW_t)$, $|u| < \varepsilon$, and any $W_1, W_2 \in T\Omega_\omega$ are the variation fields of the 2-parameter variation $\exp_{\omega(t)}(u_1W_1(t) + u_2W_2(t))$.

Energy and length

Milnor §12, p. 70

For $\omega \in \Omega$ and $0 \le a < b \le 1$, the energy from $a$ to $b$ is $E_a^b(\omega) = \int_a^b\|d\omega/dt\|^2\,dt$, $E = E_0^1$, and $L_a^b$ is the arc length. By Schwarz's inequality $(L_a^b)^2 \le (b - a)E_a^b$, with equality if and only if $\|d\omega/dt\|$ is constant, that is, if and only if the parameter $t$ is proportional to arc length.

Proved in Lean

For a map $c$ into a real normed space and $a \le b$, $E_a^b(c) = \int_a^b\|c'(t)\|^2\,dt$, $E = E_0^1$, and $L_a^b(c)$ is the length of V7.11. If $c$ is piecewise smooth on $[a, b]$, then $(L_a^b(c))^2 \le (b - a)E_a^b(c)$, with equality iff $\|c'\|$ takes one and the same value at every point of $(a, b)$ where $c$ is differentiable. An admissible path of constant speed $k$ there has $E_a^b = k^2(b - a)$.

Velocity jumps, acceleration and the first variation

restated
the sum over all of $(0, 1)$

Milnor §12, p. 71

For $\omega \in \Omega$, Milnor writes $V_t = d\omega/dt$ for the velocity, $A_t = \frac{D}{dt}\frac{d\omega}{dt}$ for the acceleration, and $\Delta_tV = V_{t^+} - V_{t^-}$ for the discontinuity of the velocity at $t$, which is zero for all but finitely many $t$ in $(0, 1)$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a map $f$ into $V$, the jump $\Delta_tf' = f'(t^+) - f'(t^-)$ is the difference of the right and the left derivative of $f$ at $t$; it vanishes where $f$ is differentiable. Along a path $\omega$, $\frac{DX}{dt}(t) = P_{\omega(t)}X'(t)$, $V = \omega'$ and $A = \frac{D}{dt}V$. The first variation of $\omega$ in the direction $W$ is $-\sum_{0 < t < 1}\langle W_t, \Delta_tV\rangle - \int_0^1\langle W_t, A_t\rangle\,dt$, the sum being finite: for $\omega$ differentiable off a finite set $B$, it is the sum over the points of $B$ in $(0, 1)$. It depends only on $W$ on $[0, 1]$.

Calculus on closed strips

Milnor §§12–13, pp. 71–76

The book has no such statement. In the proofs of Theorems 12.2 and 13.1 Milnor differentiates under the integral sign, integrates by parts on each $[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ and adds up, and interchanges partial derivatives of a variation, which is smooth only on closed strips, all without comment.

Proved in Lean

For $F$ smooth on a closed strip $U \times [a, b]$, $U \subseteq \mathbb R$ open, $a < b$: the partial derivatives $\partial F/\partial u$, $\partial F/\partial t$ computed within the strip are smooth on it, are one-sided $t$-derivatives on the edges, and the mixed partials agree on the whole closed strip, edges included. If $F$ and $F'$ are continuous on the strip and $F'$ is the $u$-derivative of $F$ inside it, then $u \mapsto \int_a^bF(u, t)\,dt$ has derivative $\int_a^bF'(u_0, t)\,dt$ at every $u_0 \in U$, also for integrands that are $C^1$ only piece by piece. If $\int_s^tg = F^-(t) - F^+(s)$ on every piece $[s, t]$ of $[a, b]$ with break points $B$, then $\int_a^bg = F^-(b) - F^+(a) - \sum_{x \in B \cap (a, b)}(F^+(x) - F^-(x))$.

the iterated partial derivativeits existence is proved$E \circ \bar\alpha$ not assumed $C^2$

Milnor §13, Theorem 13.1 · p. 75

Let $\bar\alpha : U \to \Omega$ be a 2-parameter variation of the geodesic $\gamma$ with variation fields $W_i = \frac{\partial\bar\alpha}{\partial u_i}(0, 0)$, $i = 1, 2$. Then $$\frac12\frac{\partial^2E(\bar\alpha(u_1, u_2))}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0) = -\sum_t\Big\langle W_2(t), \Delta_t\frac{DW_1}{dt}\Big\rangle - \int_0^1\Big\langle W_2, \frac{D^2W_1}{dt^2} + R(V, W_1)V\Big\rangle\,dt.$$ It is introduced on p. 74 to show that $E_{**}$ is well defined, and proved on pp. 75–76 from 12.2, the vanishing of $\Delta_tV$ and $\frac{D}{dt}V$ along a geodesic, (13.2) and (13.3).

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for a path $\gamma$ with velocity $V$ and fields $W_1, W_2$ along it, let $\Phi(W_1, W_2)$ be the right side above, where $\Delta_t\frac{DW_1}{dt} = P_{\gamma(t)}(\Delta_tW_1')$ is the jump of $\frac{DW_1}{dt} = PW_1'$. Let $\gamma$ be a geodesic (V8.10) and $\alpha(u_1, u_2, t)$ a 2-parameter variation of $\gamma$ ($\alpha(0, 0, t) = \gamma(t)$ on $[0, 1]$) with variation fields $W_1, W_2$. Then $u_1 \mapsto \frac{\partial}{\partial u_2}E(\alpha(u_1, u_2, \cdot))|_{u_2 = 0}$ is differentiable at $u_1 = 0$, with derivative $2\Phi(W_1, W_2)$. Two 2-parameter variations of $\gamma$ whose variation fields agree on $[0, 1]$ give the same value.

The Hessian $E_{**}$

restated
defined by Milnor's formulaidentified with his definitiondefined at every path of $\Omega$

Milnor §13, p. 74

For a geodesic $\gamma$, the Hessian $E_{**} : T\Omega_\gamma \times T\Omega_\gamma \to \mathbb R$ of $E$ at $\gamma$ is defined by analogy with the Hessian $f_{**}$ of a function on a manifold: given $W_1, W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$, choose a 2-parameter variation with these variation fields and put $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = \frac{\partial^2E(\bar\alpha(u_1, u_2))}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0)$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 2\Phi(W_1, W_2)$ ($\Phi$ as in V8.13) is a bilinear form on $T\Omega_\gamma$, depending only on the values of the fields on $[0, 1]$. The variation fields of a 2-parameter variation of $\gamma$ lie in $T\Omega_\gamma$. If $\gamma$ is a geodesic, every 2-parameter variation of $\gamma$ with variation fields $W_1, W_2$ has $\frac{\partial^2E}{\partial u_1\partial u_2}(0, 0) = E_{**}(W_1, W_2)$ (in the sense of V8.13), and every pair $W_1, W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ arises (V8.3). So Milnor's definition is well defined and agrees with $E_{**}$.

Linear equations have global solutions (Lemma 14.A)

stronger
proved, not assertedany continuous coefficientsany complete normed space

Milnor §14, p. 77

The Jacobi equation, a linear second-order differential equation, has $2n$ linearly independent solutions, each of which is "defined throughout $\gamma$" and of class $C^\infty$; a Jacobi field is determined by its initial conditions $J(0)$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$. Milnor gives no proof.

Proved in Lean

Let $E$ be a complete real normed space and $t \mapsto A(t)$ a continuous map from $\mathbb R$ to the continuous linear maps $E \to E$. (i) For every $t_0 \in \mathbb R$ and $x_0 \in E$ the equation $x' = A(t)x$ has a solution on all of $\mathbb R$ with $x(t_0) = x_0$, and the solution with value $\xi$ at $s$ depends linearly on $\xi$. (ii) If $a < b$ and $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and solves the equation on $(a, b)$, then for every $s \in [a, b]$, end points included, $f$ agrees on $[a, b]$ with the solution whose value at $s$ is $f(s)$. (iii) If $A$ is $C^\infty$ on $[a, b]$ (one-sided derivatives at the ends) and $f'(t) = A(t)f(t)$ at every $t \in [a, b]$, then $f$ is $C^\infty$ on $[a, b]$.

V9.2

Jacobi fields and the Jacobi system

restated
no parallel frame: a system in $V \times V$along any smooth curveinitial values at any $s$

Milnor §14, p. 77

A vector field $J$ along a geodesic $\gamma$ is a Jacobi field if it satisfies the Jacobi differential equation $\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} + R(V, J)V = 0$, $V = d\gamma/dt$. In terms of orthonormal parallel fields $P_1, \dots, P_n$ along $\gamma$, writing $J = \sum f^iP_i$, it becomes a linear system with coefficients $\langle R(V, P_j)V, P_i\rangle$; a Jacobi field is completely determined by its initial conditions $J(0)$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric. A smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ is a map $\gamma : \mathbb R \to V$ that is $C^\infty$ on $[0, 1]$, with one-sided derivatives at the ends, and has values in $N$ there; every geodesic of $\Omega$ is one. A map $J$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ if it is $C^\infty$ on $[0, 1]$, tangent along $\gamma$, and $\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} + R(V, J)V = 0$ on $(0, 1)$, $D/dt$ the covariant derivative of V8.7. With $S = P'P - PP'$ and $K(t)v = R(V, P(t)v)V$, the Jacobi system is the linear system $J' = SJ + Y$, $Y' = SY - KJ$ for $(J, Y)$ in $V \times V$; its solution with any value at any time exists on $\mathbb R$. If $s \in [0, 1]$ and both initial values are tangent at $\gamma(s)$, both components stay tangent on $[0, 1]$, the first is a Jacobi field and the second its covariant derivative. Conversely every Jacobi field $J$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with the solution whose value at $s$ is $(J(s), \frac{DJ}{dt}(s))$; in particular $J(s) = 0$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(s) = 0$ force $J = 0$ on $[0, 1]$.

The space of Jacobi fields (Corollary 14.B)

isomorphism at every $s \in [0, 1]$along any smooth curve

Milnor §14, p. 77

The Jacobi equation has $2n$ linearly independent solutions, and a Jacobi field is completely determined by $J(0)$ and $\frac{DJ}{dt}(0)$.

Proved in Lean

For every $s \in [0, 1]$, $J \mapsto (J(s), \frac{DJ}{dt}(s))$ is a linear isomorphism $\mathcal J(\gamma) \to T_{\gamma(s)}N \times T_{\gamma(s)}N$: every pair of tangent vectors at $\gamma(s)$ is the value and covariant derivative at $s$ of exactly one field of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$; and $\dim\mathcal J(\gamma) = 2n$.

Conjugate points and their multiplicity

restated
parameters, as the footnote advises

Milnor §14, p. 77

For $a \ne b$, the points $p = \gamma(a)$ and $q = \gamma(b)$ are conjugate along $\gamma$ if there is a non-zero Jacobi field $J$ along $\gamma$ which vanishes for $t = a$ and $t = b$; the multiplicity of $p$ and $q$ as conjugate points is the dimension of the vector space of all such fields. A footnote warns that if $\gamma$ has self-intersections one should rather say that the parameter values $a$ and $b$ are conjugate.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$. Parameters $a$ and $b$ are conjugate along $\gamma$ if $a, b \in [0, 1]$, $a \ne b$, and some Jacobi field along $\gamma$ vanishes at $a$ and at $b$ without vanishing identically on $[0, 1]$. Their multiplicity is the dimension of the space of fields of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ vanishing at $a$ and $b$, finite by V9.3; for $a \ne b$ in $[0, 1]$ they are conjugate iff the multiplicity is positive.

Theorem 14.1: the null vectors of $E_{**}$ are the Jacobi fields

restated
jumps of $PW_1'$ vs. jumps of $W_1'$pieces joined by a local argument

Milnor §14, Theorem 14.1 · p. 78

A vector field $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ belongs to the null space of $E_{**}$ if and only if $W_1$ is a Jacobi field. Proof (pp. 78–79): a Jacobi field vanishing at the ends is null by the second variation formula; conversely, testing against $W_2 = f(t)(\frac{D^2W_1}{dt^2} + R(V, W_1)V)$, $f$ vanishing exactly at the break points, makes $W_1$ a Jacobi field on each piece, testing against a field with values $\Delta_{t_i}\frac{DW_1}{dt}$ at the break points removes the jumps, and the pieces "fit together" since a solution is determined by $W_1(t_i)$ and $\frac{DW_1}{dt}(t_i)$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be a geodesic (V8.10) and $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$. Then $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for every $W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ iff $W_1$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$; in particular such a $W_1$ is $C^\infty$ on all of $[0, 1]$. On the way: for a Jacobi field $J$ along any curve, $\Phi(J, Y) = 0$ for every field $Y$; for a null vector the Jacobi operator vanishes off the break points and every jump of $W_1'$ is tangent and zero; and for a smooth tangent field the Jacobi equation is a second-order equation in $V$.

Theorem 14.1: the null space and the nullity

restated
null space read on $[0, 1]$parameters $0$ and $1$ for $p$ and $q$

Milnor §14, Theorem 14.1, pp. 77–79

The null space of $E_{**}$ is the space of $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ with $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for all $W_2$, the nullity $\nu$ is its dimension, and $E_{**}$ is degenerate if $\nu > 0$ (pp. 77–78). Theorem 14.1 continues: hence $E_{**}$ is degenerate if and only if the end points $p$ and $q$ are conjugate along $\gamma$, and the nullity of $E_{**}$ equals their multiplicity as conjugate points. Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, the null space of $E_{**}$ is the space of the restrictions to $[0, 1]$, extended as constants, of the $W_1 \in T\Omega_\gamma$ with $E_{**}(W_1, W_2) = 0$ for all $W_2 \in T\Omega_\gamma$, and the nullity is its dimension. If $\gamma$ is a geodesic, the null space is the space of fields of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$ vanishing at $0$ and $1$; so the nullity is the multiplicity of $0$ and $1$ as conjugate parameters (V9.4), in particular finite, and it is positive iff $0$ and $1$ are conjugate along $\gamma$.

Remark 14.2: the nullity is less than $n$

Milnor §14, Remark 14.2 · p. 79

Actually the nullity satisfies $0 \le \nu < n$: the Jacobi fields vanishing for $t = 0$ form a space of dimension precisely $n$, and $J_t = tV_t$ is a Jacobi field vanishing for $t = 0$ but not for $t = 1$.

Proved in Lean

Hence, for a geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ and $n \ge 1$, the nullity of $E_{**}$ satisfies $\nu < n$.

Example 1: no conjugate points in a flat space

narrower
only codimension $0$: open sets of $V$flat tori are not coveredproved in Chapter 10

Milnor §14, Example 1 · p. 79

Suppose that $M$ is "flat", in the sense that the curvature tensor is identically zero. Then the Jacobi equation becomes $\frac{D^2J}{dt^2} = 0$; in parallel fields, $J = \sum f^iP_i$ with $\frac{d^2f^i}{dt^2} = 0$. Evidently a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ can have at most one zero; thus there are no conjugate points, and $E_{**}$ is non-degenerate.

Proved in Lean

Let $N \subseteq V$ be a slice submanifold every tangent space of which is all of $V$ (for instance an open subset of $V$, which is a slice submanifold of codimension $0$). Then the induced metric is flat ($R = 0$); along a curve in $N$ every Jacobi field is affine, $J(t) = J(0) + t(J(1) - J(0))$ on $[0, 1]$; no two parameters are conjugate along any curve in $N$; and at every geodesic of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ the index and the nullity of $E_{**}$ are $0$.

Example 2: antipodal points of $S^n$

stronger
every great circle, every parameterJacobi fields computed, no rotationsproved in Chapter 10

Milnor §14, Example 2, pp. 79–80

Suppose that $p$ and $q$ are antipodal points on the unit sphere $S^n$, and let $\gamma$ be a great circle arc from $p$ to $q$. Then $p$ and $q$ are conjugate with multiplicity $n - 1$, so the nullity of $E_{**}$ takes its largest possible value. Proof (p. 80): rotating the sphere about the axis through $p$ and $q$ gives variations through geodesics, whose variation fields are Jacobi fields vanishing at $p$ and $q$ (Lemma 14.3); rotating in $n - 1$ different directions gives $n - 1$ linearly independent ones.

Proved in Lean

On the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n \ge 1$, with the induced metric: for unit vectors $p \perp u$ and $L \in \mathbb R$, $c(t) = \cos(Lt)\,p + \sin(Lt)\,u$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$; for every $e \perp p, u$, $t \mapsto \sin(Lt)\,e$ is a Jacobi field along $c$; and for $L > 0$ and $0 < t \le 1$, the multiplicity of $0$ and $t$ as conjugate parameters along $c$ is $n - 1$ if $Lt$ is a multiple of $\pi$, and $0$ otherwise. For $L = \pi$, $t = 1$ this is Milnor's statement for the great semicircle from $p$ to $-p$.

Lemma 14.3: variations through geodesics give Jacobi fields

hypotheses explicit
Lemmas 8.7, 9.2 on a closed strip

Milnor §14, Lemma 14.3 · p. 80

A variation of $\gamma$ through geodesics, not necessarily keeping the end points fixed, is a $C^\infty$ map $\alpha : (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1] \to M$ with $\alpha(0, t) = \gamma(t)$ and each $\bar\alpha(u)$ a geodesic (p. 79). Lemma 14.3: its variation vector field $W(t) = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$. Proof: apply $\frac{D}{\partial u}$ to $\frac{D}{\partial t}\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial t} = 0$ and use Lemmas 9.2 and 8.7.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\alpha(u, t)$ be $C^\infty$ on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1]$ (one-sided derivatives along the edges $t = 0, 1$), with values in $N$ there, such that each $t \mapsto \alpha(u, t)$, $|u| < \varepsilon$, is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$. Then $W(t) = \frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t)$ is a Jacobi field along $\alpha(0, \cdot)$. Being a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ depends only on $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$.

Lemma 14.4: every Jacobi field comes from a variation through geodesics

as in the book
proved from initial datano minimal geodesics neededgeodesic segments extend past the ends

Milnor §14, Lemma 14.4 · p. 81

Every Jacobi field along a geodesic $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ may be obtained by a variation of $\gamma$ through geodesics. Proof: in a neighbourhood $U$ of $\gamma(0)$ where any two points are joined by a unique minimal geodesic depending differentiably on the end points, with $\gamma(t) \in U$ for $0 \le t \le \delta$, minimal geodesics between the points of two curves $a(u)$, $b(u)$ give Jacobi fields along $\gamma|[0, \delta]$ with arbitrary values at $0$ and $\delta$; so $J \mapsto (J(0), J(\delta))$ is onto, hence an isomorphism (both spaces have dimension $2n$); "using the compactness of $[0, 1]$", the geodesics extend over $[0, 1]$ for small $u$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) for $x_1 \in N$ and $R > 0$ there are an open $U \ni x_1$, an $h > 0$ and $\Phi$, $C^\infty$ on $U \times \{\|w\| < R\} \times (-h, h)$, with $\exp_y(tw) = \Phi(y, w, t)$ a geodesic on $(-h, h)$ for $y \in N \cap U$, $w \in T_yN$, $\|w\| < R$. (ii) A smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ that is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $t \mapsto \exp_{\gamma(0)}(tV(0))$, a geodesic on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$. (iii) Geodesics $t \mapsto \exp_{c(u)}(t\,w(u))$ with smooth initial data depend smoothly on $(u, t)$ over any compact time interval on which the one at $u = 0$ exists. (iv) Lemma 14.4: for such a $\gamma$ and a Jacobi field $J$ along it, there are $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\alpha$ satisfying the hypotheses of Lemma 14.3 (V9.8) on $(-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \times [0, 1]$, with $\alpha(0, t) = \gamma(t)$ and $\frac{\partial\alpha}{\partial u}(0, t) = J(t)$ for $t \in [0, 1]$.

V9.13

The index and the nullity of a bilinear form

restated
a supremum, possibly $\infty$finiteness is part of Theorem 15.1

Milnor §15, p. 83; §2, p. 5

The index $\lambda$ of $E_{**}$ is the maximum dimension of a subspace of $T\Omega_\gamma$ on which $E_{**}$ is negative definite (p. 83); for a bilinear functional on a vector space, the index and the nullity are defined in §2 (p. 5).

Proved in Lean

Let $B$ be a bilinear form on a real vector space $X$. $B$ is negative (positive) definite on a subspace $S$ if $B(x, x) < 0$ ($> 0$) for every $x \ne 0$ in $S$. The index of $B$ is the supremum, in $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\} \cup \{\infty\}$, of the dimensions of the finite-dimensional subspaces on which $B$ is negative definite; a finite index is the dimension of such a subspace. A linear map $L$ with $B'(Lx, Ly) = B(x, y)$ does not decrease the index, so an isomorphism carrying $B$ to $B'$ preserves it; on a finite-dimensional space the index is Mathlib's negative index of inertia of $x \mapsto B(x, x)$. The nullity is the dimension of $\{x : B(x, y) = 0 \text{ for all } y\}$; for $E_{**}$ the null space is read on $[0, 1]$ (V9.6).

V9.14

Linear algebra for the index theorem (Lemmas 15.A and 15.B)

not in the book
used without proof on pp. 85–87independence of the compound family

Milnor §15, pp. 85–87

The book has no such statements; on pp. 85–87 Milnor uses without proof: that the index and nullity of $E_{**}$ can be computed on a summand complementary to a perpendicular subspace on which $E_{**}$ is positive definite ("the proof is straightforward", Lemma 15.4); that definiteness of $H_\tau$ on a subspace persists for $H_{\tau'}$ near $H_\tau$; a positive definite subspace of dimension $ni - \lambda(\tau) - \nu$; and a compound matrix that is "certainly negative definite" for small $c$.

Proved in Lean

Let $B$ be a bilinear form on a real vector space $X$. (1) If $\dim X = m < \infty$, a negative definite and a positive definite subspace have dimensions adding up to at most $m$. (2) (Sylvester) If $\dim X = m$ and $B$ is symmetric with index $\lambda$ and nullity $\nu$, $B$ is positive definite on a subspace of dimension $m - \lambda - \nu$. (3) If $(B_\tau)$ is a family indexed by a topological space, $S \subseteq X$ is finite-dimensional, $\tau \mapsto B_\tau(x, y)$ is continuous at $\tau_0$ for $x, y \in S$, and $B_{\tau_0}$ is negative (positive) definite on $S$, so is $B_\tau$ for $\tau$ near $\tau_0$. (4) (Lemma 15.B) If $X = A \oplus C$ with $B(a, c) = B(c, a) = 0$ and $B$ positive definite on $C$, then $B$ and $B|A$ have the same index, and the null space of $B$ is that of $B|A$. (5) (the compound matrix) If $B$ is symmetric, $U : \mathbb R^\lambda \to X$ linear with $B(Ua, Ua) < 0$ for $a \ne 0$, and $J, Y : \mathbb R^\nu \to X$ linear with $B(Jb, Ua) = 0$, $B(Jb, Jb') = 0$ and $B(Jb, Yb') = 2\langle b, b'\rangle$, then the index of $B$ is at least $\lambda + \nu$.

Broken Jacobi fields and $T'$

for every $\tau \in (0, 1]$fields vanishing outside $[0, \tau]$

Milnor §15, pp. 83–84 and 86

$T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, t_1, \dots, t_k)$ is the space of vector fields $W$ along $\gamma$ vanishing at $0$ and $1$ such that each $W|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$: a finite-dimensional space of broken Jacobi fields (p. 83). $T'$ is the space of fields with $W(t_0) = W(t_1) = \dots = W(t_k) = 0$, and "it follows from §14.5" that the broken Jacobi field with given values at the $t_i$ exists and is unique (p. 84). For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $\gamma$ be a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$. For $\tau \in \mathbb R$, the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ are the fields of $T\Omega_\gamma$ vanishing outside $[0, \tau]$. Let $0 < \tau \le 1$ and $B$ be fine for $[0, \tau]$ (V9.16). A map is a broken Jacobi field on $[0, \tau]$ for $B$ if on each piece between consecutive points of $\{0\} \cup B \cup \{\tau\}$ it agrees with a field of $\mathcal J(\gamma)$. Milnor's $T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ is the space of fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ that are broken Jacobi fields, and $T'$ the fields along $\gamma|[0, \tau]$ vanishing at the points of $B$. $W \mapsto (W(b))_{b \in B}$ is a linear isomorphism from the broken Jacobi fields onto $\bigoplus_{b \in B}T_{\gamma(b)}N$.

Lemma 15.3: the splitting of $T\Omega_\gamma$

restated
for every $\tau \in (0, 1]$positivity from the Poincaré estimate

Milnor §15, Lemma 15.3 · p. 84

$T\Omega_\gamma = T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k) \oplus T'$, the two subspaces are mutually perpendicular with respect to $E_{**}$, and $E_{**}$ restricted to $T'$ is positive definite. (iii) $E_{**}(W, W) > 0$ for every $W \ne 0$ in $T'$.

Theorem 15.1: the Morse index theorem

stronger
parameters, as the footnote advisesthe identity along any smooth curvefiniteness of the set proved first

Milnor §15, Theorem 15.1 · p. 83

(Morse.) The index $\lambda$ of $E_{**}$ is equal to the number of points $\gamma(t)$, with $0 < t < 1$, such that $\gamma(t)$ is conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$, each such conjugate point being counted with its multiplicity. The index $\lambda$ is always finite. On p. 87 the theorem "clearly follows" from Assertions (2), (3) and (4).

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) let $\ell, \nu : \mathbb R \to \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ and $h_0 > 0$, with $\ell$ non-decreasing on $(0, 1]$, $\ell = 0$ on $(0, h_0]$, $\ell$ continuous from the left on $(0, 1]$, and $\ell(\tau') = \ell(\tau) + \nu(\tau)$ for $\tau' > \tau$ near $\tau$, $0 < \tau < 1$. Then $\nu(t) \ne 0$ for only finitely many $t \in (0, 1)$, and $\ell(1) = \sum_{0 < t < 1}\nu(t)$. (ii) For every smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$, $\nu(t) \ne 0$ for only finitely many $t \in (0, 1)$, and $\lambda(1) = \sum_{0 < t < 1}\nu(t)$. (iii) Theorem 15.1: for a geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, the parameters $t \in (0, 1)$ conjugate to $0$ along $\gamma$ form a finite set, and the index of $E_{**}$ on $T\Omega_\gamma$ (V9.13) is $\lambda = \sum_{0 < t < 1}\nu(t)$, each conjugate parameter counted with its multiplicity; in particular $\lambda$ is finite.

V10.1

Milnor's metric on $\Omega$

restated
a pseudometric on maps $\mathbb R \to V$Minkowski for the triangle inequality

Milnor §16, p. 88

The path space $\Omega$ can be topologized by the distance $d(\omega, \omega') = \max_t\rho(\omega(t), \omega'(t)) + \big[\int_0^1(\frac{ds}{dt} - \frac{ds'}{dt})^2dt\big]^{1/2}$, where $s(t)$ and $s'(t)$ are the arc lengths of $\omega$ and $\omega'$ from $0$ to $t$, and $\rho$ is the distance of §10.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric and its distance $\rho$ (V7.18): for $\omega, \eta \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, with speeds $\dot s_\omega = \|\omega'\|$ and $\dot s_\eta = \|\eta'\|$, $$d(\omega, \eta) = \sup_{0 \le t \le 1}\rho(\omega(t), \eta(t)) + \Big(\int_0^1(\dot s_\omega - \dot s_\eta)^2\,dt\Big)^{1/2}.$$ This is an extended pseudometric on $\Omega$ (values in $[0, \infty]$, symmetric, with the triangle inequality), and two paths that agree on $[0, 1]$ are at distance $0$. From now on $\Omega$ and its subsets carry the topology of $d$.

The last term of $d$ is added so that the energy $E_a^b(\omega) = \int_a^b(\frac{ds}{dt})^2dt$ is a continuous function on $\Omega$. Hence $\Omega^c = E^{-1}([0, c])$ is closed and $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c = E^{-1}([0, c))$ is open.

(ii) (Lemma 16.B) If $\omega_n \to \omega$ in $\Omega$, then for every $\epsilon > 0$ there is $\delta > 0$ with $E_a^b(\omega_n) < \epsilon$ for all $n$ and all $0 \le a \le b \le 1$ with $b - a < \delta$.

The ball $S$, subdivisions, and Milnor’s choices

restated
completeness only as compactness of $S$$\delta$ also below a normal radius

Milnor §16, pp. 88–89

$\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ is the space of paths $\omega$ with each $\omega|[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ a geodesic, and $\operatorname{Int}\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)^c = (\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c) \cap \Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ (p. 88). On p. 89: every $\omega \in \Omega^c$ lies in the ball $S$ of radius $\sqrt c$ about $p$, by $L^2 \le E \le c$; $S$ is compact since $M$ is complete; by 10.8 there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that two points of $S$ at distance less than $\varepsilon$ are joined by a unique geodesic of length less than $\varepsilon$, depending differentiably on them; and the subdivision is chosen with each $t_i - t_{i-1} < \varepsilon^2/c$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $c > 0$ and $S = \{x \in N : \rho(p, x) \le \sqrt c\}$. (i) Every $\omega \in \Omega$ with $E(\omega) \le c$ maps $[0, 1]$ into $S$. (ii) $S$ is compact if $N$ is closed in $V$, or connected and complete. (iii) For every compact $K \subseteq N$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that points of $K$ at distance $< \delta$ are joined as in Corollary 10.8 at the scale $\delta$, and $\delta$ is at most a normal radius at every point of $K$. (iv) Milnor's data (V10.3): $p, q \in N$, $c > 0$ with $S = \{x \in N : \rho(p, x) \le \sqrt c\}$ compact, a scale $\delta$ as in Corollary 10.8 for $K = S$ that is also at most a normal radius on $S$ (Milnor's $\varepsilon$), and a subdivision $0 = t_0 < \dots < t_{m+1} = 1$ with $c\,(t_{i+1} - t_i) < \delta^2$. If $p, q \in N$ and $S$ is compact, every subdivision of small enough mesh, and some subdivision into equal parts, is part of such data. (v) For Milnor's data, $B = \operatorname{Int}\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)^c$ is the set of $\omega \in \Omega$ with $E(\omega) < c$ that are geodesics on each $(t_i, t_{i+1})$, and $B^a = \{\omega \in B : E(\omega) \le a\}$.

Lemma 16.1: the manifold of broken geodesics

stronger
$\Omega^c \neq \emptyset$ not neededthe manifold is $U \subseteq N^m$ itself

Milnor §16, Lemma 16.1 · p. 88

Let $M$ be complete and $c > 0$ with $\Omega^c$ non-vacuous. Then for all sufficiently fine subdivisions $(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ of $[0, 1]$, $\operatorname{Int}\Omega(t_0, \dots, t_k)^c$ can be given the structure of a smooth finite dimensional manifold "in a natural way". Proof (p. 89): for a broken geodesic $(L_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\omega)^2 = (t_i - t_{i-1})E_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\omega < \varepsilon^2$, so each segment is determined by its end points, and $\omega$ by $(\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_{k-1})) \in M \times \dots \times M$; this is a homeomorphism onto an open subset of the product, whose differentiable structure is taken over.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: fix Milnor's data. For $y = (y_1, \dots, y_m) \in V^m$ put $x_0 = p$, $x_j = y_j$, $x_{m+1} = q$, and $E'(y) = \sum_{i=0}^m\rho(x_i, x_{i+1})^2/(t_{i+1} - t_i)$; let $U$ be the set of $y \in N^m$ with every $\rho(x_i, x_{i+1})$ finite and $E'(y) < c$. (i) $U = N^m \cap O$ for an open $O \subseteq V^m$, and every such set is a slice submanifold of $V^m$, with tangent space $T_{y_1}N \times \dots \times T_{y_m}N$. (ii) For $y \in U$, the broken geodesic $\omega_y$, on $[t_i, t_{i+1}]$ the short geodesic from $x_i$ to $x_{i+1}$ run at constant speed, lies in $B$, has break points $y$, and $E(\omega_y) = E'(y)$. (iii) Every $\omega \in B$ has its break points $y$ in $U$, and $\omega_y = \omega$ on $[0, 1]$. So $y \mapsto \omega_y$ and $\omega \mapsto (\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_m))$ are inverse bijections between $U$ and $B$, paths compared on $[0, 1]$.

(ii) For $a < c$, $\{y \in U : E'(y) \le a\}$ is compact.

Milnor’s deformation $r_u$ (Lemma 16.C)

restated
“easily verified” continuity provedshort geodesic for minimal geodesic

Milnor §16, p. 91

The retraction $r : \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c \to B$ sends $\omega$ to the broken geodesic which on each $[t_{i-1}, t_i]$ is the geodesic of length less than $\varepsilon$ from $\omega(t_{i-1})$ to $\omega(t_i)$; "clearly" $E(r(\omega)) \le E(\omega) < c$. For $t_{i-1} \le u \le t_i$, $r_u(\omega)$ is $r(\omega)$ on $[0, t_{i-1}]$, the minimal geodesic from $\omega(t_{i-1})$ to $\omega(u)$ on $[t_{i-1}, u]$, and $\omega$ on $[u, 1]$; $r_0$ is the identity, $r_1 = r$, and "it is easily verified" that $r_u(\omega)$ is continuous as a function of both variables.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for Milnor's data, $\omega \in \Omega$ with $E(\omega) < c$ and $t_i \le u \le t_{i+1}$, $r_u(\omega)$ is the broken geodesic of the break points of $\omega$ on $[0, t_i]$, the short geodesic from $\omega(t_i)$ to $\omega(u)$ at constant speed on $[t_i, u]$, and $\omega$ on $[u, 1]$; the formulas of neighbouring segments agree at $u = t_{i+1}$. On $[0, 1]$: $r_u(\omega) \in \Omega$, $E(r_u(\omega)) \le E(\omega)$, $r_0(\omega) = \omega$, $r_1(\omega) = \omega_y$ for the break points $y$ of $\omega$, and $r_u(\omega) = \omega$ for $\omega \in B$. Completed by $\omega$ off $[0, 1]$, and by $\omega$ itself when $u \notin [0, 1]$ or $E(\omega) \ge c$, $(u, \omega) \mapsto r_u(\omega)$ is a map $\mathbb R \times \Omega \to \Omega$, continuous on $[0, 1] \times \operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$.

Theorem 16.2: the critical points of $E'$

restated
$E'$ read through an ambient extensionvariations through broken geodesics

Milnor §16, Theorem 16.2, pp. 90–91

The critical points of $E'$ are precisely the critical points of $E$ in $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$, namely the unbroken geodesics from $p$ to $q$ of length less than $\sqrt c$. On p. 91: every geodesic is a broken geodesic, so every critical point of $E$ in $\operatorname{Int}\Omega^c$ lies in $B$, and with the first variation formula (12.2) "it is clear" that the critical points of $E'$ are the unbroken geodesics.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: fix Milnor's data. (i) Every tangent vector of a slice submanifold is the velocity of a smooth curve in it; for a smooth curve $y(u)$ in $U$, $(u, t) \mapsto \omega_{y(u)}(t)$ is a variation through broken geodesics, smooth on each strip, whose variation field takes the value $y'(0)_j$ at $t_j$. (ii) At $\gamma = \omega_y$ the first variation in the direction $X$ is $-\sum_j\langle X(t_j), \Delta_{t_j}\gamma'\rangle$. (iii) Let $O \subseteq V^m$ be open with $N^m \cap O \subseteq U$ and $F$ smooth on $V^m$ with $F = E'$ on $N^m \cap O$. Then $dF_y(w) = -2\sum_j\langle w_j, \Delta_{t_j}\omega_y'\rangle$ for tangent $w$, and $y$ is a critical point of $E' = F|(N^m \cap O)$ iff $\omega_y$ is an unbroken geodesic. (iv) Every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega$ with $E(\gamma) < c$ has its break points $y$ in $U$, $\omega_y = \gamma$ on $[0, 1]$, and $E'(y) = E(\gamma)$.

Lemma 15.4 for the subdivision of §16

hypotheses explicit
§15 subdivisions differ from §16 onesLemma 15.4 proved anew

Milnor §16, pp. 91–92

On pp. 91–92 the tangent space $TB_\gamma$ is identified with the space $T\Omega_\gamma(t_0, \dots, t_k)$ of broken Jacobi fields of §15, and the equality of the indices and nullities "is an immediate consequence of Lemma 15.4".

(ii) For every $i$, $t_i$ and $t_{i+1}$ are not conjugate along $\gamma$. (iv) For every $\omega \in \Omega$, $E'(\omega(t_1), \dots, \omega(t_m)) \le E(\omega)$; hence $E_{**}(W, W) \ge 0$ for $W \in T\Omega_\gamma$ vanishing at the $t_j$, and $> 0$ if moreover $W \ne 0$ vanishes off $[0, 1]$. (v) The fields of $T\Omega_\gamma$ vanishing off $[0, 1]$ are the direct sum of the broken Jacobi fields and of those vanishing at the $t_j$; the index of $E_{**}$ is that of its restriction to the broken Jacobi fields, and so is the nullity.

Milnor §16, Theorem 16.3 · p. 90

If $M$ is complete and $p, q \in M$ are not conjugate along any geodesic of length $\le \sqrt a$, then $\Omega^a$ has the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex, with one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each geodesic in $\Omega^a$ along which $E_{**}$ has index $\lambda$. The full path space $\Omega^*$ and the inclusion $i$

restated
$d^*$ measured with the norm of $V$

Milnor §17, p. 93

$\Omega^*$ is the space of all continuous paths $\omega : [0, 1] \to M$ from $p$ to $q$, with the compact-open topology, which can also be described as that induced by the metric $d^*(\omega, \omega') = \max_t\rho(\omega(t), \omega'(t))$. Since $d \ge d^*$, the natural map $i : \Omega \to \Omega^*$ is continuous.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: $\Omega^*(N; p, q)$ is the set of continuous maps $\omega : [0, 1] \to V$ with values in $N$, $\omega(0) = p$ and $\omega(1) = q$, as a subspace of the continuous maps $[0, 1] \to V$ with the uniform distance $d^*(\omega, \eta) = \max_t\|\omega(t) - \eta(t)\|$, whose topology is the compact-open topology. The map $i : \Omega \to \Omega^*$ restricts a path to $[0, 1]$; $d^*(i\omega, i\eta) \le d(\omega, \eta)$, so $i$ is continuous.

Convergence in $\Omega$ controls the velocities

not in the book
$L^2$ convergence of velocitiesmaps given by smooth formulas

The book has no such statement. It is what the continuity, for $d$, of the maps in the proof of Theorem 17.1 needs, since $d$ involves only the speeds $\frac{ds}{dt}$, not the velocities.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) if $\omega_j \to \omega$ in $(\Omega, d)$, along any filter, then $\int_0^1\|\omega_j' - \omega'\|^2dt \to 0$. (ii) Conversely, if $\omega_j(s) \to \omega(s)$ for every $s \in [0, 1]$ and $\int_0^1\|\omega_j' - \omega'\|^2dt \to 0$, then $\omega_j \to \omega$ in $\Omega$. (iii) If $\Phi$ is of class $C^1$ on an open set containing $F([a, b])$, $F_j \to F$ uniformly on $[a, b]$, and the velocities $F_j'$ are bounded in $L^2$ and converge to $F'$ in $L^2$, then $(\Phi \circ F_j)' \to (\Phi \circ F)'$ in $L^2$.
