Good balls and join systems (Lemma 17.B)

not in the book
convex balls, after Whiteheadone smooth join on each whole ballneeds $\exp$ smooth everywhere (V11.1)

Milnor §17, p. 93

In the proof of Theorem 17.1, Milnor takes a continuous $f : M \to [0, \infty)$ with each $f^{-1}([0, r])$ compact, and lets $\varepsilon_1(r) \le \infty$ be the largest number such that any two points of $f^{-1}([0, r])$ at distance less than $\varepsilon_1(r)$ are joined by a unique minimal geodesic which varies differentiably with the end points.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $y, z \in V$ the minimal join vector $v(y, z)$ is the unique $v \in T_yN$ with $\exp_y(v) = z$, $\rho(y, z) = \|v\|$ and Corollary 10.8 holding at some scale $\delta > \|v\|$ ($0$ if there is none), and $\sigma_{yz}(s) = \exp_y(s\,v(y, z))$. A good ball (V7.10′) is an open $O$ such that, for one $\delta > 0$, any two points of $N \cap O$ are at distance $< \delta$ and joined as in Corollary 10.8 at the scale $\delta$, and $\sigma_{yz}([0, 1]) \subseteq N \cap O$. (i) Small balls of $V$ about points of $N$ are good. (ii) Compact subsets of $N$ have a Lebesgue number for good balls. (iii) In a good ball $\sigma_{yz}$ is the unique minimal geodesic from $y$ to $z$, its sub-arcs are minimal, and $(y, z, s) \mapsto \sigma_{yz}(s)$ is locally the restriction of a smooth map. (iv) Local smooth extensions glue, by a partition of unity, into a join system: open good sets, convex for the joins, with one smooth map of $(y, z, s)$ on each and a Lebesgue number for every compact subset of $N$.

Milnor §17, p. 94

For $\omega \in \Omega^*$, $h(\omega)$ is the broken geodesic which agrees with $\omega$ at $t = 0, A(\omega), 2A(\omega), \dots, kA(\omega)$ and $1$; "an argument similar to that in §16" shows that $h \circ i$ and $i \circ h$ are homotopic to the identity maps of $\Omega$ and $\Omega^*$.

(ii) For $\omega \in Y_k$ let $b(\omega)$ be the broken geodesic with vertices $\omega(j2^{-k})$, joined by the joins, and $H(\omega, u)(s)$ the point at time $u$ of the join from $\omega(s)$ to $b(\omega)(s)$. Then $H$ is continuous from $Y_k \times [0, 1]$ to $Y_k$ for $d^*$ and from $X_k \times [0, 1]$ to $X_k$ for $d$, and $b$ is continuous from $(Y_k, d^*)$ to $(X_k, d)$. Theorem 17.1: $\Omega$ and $\Omega^*$ are homotopy equivalent

as in the book
the theorem is true; the proof is notproved by Theorem A on telescopesno completeness

Milnor §17, Theorem 17.1 · p. 93

Let $M$ be a Riemannian manifold, not necessarily complete, and $p, q \in M$. The natural map $i : \Omega \to \Omega^*$ is a homotopy equivalence between $\Omega$, with the metric $d$, and the space $\Omega^*$ of continuous paths. The proof (pp. 93–94) builds a continuous $A : \Omega^* \to (0, 1]$ and the broken geodesic $h(\omega)$ through $\omega(0), \omega(A), \dots, \omega(kA), \omega(1)$, asserts "Clearly $h$ is continuous", and shows $h \circ i \simeq \mathrm{id}$, $i \circ h \simeq \mathrm{id}$ by "an argument similar to that in §16".

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) if $Y$ is paracompact and Hausdorff, $B_0 \subseteq B_1 \subseteq \cdots$ are subsets of $Y$ such that every point lies in the interior of some $B_n$, and $g : X \to Y$ is continuous, then $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of the sets $g^{-1}(B_n)$. (ii) For every join system, $i : \Omega(N; p, q) \to \Omega^*(N; p, q)$ is a homotopy equivalence. (iii) Theorem 17.1: for every slice submanifold $N$ of $V$, complete or not, and all $p, q$, the inclusion $i : \Omega \to \Omega^*$, with Milnor's metric $d$ on $\Omega$ and the compact-open topology on $\Omega^*$, is a homotopy equivalence.

What differs

  • The statement is Milnor's, and it holds without completeness, as in the book. One step of the printed proof does not hold as we read it: "Clearly $h$ is continuous" fails for the metric $d$ (V10.19′), so what is verified is the theorem itself, by the exposition's modified proof.
  • The modified proof: the open sets $Y_k$ exhaust the metric, hence paracompact, space $\Omega^*$, which is therefore the homotopy direct limit of the $Y_k$ (Example 1 of the Appendix), and $\Omega$ is that of the $X_k = i^{-1}(Y_k)$ by (i); $i$ carries each $X_k$ into $Y_k$ by a homotopy equivalence (V10.18); Theorem A with no closedness hypothesis (VA.15) concludes.
  • $\Omega$ is not Hausdorff for $d$, so Example 1 is applied to $\Omega^*$ and pulled back by $i$; Theorem A is needed for open, not closed, pieces.

Milnor’s map $h$ is not continuous: a step in the proof of Theorem 17.1

not in the book
a step of the book that does not hold as we read itcounterexample on $M = \mathbb R$Theorem 17.1 itself is true (V10.19)

Milnor §17, proof of Theorem 17.1, p. 94

In the proof of Theorem 17.1, with $\varepsilon(\omega) = \varepsilon_2(\max_tf(\omega(t)))$ and $F(\omega, \alpha) = (\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\omega) + \max_{|t - t'| \le \alpha}\rho(\omega(t), \omega(t'))$, the zero $\alpha = 2A(\omega)$ of $F(\omega, \cdot)$ defines a continuous $A : \Omega^* \to (0, 1]$. Then $h(\omega) \in \Omega$ is the path which agrees with $\omega$ at $t = 0, A(\omega), 2A(\omega), \dots, kA(\omega)$, $k$ the largest integer $\le 1/A(\omega)$, and at $t = 1$, and is a geodesic on each intermediate interval. Milnor writes: "Clearly $h$ is continuous."

Proved in Lean

Take $M = \mathbb R$, $p = q = 0$ (so $\rho(x, y) = |x - y|$), Milnor's $f(x) = |x|$ and the admissible choice $\varepsilon_2 \equiv 1$; $2A(\omega)$ is the unique zero of $F(\omega, \cdot)$ in $[0, 1]$, as Milnor claims, and $h(\omega)$ is the piecewise affine interpolation of $\omega$ at $0, A, \dots, kA, 1$, a map $h : \Omega^* \to \Omega$. Let $\omega_\lambda(t) = \lambda((1 - t)^{1/3} - (1 - t))$ and $\lambda_* = \sqrt3/2$. Then $\omega_\lambda \to \omega_{\lambda_*}$ uniformly as $\lambda \to \lambda_*$, while $E(h(\omega_\lambda)) \to \infty$ as $\lambda \downarrow \lambda_*$ ($E(h(\omega_{\lambda_*})) \le 1$). Since $\sqrt E$ is $1$-Lipschitz for $d$, $d(h(\omega_\lambda), h(\omega_{\lambda_*})) \to \infty$: $h$ is not continuous at $\omega_{\lambda_*}$, hence not continuous.

What differs

  • This row records a step that does not hold as we read it, not a difference of formulation: Milnor's "Clearly $h$ is continuous" (p. 94) is false for the metric $d$ of $\Omega$, the topology in which Theorem 17.1 is stated; $h$ is continuous only for $d^*$. The counterexample is machine-checked for an admissible instance of Milnor's own choices: $f(x) = |x|$ and $\varepsilon_2 \equiv 1$, legitimate because on $\mathbb R$ any two points are joined by a unique minimal geodesic depending smoothly on them, so $\varepsilon_1 \equiv \infty$. Other constants $\varepsilon_2 \equiv c$ only rescale the family (a remark, not formalized).
  • The failure is in the $L^2$ term of $d$. When $1/A(\omega)$ crosses an integer, $h(\omega)$ acquires a new last segment of duration $\delta \to 0$ and length $\ell \to 0$, whose energy $\ell^2/\delta$ need not tend to $0$: here $\ell = \lambda(\delta^{1/3} - \delta)$ gives energy at least $\frac{27}{64}\delta^{-1/3}$. Milnor's $A$ is not at fault: $A(\omega_\lambda) = (1 - \lambda c_0)/2$, with $c_0 = 2\sqrt3/9$ the maximum of $(1 - t)^{1/3} - (1 - t)$ on $[0, 1]$, depends continuously on $\lambda$, and $k = 3$ for $\lambda_* \le \lambda \le \frac54\lambda_*$; what moves is the last break point $kA = 3A$, which leaves $1$.
  • Only this step fails: the theorem is proved by a different route (V10.17–V10.19), with subdivisions kept fixed on open sets and Theorem A of the Appendix. (Also, $A$ takes its values in $(0, \frac12]$, not $(0, 1]$.)

Relative cell complexes and the tower

restated
a tower up to homotopy sufficesno nested subdivisionsa relative Theorem 3.5

Milnor §17, p. 95

In the proof of Theorem 17.3: by 16.2 together with 3.3 and 3.7, each $\Omega^{a_i}$ has the homotopy type of $\Omega^{a_{i-1}}$ with finitely many cells attached; "just as in the proof of 3.5", one constructs CW-complexes $K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots$ with cells of the required description and homotopy equivalences $\Omega^{a_i} \to K_i$, each extending the previous one, forming a commutative diagram.

Proved in Lean

(i) A map $\iota : A \to X$ is, up to homotopy, the inclusion of $A$ with cells $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ attached if there are a space $K$ obtained from $A$ by attaching a $\lambda_1$-cell, then a $\lambda_2$-cell, and so on, with $j : A \to K$ the inclusion, and a homotopy equivalence $e : X \to K$ with $e \circ \iota \simeq j$. (ii) (Lemma 3.7, relative and iterated) such attachments transport along homotopy equivalences, and the notion is invariant under homotopy-commutative squares of homotopy equivalences. (iii) (relative Theorem 3.5) for $f = F|N$ on a slice submanifold, $F$ smooth, and levels $b \le a_0$, neither critical, with $N^{a_0}$ compact and the critical points in it non-degenerate, $N^b \to N^{a_0}$ is, up to homotopy, $N^b$ with one cell of dimension the index for each critical point in $f^{-1}(b, a_0)$, in order of value. (iv) (the tower) if $E : X \to \mathbb R$ is continuous, $a_n \to \infty$, $X^{a_0}$ has the homotopy type of a finite cell complex with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0$, and each $X^{a_n} \to X^{a_{n+1}}$ is, up to homotopy, the inclusion with cells $\mathrm{cells}_{n+1}$ attached, then $X$ has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0, \mathrm{cells}_1, \dots$ (VA.18).

The step from $\Omega^a$ to $\Omega^b$

restated
any finite number of critical valuesits own $B$ for each step

Milnor §17, p. 95

Each $\Omega^{a_i}$ has the homotopy type of $\Omega^{a_{i-1}}$ with one $\lambda$-cell attached for each geodesic of index $\lambda$ with energy in $(a_{i-1}, a_i)$, by 16.2 together with 3.3 and 3.7.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) for Milnor's data and levels $a \le b < c$, if neither $a$ nor $b$ is $E'(y)$ for a $y \in U$ with $\omega_y$ a geodesic, and every such $\omega_y$ with $E'(y) \le b$ has nullity $0$, then $\Omega^a \to \Omega^b$ is, up to homotopy, $\Omega^a$ with one cell of dimension the index of $E_{**}$ at $\omega_y$ for each such $y$ with $a < E'(y) < b$, attached in order of energy; the homotopy equivalences $\Omega^t \simeq \{y \in U : E'(y) \le t\}$ are all given by $\omega \mapsto$ the break points of $r_1(\omega)$, so they commute with the inclusions. (ii) Under nullity $0$, such geodesics are finitely many; if $N$ is closed in $V$, $p, q \in N$, and every geodesic in $\Omega$ has nullity $0$, the energies at most $b$ of the geodesics in $\Omega$ are finitely many, for every $b$. (iii) The index of a geodesic, as a natural number, equals the index of $E_{**}$ at it (finite by Theorem 15.1).

Theorem 17.3: the fundamental theorem of Morse theory

narrower
$N$ closed in $V$, for completenessfor $\Omega$, not $\Omega^*$countable cell complex: a telescope

Milnor §17, Theorem 17.3 · p. 95

If $M$ is complete and $p, q \in M$ are not conjugate along any geodesic, then $\Omega(M; p, q)$ (or $\Omega^*(M; p, q)$) has the homotopy type of a countable CW-complex which contains one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each geodesic from $p$ to $q$ of index $\lambda$. Proof: levels $a_0 < a_1 < \cdots$, not critical values, with "precisely one" critical value in each interval and $\Omega^{a_0}$ empty; the tower of CW-complexes; the direct limit map $\Omega \to K$ induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups, hence is a homotopy equivalence by Whitehead's theorem, $\Omega$ having the homotopy type of a CW-complex by 17.2. A different proof, not using 17.1, is referred to the Appendix.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric, closed in $V$, and $p, q \in N$: (i) suppose every geodesic in $\Omega$ has nullity $0$, and let $a_0 \le a_1 \le \cdots$ be levels tending to $\infty$, $a_0 < 0$, none of which is the energy of a geodesic. Then there are finite lists $\mathrm{geo}_0 = \emptyset, \mathrm{geo}_1, \dots$ of geodesics, $\mathrm{geo}_{n+1}$ containing exactly one representative of each geodesic with energy in $(a_n, a_{n+1})$, ordered by energy, such that $\Omega$, with Milnor's metric, has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex (VA.18) with one cell of dimension the index of $E_{**}$ at $\gamma$ for each entry $\gamma$. (ii) Theorem 17.3: if every geodesic in $\Omega$ has nullity $0$, there are finite lists of geodesics from $p$ to $q$ such that every geodesic agrees on $[0, 1]$ with exactly one entry of exactly one list, energies increase strictly from list to list and weakly within a list, and $\Omega(N; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex with one cell of dimension $\lambda$ for each entry of index $\lambda$. (iii) The same holds if $q$ is not conjugate to $p$ along any geodesic (V11.4).

V10.23

The geodesics from $p$ to $q$ on $S^n$, and their indices

restated
“$k$ occurrences” as $k\pi < L_k < (k+1)\pi$the list of geodesics shown complete

Milnor §17, pp. 95–96; §14, Example 2

For $q \ne p, p'$ on $S^n$, $p'$ the antipode of $p$, the geodesics from $p$ to $q$ are $\gamma_0$, the short great circle arc, $\gamma_1$, the long arc $pq'p'q$, $\gamma_2 = pqp'q'pq$, and so on. The index $\lambda(\gamma_k)$ is $k(n - 1)$: $k$ is the number of times $p$ or $p'$ occurs in the interior of $\gamma_k$, and each of these points is conjugate to $p$ with multiplicity $n - 1$ (Example 2 of §14).

Proved in Lean

On the unit sphere $S^n \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+1}$, $n \ge 1$: (i) for unit $p \perp u$ and $L \in \mathbb R$, $c(t) = \cos(Lt)\,p + \sin(Lt)\,u$ is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$ of energy $L^2$ on $[0, 1]$, and every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(S^n; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with such a $c$, $L \ge 0$. (ii) The conjugate parameters along $c$ are as in V9.7″. (iii) Let $q \ne \pm p$, $\theta \in (0, \pi)$ the angle between $p$ and $q$, $u \perp p$ the unit vector with $q = \cos\theta\,p + \sin\theta\,u$; let $\gamma_{2j}$ be the great circle along $u$ with $L_{2j} = \theta + 2\pi j$, and $\gamma_{2j+1}$ the one along $-u$ with $L_{2j+1} = 2\pi(j + 1) - \theta$. These are geodesics in $\Omega(S^n; p, q)$ with $E(\gamma_k) = L_k^2$ and $k\pi < L_k < (k + 1)\pi$; every geodesic in $\Omega(S^n; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with some $\gamma_k$; $q$ is not conjugate to $p$ along any geodesic; and the index of $E_{**}$ at $\gamma_k$, and at every geodesic that agrees with it on $[0, 1]$, is $k(n - 1)$.

Milnor §17, Corollary 17.4 · p. 96

The loop space $\Omega(S^n)$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex with one cell each in the dimensions $0, n - 1, 2(n - 1), 3(n - 1), \dots$. It is derived from Theorem 17.3 and the example of the geodesics from $p$ to a point $q \ne p, p'$.

Proved in Lean

(i) Let $N \subseteq V$ be closed in $V$, $p, q \in N$, every geodesic in $\Omega$ of nullity $0$, and suppose the geodesics in $\Omega$ are, up to their values off $[0, 1]$, a sequence $g_0, g_1, \dots$ with strictly increasing energies tending to $\infty$, every geodesic agreeing with $g_k$ on $[0, 1]$ having index $d_k$. Then $\Omega$ has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex with one cell of dimension $d_k$ at stage $k + 1$. (ii) Corollary 17.4: for $n \ge 2$ and $p, q \in S^n$ with $q \ne p$ and $q \ne -p$, the path space $\Omega(S^n; p, q)$, with Milnor's metric, has the homotopy type of the countable cell complex with one cell in each of the dimensions $0, n - 1, 2(n - 1), \dots$, attached in this order.

restated
filtration by energy, not cellular homologycoefficients in a field

Milnor §17, p. 96

For $n > 2$, the homology of $\Omega(S^n)$ "can be computed immediately" from the cell structure of Corollary 17.4.

Proved in Lean

Homology is singular homology with coefficients in a field $\Bbbk$, and $b_i = \dim_\Bbbk H_i$. (i) Let $A_0 \subseteq A_1 \subseteq \cdots$ be subsets of a space $X$ such that every compact subset of $X$ lies in some $A_k$. If $H_j(A_k, A_{k_0}) = 0$ for all $k \ge k_0$, then $H_j(X, A_{k_0}) = 0$; and if the steps $H_*(A_{k+1}, A_k)$ vanish in degrees $i$ and $i + 1$ for all $k \ge k_0$, then $b_i(X) = \dim H_i(A_{k_0})$. (ii) For Milnor's data and levels $a \le b < c$, neither the energy of a geodesic, with at most one energy of a geodesic in $(a, b)$ and every geodesic of energy at most $b$ of nullity $0$, $H_j(\Omega^b, \Omega^a)$ is finite-dimensional, of dimension the number of geodesics with energy in $(a, b)$ and index $j$. (iii) In the situation of V10.24 (i) with $d_k = kr$, $r \ge 2$, $b_i(\Omega) = 1$ when $r$ divides $i$ and $0$ otherwise.

Corollary 17.5 needs completeness

not in the book
punctured space: a counterexamplecompleteness is a missing hypothesis

Milnor §17, Corollary 17.5 · p. 96

Corollary 17.5: if $M$ has the homotopy type of $S^n$, $n > 2$, then any two non-conjugate points of $M$ are joined by infinitely many geodesics. Completeness is not among its hypotheses, although the proof rests on Theorem 17.3, which assumes it; the Remark that follows (p. 97) assumes it.

Proved in Lean

(i) An open subset of $V$ is a slice submanifold of codimension $0$, every tangent space being $V$. (ii) If every tangent space of $N$ is $V$, the induced metric is flat; every geodesic in $\Omega(N; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with the segment $t \mapsto p + t(q - p)$; no two parameters are conjugate along a curve in $N$, and every geodesic has index $0$ and nullity $0$; and if the segment from $p$ to $q$ lies in $N$, it is the unique geodesic in $\Omega(N; p, q)$ up to values off $[0, 1]$. (iii) For $n \ge 1$, $N = \mathbb R^{n+1} \setminus \{0\}$ with the induced metric is homotopy equivalent to $S^n$ and path-connected; it is neither closed in $\mathbb R^{n+1}$ nor geodesically complete; no point of $N$ is conjugate to another along any geodesic; and there are $p \ne q$ in $N$ joined by exactly one geodesic.

V11.1

$\exp$ is smooth on its whole domain

stronger

Milnor §18, p. 98

A critical point is defined for a smooth map between manifolds of the same dimension and applied to $\exp = \exp_p : TM_p \to M$, so $\exp_p$ is treated as smooth on all of $TM_p$. $M$ is assumed complete so that $\exp$ is everywhere defined, "although this assumption could easily be eliminated".

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) let $E$ be a real normed space, $U_0 \subseteq E$ open, $u_0 \in U_0$, and $c, w$ of class $C^\infty$ on $U_0$ with $c(u) \in N$, $w(u) \in T_{c(u)}N$. If $t \mapsto \exp_{c(u_0)}(t\,w(u_0))$ is a geodesic on $(-\delta, B + \delta)$, $B \ge 0$, there are $\varepsilon, \eta > 0$ such that every $t \mapsto \exp_{c(u)}(t\,w(u))$ with $\|u - u_0\| < \varepsilon$ is a geodesic on $(-\eta, B + \eta)$ and $(u, t) \mapsto \exp_{c(u)}(t\,w(u))$ is $C^\infty$ there. (ii) Every point of $N$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ in $V$ with a $C^\infty$ retraction $U \to N$. (iii) The domain of $\exp$ lies in $TN$, contains $(y, w)$ as soon as $t \mapsto \exp_y(tw)$ is a geodesic on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$, and equals $TN \cap O'$ for an open $O' \subseteq V \times V$; near each of its points $\exp$ is the restriction of a $C^\infty$ map on an open set of $V \times V$, and $(q, v) \mapsto \exp_q(v)$ is $C^\infty$ on it as a map on the manifold $TN$.

V11.2

$\exp_q$, its derivative, and critical points of $\exp_q$

Milnor §18, p. 98

A smooth map $f : N \to M$ between manifolds of the same dimension is critical at $x$ if $f_* : TN_x \to TM_{f(x)}$ is not one-to-one. This is applied to $\exp = \exp_p : TM_p \to M$, with $X \in T(TM_p)_v$ the tangent space at $v$ of $TM_p$ "considered as a manifold"; $\gamma_v$ is the geodesic $t \mapsto \exp(tv)$ from $p$ to $\exp v$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $q \in N$ let $\mathcal D_q \subseteq T_qN$ be the set of $v$ with $(q, v)$ in the domain of $\exp$. For $v \in \mathcal D_q$, $\gamma_v(t) = \exp_q(tv)$ is a geodesic on an open interval containing $[0, 1]$ and a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$. If $N$ is geodesically complete, $\mathcal D_q = T_qN$.

V11.3

Theorem 18.1: conjugate points are critical values of $\exp$

stronger
multiplicity $= \dim\ker d(\exp_q)_v$no completenessneeds $\exp$ smooth (V11.1)

Milnor §18, Theorem 18.1 · p. 98

The point $q = \exp v$ is conjugate to $p$ along the geodesic $\gamma_v$ from $p$ to $\exp v$ if and only if the mapping $\exp$ is critical at $v$. Proof (pp. 98–99): if $\exp_*X = 0$ with $X \ne 0$, the variation $\alpha(u, t) = \exp tv(u)$ through geodesics, for a path $v(u)$ with $v(0) = v$ and $\frac{dv}{du}(0) = X$, has a variation field $W$ with $W(0) = 0$, $W(1) = \exp_*X = 0$ and $\frac{DW}{dt}(0) \ne 0$; conversely, if $\exp_*$ is non-singular at $v$, independent $X_1, \dots, X_n$ give $n$ Jacobi fields vanishing at $p$ with independent values at $\exp v$, and "clearly" no non-trivial Jacobi field vanishes at both ends.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $q \in N$ and $v \in \mathcal D_q$ (V11.2). For $X \in T_qN$ let $W_X(t) = t\,d(\exp_q)_{tv}(X)$ on $[0, 1]$, constant off $[0, 1]$. (i) $X \mapsto W_X$ is linear and each $W_X$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma_v$ with $W_X(0) = 0$, $\frac{DW_X}{dt}(0) = X$ and $W_X(1) = d(\exp_q)_v(X)$. (ii) $X \mapsto W_X$ is injective, and every Jacobi field along $\gamma_v$ vanishing at $0$ is a $W_X$. (iii) The Jacobi fields vanishing at $0$ and $1$ are the $W_X$ with $X \in \ker d(\exp_q)_v$, so the multiplicity of the conjugate parameters $0$ and $1$ is $\dim\ker d(\exp_q)_v$. (iv) Theorem 18.1: $0$ and $1$ are conjugate along $\gamma_v$ iff $\exp_q$ is critical at $v$.

V11.4

The conjugate locus is the set of critical values of $\exp_p$

not in the book
every geodesic from $p$ is radialthe conjugate locus named

Milnor §18, p. 99

The book has no such statement. Milnor says that Corollary 18.2 "follows immediately from 18.1 together with Sard's theorem (6.1)", which needs every point conjugate to $p$ along some geodesic to be a critical value of $\exp_p$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $p \in V$, the conjugate locus $C(p)$ is the set of $q$ for which there is a geodesic $\gamma$ from $p$ (a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ that is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$, $\gamma(0) = p$) with $\gamma(1) = q$ along which $0$ and $1$ are conjugate. Let $p \in N$. For every geodesic $\gamma$ from $p$, its initial velocity $v$ lies in $\mathcal D_p$, $\exp_p(v) = \gamma(1)$, and $0$ and $1$ are conjugate along $\gamma$ iff $\exp_p$ is critical at $v$. Hence $C(p) = \exp_p(\{v \in \mathcal D_p : \exp_p \text{ critical at } v\})$, the set of critical values of $\exp_p$; if $N$ is geodesically complete, $\mathcal D_p = T_pN$.

Milnor §19, Lemma 19.1 · p. 100

Suppose that the sectional curvature of $M$ is everywhere $\le 0$, i.e. $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$ for every pair of vectors $A, B$ in $TM_p$ and every $p$. Then no two points of $M$ are conjugate along any geodesic. Proof: $\langle\frac{D^2J}{dt^2}, J\rangle = -\langle R(V, J)V, J\rangle \ge 0$, so $\langle\frac{DJ}{dt}, J\rangle$ is monotonically increasing, strictly so unless $\frac{DJ}{dt} = 0$; if $J(0) = J(t_0) = 0$ it vanishes on $[0, t_0]$, so $J(0) = \frac{DJ}{dt}(0) = 0$ and $J \equiv 0$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: $N$ has non-positive curvature if $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$ for all $A, B \in T_qN$ and all $q \in N$; equivalently, every sectional curvature of $N$ is $\le 0$. (i) For a smooth curve $\gamma$ in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ and a Jacobi field $J$ along it, $\frac{d}{dt}\langle\frac{DJ}{dt}, J\rangle = \|\frac{DJ}{dt}\|^2 - \langle R(V, J)V, J\rangle$ on $(0, 1)$. (ii) If $N$ has non-positive curvature and $\gamma$ is a smooth curve in $N$ on $[0, 1]$ which is a geodesic on $(0, 1)$, a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ vanishing at two parameters $a < b$ of $[0, 1]$ vanishes on $[0, 1]$: no two parameters are conjugate along $\gamma$.

The Ricci tensor and Milnor’s Assertion

as in the book

Milnor §19, p. 104

Definition: the Ricci tensor at a point $p$ of a Riemannian manifold is the bilinear pairing $K : TM_p \times TM_p \to \mathbb R$, $K(U_1, U_2)$ the trace of the linear transformation $W \mapsto R(U_1, W)U_2$ of $TM_p$; "it follows easily from 9.3 that $K$ is symmetric". Assertion: for an orthonormal basis $U_1, \dots, U_n$ of $TM_p$, $K(U_n, U_n)$ is the sum of the sectional curvatures $\langle R(U_n, U_i)U_n, U_i\rangle$, $i = 1, \dots, n - 1$, because the $n$-th diagonal term of the matrix $(\langle R(U_n, U_i)U_n, U_j\rangle)$ is zero.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: for $q \in N$ and $U_1, U_2 \in T_qN$, $K(U_1, U_2)$ is the trace of $W \mapsto R(U_1, W)U_2$ on $T_qN$. For an orthonormal basis $E_1, \dots, E_n$ of $T_qN$, $K(U_1, U_2) = \sum_i\langle R(U_1, E_i)U_2, E_i\rangle$, and $K(U_1, U_2) = K(U_2, U_1)$. Assertion: for an orthonormal basis $U_1, \dots, U_n$, $K(U_n, U_n) = \sum_{i \ne n}\langle R(U_n, U_i)U_n, U_i\rangle$.

Milnor §19, proof of Theorem 19.4, p. 104

In the proof of Theorem 19.4: for a geodesic $\gamma : [0, 1] \to M$ of length $L$, choose parallel vector fields $P_1, \dots, P_n$ along $\gamma$ which are orthonormal at one point, and hence everywhere, with $P_n$ pointing along $\gamma$, so that $V = \frac{d\gamma}{dt} = LP_n$ and $\frac{DP_i}{dt} = 0$.

(ii) If $L > 0$, there are such $c$ and $V$ and $n - 1$ parallel unit fields $P_1, \dots, P_{n-1}$ along $c$ such that, for every $r$ for which $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$, $\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\langle R(V, P_i)V, P_i\rangle \ge L^2(n - 1)/r^2$ at every $t$.

The test fields $\sin(\pi t)P_i(t)$

restated
$\cos^2$ in place of $\sin^2$, same integral$n \ge 2$

Milnor §19, proof of Theorem 19.4, p. 105

With $W_i(t) = (\sin\pi t)P_i(t)$, $\frac12E_{**}(W_i, W_i) = -\int_0^1\langle W_i, \frac{D^2W_i}{dt^2} + R(V, W_i)V\rangle\,dt = \int_0^1(\sin\pi t)^2(\pi^2 - L^2\langle R(P_n, P_i)P_n, P_i\rangle)\,dt$. Summing for $i = 1, \dots, n - 1$ gives $\int_0^1(\sin\pi t)^2((n - 1)\pi^2 - L^2K(P_n, P_n))\,dt$, which is negative if $K(P_n, P_n) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ and $L > \pi r$; hence $E_{**}(W_i, W_i) < 0$ for some $i$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ agree on $[0, 1]$ with a $C^\infty$ curve $c : \mathbb R \to N$, $P$ a parallel unit field along $c$, and $V$ a field equal to $\gamma'$ on $(0, 1)$. Then $W(t) = \sin(\pi t)P(t)$ lies in $T\Omega_\gamma$ and $\frac12E_{**}(W, W) = \int_0^1(\pi^2\cos^2(\pi t) - \sin^2(\pi t)\langle R(V, P)V, P\rangle)\,dt$. (ii) If $n \ge 2$, $r > 0$, $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$, and $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ is a geodesic of length $> \pi r$, then $E_{**}(X, X) < 0$ for some $X \in T\Omega_\gamma$.

Theorem 19.4 (Myers)

$n \ge 2$, which the book omitsdoes not hold as printed for $n = 1$

Milnor §19, Theorem 19.4 · p. 104

(Myers.) Suppose that the Ricci curvature $K$ satisfies $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit vector $U$ at every point of $M$, where $r$ is a positive constant. Then every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ of length $> \pi r$ has a parameter $t \in (0, 1)$ conjugate to $0$, and is not minimal: some path of $\Omega(N; p, q)$ is shorter (V8.6).

Corollary 19.5: compactness and diameter

hypotheses explicit
connectedness, for minimal geodesics$n \ge 2$ forced by $(n - 1)/r^2 > 0$

Milnor §19, Corollary 19.5 · p. 105

If $M$ is complete, and $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2 > 0$ for all unit vectors $U$, then $M$ is compact, with diameter $\le \pi r$. Proof: a minimal geodesic from $p$ to $q$ has length $\le \pi r$, and closed bounded sets in a complete manifold are compact.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: a minimal geodesic on $[0, 1]$ (V7.24) is a geodesic of $\Omega(N; \gamma(0), \gamma(1))$ minimal in the sense of V8.6. Let $N$ be (pre)connected, $(N, \rho)$ complete, $r > 0$ with $(n - 1)/r^2 > 0$, and $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$. Then $\rho(p, q) \le \pi r$ for all $p, q \in N$, and $N$ is compact.

Milnor §19, proof of Theorem 19.6, p. 106

For a geodesic of length $> k\pi r$, "a similar argument" gives, for each $i = 1, \dots, k$, a vector field $X_i$ along $\gamma$ which vanishes outside the interval $(\frac{i-1}k, \frac ik)$ and has $E_{**}(X_i, X_i) < 0$; "clearly" $E_{**}(X_i, X_j) = 0$ for $i \ne j$.

The field $X$ equal to $\sin(\kappa(t - a))P(t)$, $\kappa = \pi/(b - a)$, on $[a, b]$ and to $0$ elsewhere lies in $T\Omega_\gamma$, and if $\|P\| = 1$, $\frac12E_{**}(X, X) = \int_a^b(\kappa^2\cos^2(\kappa(t - a)) - \sin^2(\kappa(t - a))\langle R(V, P)V, P\rangle)\,dt$. Two such fields on $[a, b]$ and $[a', b']$ with $b \le a'$ have $E_{**}(X, X') = 0$. If $n \ge 2$, $r > 0$, the $P_i$ are as in V11.10 (ii) and $L(\gamma)(b - a) > \pi r$, the field built on $[a, b]$ from some $P_i$ has $E_{**}(X, X) < 0$.

Theorem 19.6: the index estimate

hypotheses explicit
continuity of $K(U, U)$ proved$n \ge 2$the $X_i$ independent: disjoint supports

Milnor §19, proof of Theorem 19.6, p. 106

Since the space of all unit vectors $U$ on the compact $M$ is compact, the continuous function $K(U, U) > 0$ takes on a minimum, which can be denoted by $(n - 1)/r^2 > 0$. Then every geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(M; p, q)$ of length $> \pi r$ has index $\lambda \ge 1$; more generally one of length $> k\pi r$ has index $\lambda \ge k$, since $X_1, \dots, X_k$ span a $k$-dimensional subspace of $T\Omega_\gamma$ on which $E_{**}$ is negative definite.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) if $N$ is compact, $n = \dim N \ge 2$, and the Ricci tensor is positive definite at every point, there is $r > 0$ with $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$. (ii) Let $n \ge 2$, $r > 0$ and $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$; let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be a geodesic and $k \ge 0$ an integer. If $L(\gamma) > k\pi r$, the index of $E_{**}$ at $\gamma$ is at least $k$, and the parameters $t \in (0, 1)$ conjugate to $0$, counted with multiplicity, number at least $k$. Equivalently, a geodesic of index $< k$ has length $\le k\pi r$.

Theorem 19.2 (Cartan–Hadamard)

as in the book
proved through the covering $\exp_p$the argument runs in reverse order

Milnor §19, Theorem 19.2 · p. 102

(Cartan.) Suppose that $M$ is a simply connected, complete Riemannian manifold, and that the sectional curvature $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle$ is everywhere $\le 0$. Then any two points of $M$ are joined by a unique geodesic. Furthermore, $M$ is diffeomorphic to the Euclidean space $\mathbb R^n$. Proof (pp. 102–103): by the index theorem and 17.3, $\Omega(M; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a $0$-dimensional complex with one vertex for each geodesic; it is connected since $M$ is simply connected, so there is precisely one geodesic from $p$ to $q$. Therefore $\exp_p : TM_p \to M$ is one-one and onto; by 18.1 it is non-critical, hence locally a diffeomorphism, hence a global diffeomorphism.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $N$ be geodesically complete (for instance closed in $V$), simply connected (as a topological space, with the topology of $V$), and of non-positive curvature. Then any two points $p, q \in N$ are joined by a geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$, and every geodesic in $\Omega(N; p, q)$ agrees with $\gamma$ on $[0, 1]$; and $N$ is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$, $n = \dim N$, for its manifold structure as a slice submanifold. More precisely, $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ is itself a diffeomorphism: it is a covering map (V11.19), injective because $N$ is simply connected, and onto by the Hopf–Rinow theorem.

  • The statement is Milnor's. The order of the argument is reversed: Milnor deduces the uniqueness of geodesics from the connectedness of the path space and then the injectivity of $\exp_p$; here the covering $\exp_p$ (V11.19) gives injectivity directly (the image of a segment of $T_pN$ with both ends over one point is a null-homotopic loop, whose lift is closed), and uniqueness follows. The path space in non-positive curvature

stronger
simply connected or nota discrete space, through the coveringcontractible when simply connected

Milnor §19, proof of Theorem 19.2, p. 102

In the proof of Theorem 19.2: since every geodesic from $p$ to $q$ has index $0$, Theorem 17.3 asserts that the path space $\Omega(M; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a $0$-dimensional CW-complex, with one vertex for each geodesic. The hypothesis that $M$ is simply connected implies that $\Omega(M; p, q)$ is connected, and a connected $0$-dimensional CW-complex must consist of a single point.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric, of non-positive curvature: (i) if $N$ is closed in $V$ and $p, q \in N$, $\Omega(N; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a countable cell complex (VA.18) all of whose cells are $0$-cells, one for each geodesic from $p$ to $q$ (Theorem 17.3 with all indices $0$). (ii) If $N$ is geodesically complete, the fibre of $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ over $q$ is discrete and countable, its points $v$ correspond bijectively to the geodesics $t \mapsto \exp_p(tv)$ from $p$ to $q$, and $\Omega(N; p, q)$, with Milnor's metric, is homotopy equivalent to it. (iii) If moreover $N$ is simply connected, $\Omega(N; p, q)$ is contractible, and (for $N$ closed) it has the homotopy type of a cell complex with exactly one cell, a $0$-cell.

V11.19

$\exp_p$ is a covering map

not in the book
$T_pN$ is the universal coveringGauss lemma beyond a normal ball“it is clear” made precise

Milnor §19, p. 103

The book has no such statement. At the end of the proof of 19.2 Milnor notes that by 18.1 $\exp_p$ is non-critical everywhere, "so that $\exp_p$ is locally a diffeomorphism". For a complete $M$ of curvature $\le 0$ that is not simply connected, Theorem 19.2 is applied to the universal covering space $\tilde M$, which, "it is clear", inherits from $M$ a Riemannian metric that is geodesically complete and of curvature $\le 0$.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: (i) the Gauss lemma holds on the whole domain of $\exp_p$: $\langle d(\exp_p)_w(w), d(\exp_p)_w(x)\rangle = \langle w, x\rangle$ for $w \in \mathcal D_p$, $x \in T_pN$. (ii) $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ is a local diffeomorphism at every point where $d(\exp_p)$ is one-to-one. Now let $N$ be geodesically complete and $\exp_p$ nowhere critical. (iii) A lift $\Gamma$ through $\exp_p$ of a smooth curve of speed $\le L$ on $[0, T]$ satisfies $\|\Gamma(t)\| \le \|\Gamma(0)\| + 1 + Lt$. (iv) Smooth curves in $N$ lift through $\exp_p$, uniquely, from any point over the initial point. (v) $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ is a covering map. In non-positive curvature (V11.8) all of this applies.

Milnor §19, p. 103

More generally, suppose that $M$ is complete with sectional curvature $\le 0$ but not simply connected (for example a flat torus, or a compact surface of genus $\ge 2$ with constant negative curvature). Theorem 19.2 applies to the universal covering space $\tilde M$; given two points $p, q \in M$, it follows that each homotopy class of paths from $p$ to $q$ contains precisely one geodesic.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $N$ be geodesically complete and of non-positive curvature, and $p, q \in N$. Every continuous path $c$ in $N$ from $p$ to $q$ is homotopic, relative to its end points, to a geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$; and two geodesics in $\Omega(N; p, q)$ that are both homotopic to $c$ agree on $[0, 1]$.

Milnor §19, Corollary 19.3 · p. 103

If $M$ is complete with $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$, then the homotopy groups $\pi_i(M)$ are zero for $i > 1$, and $\pi_1(M)$ contains no element of finite order other than the identity. Proof: clearly $\pi_i(M) = \pi_i(\tilde M) = 0$ for $i > 1$, $\tilde M$ being contractible; and since the cohomology of $M$ is that of the group $\pi_1(M)$ (Hu), a non-trivial finite cyclic subgroup $G$ would give a covering $\hat M$ with $H^k(G) = H^k(\hat M) = 0$ for $k > n$, while the cohomology of a finite cyclic group is non-trivial in arbitrarily high dimensions.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: if $N$ is geodesically complete and of non-positive curvature, then $\pi_i(N, x) = 0$ for every $i > 1$ and every base point $x \in N$ (Mathlib's homotopy groups); on the way, every map of the cube $I^i$, $i \ge 2$, constant on the boundary, is null-homotopic relative to the boundary.

Theorem 19.6: positive Ricci curvature and the path space

narrower

Milnor §19, Theorem 19.6 · p. 106

If $M$ is a compact manifold, and if the Ricci tensor $K$ of $M$ is everywhere positive definite, then the path space $\Omega(M; p, q)$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex having only finitely many cells in each dimension. Proof: by the index estimate a geodesic of length $> k\pi r$ has index $\ge k$; if $p$ and $q$ are not conjugate along any geodesic, then by 16.3 there are only finitely many geodesics of length $\le k\pi r$, hence only finitely many with index $< k$; together with 17.3 this completes the proof.

Proved in Lean

For a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$, with the induced metric: let $N$ be compact, $n = \dim N \ge 2$, with Ricci tensor positive definite at every point, and $p, q \in N$ with $q$ not conjugate to $p$ along any geodesic ($q \notin C(p)$, V11.4). Then $\Omega(N; p, q)$, with Milnor's metric, has the homotopy type of a countable cell complex (VA.18) in which each dimension $d$ occurs at only finitely many of the stages, each stage attaching finitely many cells: only finitely many cells of each dimension. The same holds for $N$ closed in $V$ with $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$ for some $r > 0$; on the way, a geodesic of index $\le d$ has energy $\le ((d + 1)\pi r)^2$.

The homology of the path space in positive Ricci curvature

not in the book
finite Betti numbers, field coefficientsenergy filtration, not cellular homology

Milnor §19, cf. Theorem 19.6, p. 106

The book draws no homological consequence from Theorem 19.6; with cellular homology it would be immediate that each $H_i(\Omega(M; p, q))$ is finitely generated, as on p. 96 Milnor reads the homology of $\Omega(S^n)$ off its cells.

Hence, if $n = \dim N \ge 2$, $r > 0$, $K(U, U) \ge (n - 1)/r^2$ for every unit tangent vector $U$ at every point, $n = \dim N$, and $q \notin C(p)$, then $H_i(\Omega(N; p, q); \Bbbk)$ is finite-dimensional for every $i$ and every field $\Bbbk$; in particular under Milnor's hypotheses of Theorem 19.6 (compact $N$, positive definite Ricci tensor).

V12.1

The algebraic model of a bi-invariant metric

restated
an abstract Lie algebra with a form

Milnor §21, p. 113

Milnor works with the Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant vector fields on a Lie group $G$ with a left and right invariant metric, the bracket of vector fields, and the connection $X \vdash Y$ of the metric; Theorem 21.3 (a) is the identity $\langle[X, Y], Z\rangle = \langle X, [Y, Z]\rangle$.

Proved in Lean

For a real Lie algebra $L$ (standing for Milnor's $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant fields) with a bilinear form $B$ (his inner product on $\mathfrak g$): $B$ is ad-invariant if $B([X, Y], Z) = B(X, [Y, Z])$ for all $X, Y, Z$, which is Mathlib's Lie invariance. A bilinear $D : L \times L \to L$, standing for $X \vdash Y$, is Levi-Civita for $B$ if $D(X, Y) - D(Y, X) = [X, Y]$ and $B(D(X, Y), Z) + B(Y, D(X, Z)) = 0$.

The non-zero eigenvalues of $K_V$ occur in pairs

restated
a complex structure, not the normal form

Milnor §21, proof of Theorem 21.7, p. 117

Choosing an orthonormal basis that puts $\operatorname{Ad}V$ in block form with blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0 & a_i\\ -a_i & 0\end{pmatrix}$, $(\operatorname{Ad}V)^2$ is diagonal with entries $-a_1^2, -a_1^2, -a_2^2, \dots$; so the non-zero eigenvalues of $K_V$ are positive and occur in pairs.

Proved in Lean

For a real Lie algebra $L$ (standing for Milnor's $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant fields) with a bilinear form $B$ (his inner product on $\mathfrak g$) ad-invariant and positive definite, $L$ finite-dimensional: $K_VW = \mu W$ iff $[V, [V, W]] = -4\mu W$; $\operatorname{ad}_V$ preserves each eigenspace $E_\mu$; for $\mu > 0$, $J = (2\sqrt\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{ad}_V$ satisfies $J^2 = -1$ on $E_\mu$ and preserves $B$; so every eigenspace of $K_V$ for $\mu \neq 0$ has even dimension.

Matrix groups and their bi-invariant metric

narrower
groups given as matrices onlyno Haar averaging

Milnor §21, p. 112; §23, p. 125

A Lie group $G$ with a metric invariant under left and right translations; if $G$ is compact such a metric exists, by averaging any metric with the Haar measure (p. 112). For $U(n)$ the tangent space at $I$ is the space of skew-Hermitian matrices (p. 125, (6)).

Proved in Lean

Multiplication by a unitary matrix is a linear isometry of $M_n(\mathbb K)$. A matrix group is a slice submanifold $G \subseteq M_n(\mathbb K)$ with a real Lie subalgebra $\mathfrak g$ such that every $g \in G$ is unitary, $G$ is closed under products and adjoints, $\mathfrak g$ consists of skew-Hermitian matrices and is invariant under $X \mapsto gXg^*$, $\exp\mathfrak g \subseteq G$, and $\dim G = \dim\mathfrak g$. Then $T_gG = g\mathfrak g$, left and right translations by elements of $G$ are isometries of $M_n(\mathbb K)$ preserving $G$ (the metric is bi-invariant), and the inner product on $\mathfrak g$ is ad-invariant and positive definite.

The geodesics $\gamma$ with $\gamma(0) = e$ are precisely the one-parameter subgroups of $G$. (By Corollary 20.2, p. 110, a symmetric space is complete.)

Proved in Lean

(i) A geodesic $\gamma : \mathbb R \to G$ with $\gamma(0) = I$ is $t \mapsto \exp(t\gamma'(0))$ and satisfies $\gamma(s + t) = \gamma(s)\gamma(t)$. (ii) A differentiable $\theta : \mathbb R \to G$ with $\theta(0) = I$ and $\theta(s + t) = \theta(s)\theta(t)$ is a geodesic. $\exp_g(gX) = g\exp X$, and $G$ is geodesically complete.

Milnor §21, Lemma 21.1 · p. 112

If $G$ has a bi-invariant metric, then for each $\tau$ the map $I_\tau(\sigma) = \tau\sigma^{-1}\tau$ is an isometry which fixes $\tau$ and reverses geodesics through $\tau$; so $G$ is a symmetric space.

Theorem 21.3 and Corollary 21.4 for matrix groups

narrower
matrix groupsby the Gauss equation

Milnor §21, Theorem 21.3 and Corollary 21.4 · p. 113

Let $G$ have a bi-invariant metric and $X, Y, Z, W \in \mathfrak g$. Then (a) $\langle[X, Y], Z\rangle = \langle X, [Y, Z]\rangle$, (b) $R(X, Y)Z = \frac14[[X, Y], Z]$, (c) $\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle = \frac14\langle[X, Y], [Z, W]\rangle$; in the proof, (d) $X \vdash Y = \frac12[X, Y]$. Corollary 21.4 (p. 115): $\langle R(X, Y)X, Y\rangle = \frac14\langle[X, Y], [X, Y]\rangle \ge 0$.

Proved in Lean

For a matrix group $(G, \mathfrak g)$ — a slice submanifold $G$ of the space $M_n(\mathbb K)$ of matrices ($\mathbb K = \mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$), with the induced metric of $\langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^*B)$, and a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of skew-Hermitian matrices (V12.14), $g \in G$, $X, Y, Z, W \in \mathfrak g$: (a) holds; (d) the covariant derivative of $q \mapsto qY$ in the direction $gX$ is $g\cdot\frac12[X, Y]$; the second fundamental form is $\mathrm{II}_g(gX, gY) = \frac12g(XY + YX)$; (b) $R(gX, gY)gZ = \frac14g[[X, Y], Z]$ (Milnor's sign), which is $g$ times the algebraic curvature of V12.5, and $R(gA, gW)gA = g\,K_A(W)$; (c) $\langle R(gX, gY)gZ, gW\rangle = \frac14\langle[X, Y], [Z, W]\rangle$; and $\langle R(gX, gY)gX, gY\rangle = \frac14\|[X, Y]\|^2 \ge 0$, zero iff $XY = YX$.

Theorem 20.5 for matrix groups: the Jacobi equation along $\exp(tA)$

narrower
one-parameter subgroups of matrix groupsno eigenbasismultiplicities: $SU(n)$ only (V14.18)

Milnor §20, Theorem 20.5 · p. 110

Let $\gamma$ be a geodesic in a locally symmetric manifold with $\gamma(0) = p$, $\gamma'(0) = V$, and $e_1, \dots, e_n$ the eigenvalues of $K_V(W) = R(V, W)V$. The conjugate points to $p$ along $\gamma$ are the $\gamma(\pi k/\sqrt{e_i})$, $k$ a non-zero integer, $e_i > 0$; the multiplicity of $\gamma(t)$ is the number of $e_i$ such that $t$ is a multiple of $\pi/\sqrt{e_i}$. Proof (p. 111): in a parallel orthonormal eigenframe the Jacobi equation is $w_i'' + e_iw_i = 0$.

Proved in Lean

For a matrix group $(G, \mathfrak g)$ — a slice submanifold $G$ of the space $M_n(\mathbb K)$ of matrices ($\mathbb K = \mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$), with the induced metric of $\langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^*B)$, and a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of skew-Hermitian matrices (V12.14), $A \in \mathfrak g$, $\gamma(t) = \exp(tA)$, $h(t) = \exp(tA/2)$: the covariant derivative of $hUh$ along $\gamma$ is $hU'h$ for $\mathfrak g$-valued $U$, and $R(\gamma', hMh)\gamma' = h\,K_A(M)\,h$ with $K_A(M) = \frac14[[A, M], A]$. Hence if $U$ is smooth with $U'' + K_A(U) = 0$, $hUh$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ with covariant derivative $U'(0)$ at $0$.

Theorem 22.1

narrower
neighbourhood retract assumed (no Hanner)relative form, every compact $P$compact balls for completeness

Milnor §22, Theorem 22.1 · p. 118

If the space $\Omega^d$ of minimal geodesics from $p$ to $q$ is a topological manifold, and if every non-minimal geodesic from $p$ to $q$ has index $\ge \lambda_0$, then $\pi_i(\Omega, \Omega^d) = 0$ for $0 \le i < \lambda_0$. ($M$ is complete throughout §22; proof pp. 122–123.)

Proved in Lean

For a slice submanifold $N$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$, with the induced metric, $p, q \in N$ and $\Omega = \Omega(N; p, q)$ with Milnor's metric (V10.1): let the closed balls about $p$ be compact, let every geodesic of $\Omega$ not of least energy have index $\ge \lambda_0$, and let $\Omega^d$ be a retract of an open neighbourhood in $\Omega$ (an open $O \supseteq \Omega^d$ and $\rho : O \to \Omega^d$, continuous on $O$, the identity on $\Omega^d$). Let $P$ be compact with a continuous injection into a real vector space of dimension $< \lambda_0$ (e.g. $I^i$, $i < \lambda_0$). Then every map $h : P \to \Omega$ is homotopic, relative to $h^{-1}(\Omega^d)$, to a map into $\Omega^d$; equivalently the inclusion $\Omega^d \to \Omega$ compresses maps from $P$.

Lemma A: the minimal geodesics between antipodes are the equator

Milnor §22, proof of Corollary 22.3, p. 119

Let $p, q = -p$ be antipodal on $S^{n+1}$. Then the space $\Omega^{\pi^2}$ of minimal geodesics from $p$ to $q$ "can be identified with" the equator $S^n$. (The exposition states this as Lemma A, with the list of all geodesics from $p$ to $-p$.)

On the unit sphere $S^{n+1} \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+2}$: every geodesic from $p$ to $-p$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $t \mapsto \cos(Lt)p + \sin(Lt)u$, $u \perp p$ a unit vector, $L = (2m + 1)\pi$, and each of these is one; every path from $p$ to $-p$ has energy $\ge \pi^2$; the paths of least energy are the semicircles $\gamma_u$ ($L = \pi$), $u$ in the equator. $u \mapsto \gamma_u$ is continuous for Milnor's metric, a homotopy equivalence from the equator to $\Omega^d$ with homotopy inverse $\gamma \mapsto \gamma(\frac12)$, and a homeomorphism of the equator onto the separation quotient of $\Omega^d$.

Lemma 22.4

stronger
$f$ only $C^2$operator norms for partialsno eigenvalues

Milnor §22, Lemma 22.4 · p. 119

Let $K$ be a compact subset of an open $U \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ and $f : U \to \mathbb R$ smooth, all of whose critical points in $K$ have index $\ge \lambda_0$. If $g : U \to \mathbb R$ is smooth and its first and second partial derivatives are within $\varepsilon$ of those of $f$ uniformly on $K$, $\varepsilon$ small, then every critical point of $g$ in $K$ has index $\ge \lambda_0$. Proof (pp. 120–121): the $\lambda$-th eigenvalue of the Hessian is continuous, and "a uniform continuity argument which will be left to the reader".

Proved in Lean

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $K \subseteq U \subseteq E$ with $K$ compact and $U$ open, and $f : E \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^2$ on $U$ with every critical point in $K$ of index $\ge \lambda_0$. There is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every $g$ with $\|dg_x - df_x\| < \varepsilon$ and $\|d^2g_x - d^2f_x\| < \varepsilon$ (operator norms) at each $x \in K$ has all its critical points in $K$ of index $\ge \lambda_0$; likewise for $g = f + h$ with the first two derivatives of $h$ smaller than $\varepsilon$ on $K$.

Pushing maps, and pushing off cells

not in the book
replaces $\pi_r(X, A) = 0$push-off lemma of cellular approximation

Milnor §22, proof of Lemma 22.5, p. 122

"Since $r < \lambda_0$ it follows that $h$ is homotopic within $(M^c, M^0)$ to a map $h'$ into $g^{-1}(-\infty, 2\delta]$": maps of dimension below $\lambda_0$ can be pushed off cells of dimension $\ge \lambda_0$.

Proved in Lean

$A$ pushes maps from $P$ out of $X$ ($A, X \subseteq T$) if every map $P \to T$ with values in $X$ is homotopic in $T$, relative to the preimage of $A$, to a map into $A$. This is transitive and monotone; a strong deformation retract pushes maps from every $P$; and if $T$ is Hausdorff, $A$ closed, $P$ compact with a continuous injection into a real vector space of dimension $d$, and $e_1, \dots, e_k$ are disjoint embedded closed cells of dimensions $> d$ meeting $A$ exactly in their boundary spheres, then $A$ pushes maps from $P$ out of $A \cup e_1 \cup \dots \cup e_k$.

Jacobi's formula $d(\det)_A(AX) = \det A\operatorname{tr}X$, and $\det\exp(tX) = 1$ for $\operatorname{tr}X = 0$.

Theorem 20.5 for $SU(n)$

$SU(n)$ onlyno eigenbasis$T$ carried through, no reduction

Milnor §20, Theorem 20.5, p. 110; §23, pp. 130–131

By Theorem 20.5 the conjugate points along $t \mapsto \exp tA$ are determined by the eigenvalues of $K_A(W) = \frac14[[A, W], A]$: an eigenvalue $e > 0$ gives conjugate points at the multiples of $\pi/\sqrt e$, the multiplicity counting the eigenvalues; "adding over all $j, l$".

Proved in Lean

For $A = T\operatorname{diag}(ia_j)T^* \in \mathfrak{su}(n)$, $T$ unitary, and $C \in \mathfrak{su}(n)$, $J_C(t) = e^{tA/2}T(S(t) \odot T^*CT)T^*e^{tA/2}$, with $S(t) \odot W$ the matrix of $\frac{\sin(b_{jl}t)}{b_{jl}}w_{jl}$, $b_{jl} = (a_j - a_l)/2$, is a Jacobi field along $\exp(tA)$ with $J_C(0) = 0$, $DJ_C/dt(0) = C$. The multiplicity of $t_0 \in [0, 1]$ as a parameter conjugate to $0$ is $\dim\{W \in \mathfrak{su}(n) : S(t_0) \odot W = 0\}$, which for $a = \pi k$ and $0 < t_0 < 1$ equals the multiplicity computed from Milnor's spectrum (V14.8–V14.9).

not in the book
Hanner replaced by a spectral projection

Milnor §23, p. 128

By Lemma 23.1, $\Omega^d$ is a manifold, and by Lemma 23.2 every non-minimal geodesic has index $\ge 2m + 2$; with Theorem 22.1 this gives the result. No retraction is written down.

Hence $\pi_i(\Omega^d, \gamma) \cong \pi_{i+1}(SU(2m), I)$ for $i \le 2m$, as groups for $1 \le i \le 2m$.

An equivariant map onto a space with a transitive group action is locally trivial with fibre the fibre over $b_0$ if the orbit map at $b_0$ has a continuous local section. $U(n)$ acts transitively on the Stiefel manifold $V_k(\mathbb K^n) = \{F : F^*F = I\}$, with an explicit continuous local section near the base frame. Restricting frames to their last vectors is locally trivial with fibre a Stiefel manifold, $g \mapsto gF_0$, $U(n) \to V_k(\mathbb K^n)$, is locally trivial with fibre $U(n - k)$, and $V_1(\mathbb K^n)$ is the unit sphere, so $U(m + 1) \to S^{2m+1}$ is locally trivial with fibre $U(m)$.

stronger
every $V_k(\mathbb C^n)$all base points

Lemma 24.2, from Milnor's spectrum

the spectrum is the inputgeodesics: V15.30

Milnor §24, Lemma 24.2 · p. 135

Any non-minimal geodesic from $I$ to $-I$ in $O(2m)$ has index $\ge 2m - 2$. For $A$ with blocks $a_j\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, $a_1 \ge \dots \ge a_m > 0$ odd, the non-zero eigenvalues of $K_A$ are $(a_i + a_j)^2/4$ for $i < j$ and $(a_i - a_j)^2/4$ for $i < j$ with $a_i \neq a_j$, each counted twice; so $\lambda = \sum_{i<j}(a_i + a_j - 2) + \sum_{a_i > a_j}(a_i - a_j - 2)$.

Proved in Lean

For integers $a_1, \dots, a_m$ put $\lambda(a) = \sum_{i < j}(a_i + a_j - 2) + \sum_{a_i > a_j}(a_i - a_j - 2)$, the second sum over ordered pairs. Let all $a_j$ be odd and positive. (i) The index, in the sense of Chapter 14 (V14.8), of the spectrum consisting of $\tfrac{\pi^2}{4}(a_i + a_j)^2$ for $i < j$ and $\tfrac{\pi^2}{4}(a_i - a_j)^2$ for $a_i > a_j$, each counted twice, is $\lambda(a)$. (ii) If all $a_j = 1$, $\lambda(a) = 0$. (iii) If not all $a_j = 1$, $\lambda(a) \ge 2m - 2$.

Milnor §24, p. 136

With fixed anticommuting complex structures $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$, $\Omega_k(n)$ is the set of all complex structures which anticommute with them. $\Omega_k(n) \subset \Omega_{k-1}(n) \subset \dots \subset \Omega_1(n) \subset O(n)$; "clearly each $\Omega_k(n)$ is a compact set"; $\Omega_0(n) = O(n)$.

$\Omega_0(n) = O(n)$, and for $k \ge 1$, $\Omega_k(n)$ is the set of complex structures $J$ with $J_\alpha J = -JJ_\alpha$ for $1 \le \alpha \le k - 1$. For any fixed matrices $J_\alpha$, $\Omega_{k+1}(n) \subseteq \Omega_k(n)$, and every $\Omega_k(n)$ is closed and compact. $J_1, \dots, J_k$ form an anticommuting family if each is a complex structure and $J_\alpha J_\beta = -J_\beta J_\alpha$ for $\alpha \neq \beta$; then $J_k \in \Omega_k(n)$ for $k \ge 1$.

Milnor §24, proof of Lemma 24.4 and Remark, pp. 137–138

(i) If $J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$, then $A = -J_kJ'$ ($= J_k^{-1}J'$) is a complex structure that anticommutes with $J_k$ and commutes with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$, and $J' = J_kA$. (ii) Conversely, for every such $A$, $J_kA \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$. (iii) For $J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$ and every real $t$, $\cos t\,J_k + \sin t\,J' \in \Omega_k(n)$, and $J_k\exp(tA) = \cos t\,J_k + \sin t\,J'$ for $A = -J_kJ'$: the curve $t \mapsto J_k\exp(tA)$ stays in $\Omega_k(n)$, passes through $J'$ at $t = \pi/2$ and reaches $-J_k$ at $t = \pi$. (iv) A complex structure $J'$ anticommuting with a matrix $J$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(J'^{\mathsf T}J) = 0$.

Milnor §24, p. 138

Choose fixed anticommuting complex structures $J'_1, \dots, J'_k$ on $\mathbb R^{n'}$. Then each $J \in \Omega_k(n)$ determines a complex structure $J \oplus J'_k$ on $\mathbb R^n \oplus \mathbb R^{n'}$ which anticommutes with $J_\alpha \oplus J'_\alpha$ for $\alpha = 1, \dots, k - 1$.

For any fixed matrices and every $k$: if $P \in \Omega_k(n)$ for the $J_\alpha$ and $P' \in \Omega_k(n')$ for the $J'_\alpha$, then $P \oplus P' \in \Omega_k(n + n')$ for the $J_\alpha \oplus J'_\alpha$. With $P' = J'_k$ (V15.4) this is Milnor's map $J \mapsto J \oplus J'_k$.

Milnor §24, pp. 136, 139

Renaming the coordinates and repeating block-diagonally ($J_\alpha \oplus \dots \oplus J_\alpha$) preserve anticommuting families; so $\mathbb R^{16r}$ carries eight anticommuting complex structures for every $r$.

bijections with involutions

Milnor §24, Lemma 24.6 (3), (5), (6), (7), pp. 139–141

$\Omega_3(16r)$ is the quaternionic Grassmann manifold of $\mathbb H^{4r}$, through the $+1$-eigenspace $V_1$ of $J_1J_2J_3$; $\Omega_5(16r)$ the subspaces $W \subset V_1$ closed under $J_1$ with $V_1 = W \oplus J_2W$; $\Omega_6(16r)$ the real subspaces $X \subset W$ with $W = X \oplus J_1X$; $\Omega_7(16r)$ the real Grassmann manifold of $X \cong \mathbb R^{2r}$.

Proved in Lean

Let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family and $1 \le a < b \le k$. For $J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$, $\theta = J_aJ_bJ'$ is symmetric with $\theta^2 = I$, commutes with $J_a$ and $J_b$, and anticommutes with every other $J_c$, $c \le k$. Conversely, for every such $\theta$, $J' = J_bJ_a\theta$ lies in $\Omega_{k+1}(n)$ and $J_aJ_bJ' = \theta$; and $J_bJ_a(J_aJ_bJ') = J'$ for every $J'$. So $J' \mapsto J_aJ_bJ'$ is a bijection of $\Omega_{k+1}(n)$ onto the symmetric involutions with this commutation pattern. With $(a, b, k) = (1, 2, 2), (1, 4, 4), (2, 4, 5), (1, 6, 6)$ it is the passage $J_3 \mapsto \theta_3$, $J_5 \mapsto \theta_5$, $J_6 \mapsto \theta_6$, $J_7 \mapsto \theta_7$ of 24.6 (3), (5), (6), (7).

Lemma 24.6, the dimensions

stronger
equal halves are forced

Milnor §24, pp. 139–141

The splittings $V_1 \oplus V_2$, $W \oplus J_2W$, $X \oplus J_1X$, $X_1 \oplus X_2$. Milnor restricts attention to the components with $\dim_{\mathbb H}V_1 = \dim_{\mathbb H}V_2 = 2r$ and with $\dim X_1 = \dim X_2 = r$.

On a finite-dimensional real vector space $V$, if $\theta^2 = 1$ and an injective $P$ anticommutes with $\theta$, then $\dim V = 2\dim\{\theta = 1\}$ ($P$ exchanges the $\pm1$-eigenspaces of $\theta$). Hence, for Clifford $J_1, \dots, J_8$ on $V$, with $V_1 = \{\theta_3 = 1\}$, $W = V_1 \cap \{\theta_5 = 1\}$, $X = W \cap \{\theta_6 = 1\}$ and $X_1 = X \cap \{\theta_7 = 1\}$: $\dim V = 2\dim V_1 = 4\dim W = 8\dim X = 16\dim X_1$, the halvings being effected by $J_4$, $J_2$, $J_1$ and $J_7J_8$. $m_k$ defined by the table

Milnor §24, p. 143

$V$ is a minimal $(J_1, \dots, J_k)$-space if no proper, non-trivial subspace is closed under the action of $J_1, \dots, J_k$. $m_k$ is the dimension of a minimal space: $m_0, \dots, m_8 = 1, 2, 4, 4, 8, 8, 8, 8, 16$, and for $k > 8$ "it can be shown that $m_k = 16m_{k-8}$".

A real vector space $V$ with linear maps $J_1, J_2, \dots$ is minimal for $J_1, \dots, J_k$ if $V \neq 0$ and every subspace closed under $J_1, \dots, J_k$ is $0$ or $V$. The numbers $m_k$ are defined by the table $m_0, \dots, m_8 = 1, 2, 4, 4, 8, 8, 8, 8, 16$ and $m_{k+8} = 16m_k$.

Milnor §24, p. 143

Vector fields on spheres

narrower
the identities; no Hurwitz–Radon count

Milnor §24, Remark, pp. 143–144

For anticommuting $J_1, \dots, J_k$ on a space of dimension $rm_k$ and each unit vector $u$, the $k$ vectors $J_1u, \dots, J_ku$ are perpendicular to each other and to $u$: $k$ linearly independent vector fields on an $(rm_k - 1)$-sphere; $3$ on a $(4r - 1)$-sphere, $7$ on an $(8r - 1)$-sphere, $8$ on a $(16r - 1)$-sphere (Hurwitz and Radon; Adams: best possible).

Proved in Lean

If $J_1, \dots, J_k$ are anticommuting complex structures on $\mathbb R^n$, then for every $u$, $\langle J_\alpha u, J_\beta u\rangle = \delta_{\alpha\beta}|u|^2$ and $\langle J_\alpha u, u\rangle = 0$; so for $|u| = 1$ the $J_\alpha u$ are $k$ orthonormal vectors tangent to the unit sphere at $u$. This is written out for the eight structures of V15.9 on $\mathbb R^{16r}$ (eight fields on $S^{16r-1}$), and the general statement applies to the block-diagonal families on $\mathbb R^{4r}$ and $\mathbb R^{8r}$ built from V15.9 (three and seven fields).

Milnor §24, Assertions, pp. 145–146

$K_A$ has at least $s - 1$ eigenvalues which are $\ge (3 + 1)^2/4 = 4$. Each eigenvalue $e^2$ of $K_A$ gives rise to conjugate points for $t = e^{-1}, 2e^{-1}, 3e^{-1}, \dots$; hence the index of a non-minimal geodesic from $J$ to $-J$ in $\Omega_k(n)$ is $\ge n/m_{k+1} - 1$.

Proved in Lean

The index of a spectrum (in the sense of Chapter 14, V14.8) is at least the number of its eigenvalues greater than $\pi^2$. Hence, for integers $a_1, \dots, a_s \ge 1$ with some $a_{h_0} \ge 3$, the $s - 1$ eigenvalues $\tfrac{\pi^2}{4}(a_{h_0} + a_j)^2$, $j \neq h_0$, already have index at least $s - 1$.

Totally geodesic sets of orthogonal matrices

restated
the geodesics are listed directlyno comparison with $O(n)$

Milnor §24, footnote, p. 136; p. 137

A submanifold of a Riemannian manifold is called totally geodesic if each geodesic in the submanifold is also a geodesic in the larger manifold. The description of $\Omega_k(n)$ near $J$ as the points $J\exp A$, $A$ in a linear subspace, "clearly implies" that $\Omega_k(n)$ is a totally geodesic submanifold of $O(n)$.

Proved in Lean

Let $N \subseteq M_n(\mathbb R)$ be a slice submanifold consisting of orthogonal matrices, and for each $x \in N$ let $T_x$ be a space of skew matrices with $\dim T_x = \dim N$, such that $x\exp A \in N$ and $A \in T_{x\exp A}$ whenever $A \in T_x$. Then: (i) the tangent space of $N$ at $x$ is $x\,T_x$; (ii) for $A \in T_x$ the curve $t \mapsto x\exp(tA)$ is a geodesic of $N$ on all of $\mathbb R$; (iii) every unbroken geodesic $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $s \mapsto p\exp(sV)$ for some $V \in T_p$; (iv) the Riemannian exponential of $N$ is $\exp_x(xA) = x\exp A$ for $A \in T_x$, and $N$ is geodesically complete. Also, as a tool for V15.23: let $S$ be a subset of a real normed space $V$ such that near each $x \in S$ there is a smooth $\Phi : Z \times W \to V$ ($Z$, $W$ finite-dimensional) with $\Phi(0) = x$ and invertible derivative at $0$, for which, near $0$, the points $\Phi(z, 0)$ lie in $S$ and every point $\Phi(q) \in S$ equals $\Phi(g(q), 0)$ with $g(q) \to 0$ as $q \to 0$; then $S$ is a slice submanifold modelled on $Z$.

Assertions 1 and 2 in both directions; $\Omega_k(n)$ near a point

hypotheses explicit
"small": the Frobenius norm$C$ need not be assumed skew

Milnor §24, Assertions 1 and 2, p. 137

For small skew $A$: $J\exp A$ is a complex structure if and only if $A$ anticommutes with $J$; $J\exp A$ anticommutes with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$ if and only if $A$ commutes with them. Thus a neighborhood of $J$ in $\Omega_k(n)$ consists of all points $J\exp A$ where $A$ ranges over all small matrices in a linear subspace of the Lie algebra.

Proved in Lean

For a matrix $x$ let $\mathcal T_x$ be the space of skew matrices $A$ with $Ax = -xA$ and $AJ_\alpha = J_\alpha A$ for $1 \le \alpha \le k - 1$; for $k = 0$ the first condition is dropped, so that $\mathcal T_x$ is the space $\mathfrak o(n)$ of all skew matrices, the same for every $x$. (i) For any fixed matrices $J_\alpha$: if $x \in \Omega_k(n)$ and $A \in \mathcal T_x$, then $x\exp A \in \Omega_k(n)$ and $A \in \mathcal T_{x\exp A}$. (ii) There is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that $\exp$ is injective on the matrices of norm $< \varepsilon$. For every such $\varepsilon$, every anticommuting family $J_1, \dots, J_k$, every $x \in \Omega_k(n)$ and every matrix $C$ with $\|C\| < \varepsilon$: if $x\exp C \in \Omega_k(n)$, then $C \in \mathcal T_x$. (iii) Hence, for an anticommuting family and $x \in \Omega_k(n)$, there is a map $L$ with $L(y) \to 0$ as $y \to x$, such that every $y \in \Omega_k(n)$ near $x$ satisfies $L(y) \in \mathcal T_x$ and $y = x\exp(L(y))$.

Lemma 24.4, first half: a smooth, totally geodesic submanifold

restated
stratum by stratumin $M_n(\mathbb R)$, not in $O(n)$

Milnor §24, Lemma 24.4 · p. 136

Each $\Omega_k(n)$ is a smooth, totally geodesic submanifold of $O(n)$.

p. 139: $\Omega_3(16r)$ "contains components of varying dimension"; p. 141: so does $\Omega_7(16r)$.

Proved in Lean

The stratum of $\Omega_k(n)$ through a matrix $p$ is the set of $x \in \Omega_k(n)$ with $\dim\mathcal T_x = \dim\mathcal T_p$. (i) $\dim\mathcal T_{x\exp A} = \dim\mathcal T_x$ for $A \in \mathcal T_x$. Let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family. (ii) The stratum is open in $\Omega_k(n)$ (each of its points has a neighbourhood in $M_n(\mathbb R)$ whose points in $\Omega_k(n)$ belong to it), closed in $M_n(\mathbb R)$, and compact. (iii) It is a slice submanifold of $M_n(\mathbb R)$ modelled on $\mathcal T_p$, and it satisfies the hypotheses of V15.21 with $T_x = \mathcal T_x$. Consequently its tangent space at $x$ is $x\mathcal T_x$, its geodesics are the curves $t \mapsto x\exp(tA)$ with $A \in \mathcal T_x$, and it is geodesically complete. For $k = 0$ the stratum through any $p$ is $O(n)$.

(ii) In the setting of V15.25, $A \mapsto \gamma_A$ is a homotopy equivalence of $\mathcal C_p$ with $\Omega^d(N; p, -p)$, and a homeomorphism of $\mathcal C_p$ onto the quotient of $\Omega^d$ in which paths at distance $0$ are identified. (iii) If $J_1, \dots, J_{k+1}$ is an anticommuting family and $N$ is the stratum of $\Omega_k(n)$ through $J_k$, the map $\varphi : \Omega_{k+1}(n) \to \Omega(N; J_k, -J_k)$, $\varphi(J')(t) = \cos(\pi t)\,J_k + \sin(\pi t)\,J'$, is continuous, and it is the inclusion $\Omega^d \to \Omega$ composed with a homotopy equivalence $\Omega_{k+1}(n) \to \Omega^d$. For $k = 0$, $N = O(n)$ and $\Omega_1(n)$ is the set of all complex structures: this is Lemma 24.1.

Killing fields are Jacobi fields; a lower bound for the index

restated
no curvature of $\Omega_k(n)$isometries give the Jacobi fields

Milnor §24, pp. 144, 146

Since $\Omega_k(n)$ is a totally geodesic submanifold of $O(n)$, $K_A$ can be computed by $K_AB = -\tfrac14[A, [A, B]]$ on $T$. Each eigenvalue $e^2$ of $K_A$ gives rise to conjugate points for $t = e^{-1}, 2e^{-1}, 3e^{-1}, \dots$ by 20.5; then apply the index theorem.

Proved in Lean

Let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family, $p \in \Omega_k(n)$, $N$ the stratum through $p$, and $V \in \mathcal T_p$. The isotropy algebra of $p$ is the space of skew matrices commuting with $p$ and with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$. (i) For $X$ in the isotropy algebra, $K(t) = X\gamma(t) - \gamma(t)X$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma(t) = p\exp(tV)$ in $N$. (ii) Let $\gamma \in \Omega(N; p, q)$ be an unbroken geodesic equal to $t \mapsto p\exp(tV)$ on $[0, 1]$, let $\tau \in [0, 1]$, and let $\mathcal X$ be a subspace of the isotropy algebra whose elements commute with $\exp(\tau V)$ and none of whose non-zero elements commutes with $V$. Then $\gamma(\tau)$ is conjugate to $\gamma(0)$ along $\gamma$ with multiplicity (V9.4) at least $\dim\mathcal X$. (iii) For a finite set $T \subset (0, 1)$ and such subspaces $\mathcal X_\tau$, $\tau \in T$, the index of $\gamma$ is at least $\sum_{\tau \in T}\dim\mathcal X_\tau$.

The splitting into minimal pieces; Lemma 24.8 between two pieces

restated
$k \le 7$only $c \ge 1$ is useda linear isomorphism

Milnor §24, pp. 144–145

$\mathbb R^n = M_1 \oplus \dots \oplus M_s$, mutually orthogonal subspaces closed and minimal under the action of $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$, $J$ and $A$. The eigenvalues of $A$ on $M_h$ "must be all equal, except for sign": $\pm ia_h$, with $a_h$ odd and positive. $J' = a_h^{-1}JA|M_h$ makes $M_h$ a minimal $(J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J, J')$-space, so $\dim M_h = m_{k+1}$ and $s = n/m_{k+1}$. For $h \neq j$ an isometry from $M_h$ to $\bar M_j$ "exists by 24.8".

Proved in Lean

Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and $\mathcal G$ a set of operators on $E$, each self-adjoint or skew-adjoint. A subspace is minimal invariant if it is non-zero, invariant under $\mathcal G$, and contains no invariant subspace other than $0$ and itself. (i) Every invariant subspace $U$ is spanned by a list of pairwise orthogonal minimal invariant subspaces of $U$ whose dimensions add up to $\dim U$; and a self-adjoint operator that commutes with $\mathcal G$ and preserves a minimal invariant $M$ is a scalar on $M$. (ii) Let $A$ be skew-adjoint, let $J, J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$ be skew-adjoint operators with square $-1$, anticommuting with one another, and let $A$ anticommute with $J$ and commute with the $J_\alpha$ (for $k = 0$: $J = 1$ and there are no $J_\alpha$); put $\mathcal G = \{A, J, J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}\}$. On each minimal invariant $M$, $A^2 = -c$ for a real $c$; and for real $s$ with $s^2c = 1$ the restrictions of $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J, sJA$ to $M$ satisfy the Clifford relations (V15.10) and make $M$ a minimal space for $k + 1$ structures (V15.13). For matrices: if $A$ is skew, $\exp(\pi A) = -I$, and $A^2 = -c$ on a non-zero subspace of $\mathbb R^n$, then $c \ge 1$. (iii) If $k \le 7$, $k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, and $M_0$, $M_1$ are minimal invariant with $A^2 = -a_0^2$ on $M_0$ and $A^2 = -b^2$ on $M_1$, $a_0, b > 0$, there is a linear isomorphism $T : M_0 \to M_1$ that commutes with $J$ and the $J_\alpha$ and carries $a_0^{-1}JA$ to $-b^{-1}JA$. (iv) If moreover $c \ge 1$ on every minimal invariant subspace and $A^2 \neq -1$, then in a splitting (i) of $E$ some piece $M_0$ has $c > 1$; and there are an integer $s$ with $(s + 1)m_{k+1} = \dim E$, reals $a_0 > 1$ and $b_1, \dots, b_s \ge 1$, and operators $D_1, \dots, D_s$ on $E$ (each the projection onto $M_0$ followed by an isomorphism (iii) onto another piece) which commute with $J$ and the $J_\alpha$, satisfy $b_jD_jA = -a_0AD_j$, $A^2D_j = -b_j^2D_j$ and $D_jA^2 = -a_0^2D_j$, and for which the $AD_j$ are separated by projections (for $k = 0$ there are two for each $j$, $D_j$ and $D_jA$).

Milnor §24, Lemma 24.2, p. 135; Assertion, p. 146

Any non-minimal geodesic from $I$ to $-I$ in $O(2m)$ has index $\ge 2m - 2$ (Lemma 24.2). For $k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, the index of a non-minimal geodesic from $J$ to $-J$ in $\Omega_k(n)$ is $\ge n/m_{k+1} - 1$ (Assertion).

Proved in Lean

Let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family on $\mathbb R^n$ with $\mathcal C_{J_k} \neq \emptyset$ (equivalently $\Omega_{k+1}(n) \neq \emptyset$, V15.26), let $k \le 7$ and $k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, and let $N$ be the stratum through $J_k$. If $\gamma \in \Omega(N; J_k, -J_k)$ is an unbroken geodesic which is not of least energy, then $m_{k+1}$ divides $n$ and the index of $\gamma$ is at least $n/m_{k+1} - 1$; for $k = 0$ it is at least $2(n/2 - 1) = n - 2$.

Milnor §24, p. 146; Theorem 24.5, p. 138

The inclusion map $\Omega_{k+1}(n) \to \Omega\Omega_k(n)$ induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups in dimensions $\le n/m_{k+1} - 3$. (Theorem 24.5: $\pi_hO \cong \pi_{h-1}\Omega_1 \cong \pi_{h-2}\Omega_2 \cong \dots \cong \pi_1\Omega_{h-1}$.)

Let $J_1, \dots, J_{k+1}$ be an anticommuting family on $\mathbb R^n$, $k \le 7$, $k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, let $N$ be the stratum of $\Omega_k(n)$ through $J_k$, and let $i + 2 \le n/m_{k+1} - 1$ (for $k = 0$: $i + 2 \le n - 2$). Then: (i) the inclusion $\Omega^d \to \Omega(N; J_k, -J_k)$ induces a bijection on $\pi_i$ at every minimal path; (ii) for every $J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$, the map $\varphi$ of V15.26 induces a bijection $\pi_i(\Omega_{k+1}(n), J') \to \pi_i(\Omega(N; J_k, -J_k), \varphi(J'))$; (iii) for every $J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$ there is a bijection $\pi_i(\Omega_{k+1}(n), J') \cong \pi_{i+1}(\Omega_k(n), J_k)$. On the way: $N$ is open and closed in $\Omega_k(n)$, and $\pi_{j+1}(N, x) \cong \pi_{j+1}(\Omega_k(n), x)$ for $x \in N$ and $j \ge 0$.

Angles, and the paths with a given end angle

not in the book
classes open and closed

Milnor §24, pp. 147–148

$f$ maps the geodesic into a closed loop on $S^1$ "which is completely determined by the trace of $A$. It follows that this trace is invariant under homotopy of the geodesic within the path space". Then: "restrict attention to some fixed component of $\Omega\Omega_k(n)$".

Proved in Lean

Let $F$ be a complex-valued function on a finite-dimensional real inner product space $V$ and $\omega : \mathbb R \to V$. An angle of $F \circ \omega$ is a continuous $\theta : [0, 1] \to \mathbb R$ with $\theta(0) = 0$ and $F(\omega(t)) = e^{i\theta(t)}$ for $t \in [0, 1]$. An angle is unique, and it exists whenever $t \mapsto F(\omega(t))$ is continuous on $[0, 1]$, of modulus $1$, with $F(\omega(0)) = 1$. For $N \subseteq V$, points $p$, $q$ and a real $w$, let $\Omega_w \subseteq \Omega(N; p, q)$ be the set of paths $\omega$ for which $F \circ \omega$ has an angle with $\theta(1) = w$. If $F$ is continuous and $|F| = 1$ on a compact set containing $N$, every $\Omega_w$ is open and closed in $\Omega(N; p, q)$; and $\Omega_w$, $\Omega_{w'}$ are disjoint for $w \neq w'$.

The complex determinant of a real matrix

restated
no complex basis

Milnor §24, pp. 146–147

Make $\mathbb R^n$ into an $(n/2)$-dimensional complex vector space by $iv = J_1J_2\cdots J_{k-1}v$. A unitary complex linear transformation "has a well defined complex determinant", and $f(J\exp(\pi tA)) = \det(\exp(\pi tA)) = e^{\pi t\operatorname{trace}A}$.

Proved in Lean

For real $n \times n$ matrices $\mathbf i$ and $M$ put $\det_{\mathbb C}M = \det(M_{\mathbb C}P_+ + P_-)$, a complex number, where $M_{\mathbb C}$ is $M$ read as a complex matrix and $P_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \mp \sqrt{-1}\,\mathbf i_{\mathbb C})$. Then $\det_{\mathbb C}I = 1$, and, if $\mathbf i^2 = -I$: $\det_{\mathbb C}(MN) = \det_{\mathbb C}M\,\det_{\mathbb C}N$ whenever $N$ commutes with $\mathbf i$; $|\det_{\mathbb C}M| = 1$ when $\mathbf i$ is skew and $M$ is orthogonal and commutes with $\mathbf i$; and $\det_{\mathbb C}\exp(tV) = e^{-\sqrt{-1}\,t\operatorname{tr}(V\mathbf i)/2}$ for every real $t$, when $V$ commutes with $\mathbf i$ and $\operatorname{tr}V = 0$.

Milnor's $i$ and $f$, and the classes $\Omega^{(c)}$

restated
$i$ axiomatized; proved for $k = 2, 6$$m_{k+1} = m_k$ for $k = 2, 6$

Milnor §24, pp. 146–148

$iv = J_1J_2\cdots J_{k-1}v$; "the condition $k \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ guarantees that $i^2 = -1$, and that $J_1, J_2, \dots, J_{k-1}$ commute with $i$". For $J' \in \Omega_k(n)$ the composition $J^{-1}J'$ commutes with $i$, and $f(J') = \det_{\mathbb C}(J^{-1}J') \in S^1$. A component of $\Omega\Omega_k(n)$ is fixed by $\operatorname{trace}A = icm_k/2$.

Proved in Lean

Call a matrix $\mathbf i$ central for $k$ if $\mathbf i^2 = -I$, $\mathbf i^{\mathsf T} = -\mathbf i$, $\mathbf i$ commutes with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$ and with every matrix that commutes with all of them, and $\mathbf i$ anticommutes with every matrix that anticommutes with all of them. The product $\mathbf i = J_1J_2\cdots J_{k-1}$ is central for $k = 2$ when $J_1$ is a complex structure, and for $k = 6$ when $J_1, \dots, J_5$ is an anticommuting family. Let $\mathbf i$ be central for $k \ge 1$, $p \in \Omega_k(n)$, and $f(X) = \det_{\mathbb C}(p^{\mathsf T}X)$ (V15.34 with this $\mathbf i$). Then $|f| = 1$ on $\Omega_k(n)$, $f(p) = 1$, and $f(p\exp(tV)) = e^{-\sqrt{-1}\,t\operatorname{tr}(V\mathbf i)/2}$ for $V \in \mathcal T_p$. Now let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be an anticommuting family, $k \ge 1$, $p = J_k$, $N$ the stratum through $J_k$, and let $\Omega_w \subseteq \Omega(N; J_k, -J_k)$ be the set of paths whose $f$-angle ends at $w$ (V15.33). Each $\Omega_w$ is open and closed, different $w$ give disjoint sets, and a path that agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $t \mapsto J_k\exp(tV)$, $V \in \mathcal T_{J_k}$, lies in $\Omega_w$ if and only if $w = -\operatorname{tr}(V\mathbf i)/2$. For an integer $c$, $\Omega^{(c)}$ denotes $\Omega_w$ with $w = \pi m_{k+1}c/2$.

The pieces for $k \equiv 2 \pmod 4$

restated
no complex eigenspacesa linear isomorphism

Milnor §24, p. 147

On each $M_h$ the complex linear transformation $A|M_h$ "can have only one eigenvalue, say $ia_h$", so $A|M_h$ coincides with $a_hJ_1J_2\cdots J_{k-1}|M_h$. $M_h$ is minimal under $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}, J$, of complex dimension $m_k/2$; therefore $\operatorname{trace}A = i(a_1 + \dots + a_r)m_k/2$. By 24.8 there is an isometry $M_h \to M_j$ which commutes with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$ and anticommutes with $J$.

Proved in Lean

In the setting of V15.29 (ii) with $k \ge 1$, let $\mathbf i = J_1\cdots J_{k-1}$ and suppose that $\mathbf i$ is skew-adjoint with $\mathbf i^2 = -1$, commutes with $A$ and the $J_\alpha$, and anticommutes with $J$. (i) On each minimal invariant $M$, $A = c\,\mathbf i$ for a real $c$. (ii) For matrices: if $\mathbf i$ is skew with $\mathbf i^2 = -I$ and commutes with $A$, $\exp(\pi A) = -I$, and $Aw = c\,\mathbf iw$ for a vector $w \neq 0$, then $c$ is an odd integer. (iii) If $k \le 7$ and the scalars $c$ of (i) are odd integers, then there are pairwise orthogonal minimal invariant subspaces $M_1, \dots, M_\nu$ of $E$ with $A = a_h\mathbf i$ on $M_h$, $a_h$ an odd integer, $\nu m_{k+1} = \dim E$, $\operatorname{tr}(A\mathbf i) = -m_{k+1}\sum_h a_h$, and $A^2 = -1$ if every $a_h = \pm1$. (iv) If $k \le 8$, $k \not\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and $M_0$, $M_1$ are minimal invariant with $A = c_0\mathbf i$ on $M_0$ and $A = c_1\mathbf i$ on $M_1$, $c_0, c_1 \neq 0$, there is a linear isomorphism $M_0 \to M_1$ that commutes with the $J_\alpha$ and anticommutes with $J$.

The structures on $\mathbb R^{16r}$, and stabilization

narrower
no limit mapthe class $c$ is stable

Milnor §24, pp. 138–139

$\Omega_k(n)$ can be imbedded in $\Omega_k(n + n')$ by $J \mapsto J \oplus J'_k$. "It is not difficult to see that the inclusions $\Omega_{k+1}(n) \to \Omega\Omega_k(n)$ give rise, in the limit, to inclusions $\Omega_{k+1} \to \Omega\Omega_k$." Later it is convenient to set $n = 16r$.

Proved in Lean

On $\mathbb R^{16r} = \mathbb R^{16} \otimes \mathbb R^r$ let $J_\alpha = J'_\alpha \oplus \dots \oplus J'_\alpha$ ($r$ summands), where $J'_1, \dots, J'_8$ are the structures of V15.9 on $\mathbb R^{16}$; $J_1, \dots, J_8$ is an anticommuting family. Identify $\mathbb R^{16r} \oplus \mathbb R^{16}$ with $\mathbb R^{16(r+1)}$, the new block last, and put $s(X) = X \oplus J'_k$ (for $k = 0$: $X \oplus I_{16}$). Then: (i) for $k \le 8$, $s$ maps $\Omega_k(16r)$ into $\Omega_k(16r + 16)$ and carries $J_k$ to $J_k$; (ii) for $k \le 7$ and $J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(16r)$, $\varphi(J' \oplus J'_{k+1})(t) = \varphi(J')(t) \oplus \bigl(\cos(\pi t)\,J'_k + \sin(\pi t)\,J'_{k+1}\bigr)$ for all $t$; (iii) for $k = 2, 6$ and every matrix $X$ on $\mathbb R^{16r}$, $\operatorname{tr}\bigl(J_k^{\mathsf T}(X \oplus J'_{k+1})\,\mathbf i\bigr) = \operatorname{tr}(J_k^{\mathsf T}X\mathbf i)$, the left side computed on $\mathbb R^{16(r+1)}$, so that by V15.39 (i) the class $c$ of $\varphi(J')$ does not change under stabilization; (iv) for $k = 2, 6$, $\varphi(J_{k+1}) \in \Omega^{(0)}$.

Lemma 24.6 (8): $\Omega_8(16r) \cong O(r)$

restated
by the commutant of $J_1, \dots, J_7$a homeomorphism

Milnor §24, Lemma 24.6 (8), pp. 141–142

$\Omega_8(16r)$ can be identified with the set of all real isometries from $X_1$ to $X_2$: $J_7J_8$ maps $X_1$ isomorphically onto $X_2$, and "clearly this isomorphism determines $J_8$ uniquely". Thus $\Omega_8(16r)$ is diffeomorphic to the orthogonal group $O(r)$.

Proved in Lean

(i) A $16 \times 16$ matrix that commutes with $J'_1, \dots, J'_7$ is $b\,I + c\,W$ for real $b$, $c$, where $W = 1 \otimes 1 \otimes 1 \otimes \tau$ in the notation of V15.9. (ii) With $P_\pm = \tfrac12(1 \pm W)$ and $q(U, V) = P_+ \otimes U + P_- \otimes V$ for $r \times r$ matrices $U$, $V$: every matrix on $\mathbb R^{16r}$ that commutes with $J_1, \dots, J_7$ (V15.41) is $q(U, V)$ for some $U$, $V$. (iii) $\Omega_8(16r)$, for the structures of V15.41, is homeomorphic to $O(r)$: $J$ corresponds to the $U$ with $-J_8J = q(U, U^{\mathsf T})$, and $U$ to $J_8\,q(U, U^{\mathsf T})$; the base point $J_8$ corresponds to $I$.

Stability of $\pi_iO(n)$ and $\pi_iU(n)$

not in the book

$\pi_{i-1}U(m) \cong \pi_{i-1}U(m + 1)$ for $i \le 2m$, from the fibration $U(m) \to U(m + 1) \to S^{2m+1}$. For $O$ no such statement is made: $\pi_iO$ is the homotopy group of the direct limit.

So $\pi_iO(n) \cong \pi_iO(n')$ whenever $i + 2 \le n$ and $i + 2 \le n'$, and $\pi_iU(n) \cong \pi_iU(n')$ whenever $i < 2n$ and $i < 2n'$.
