Milnor Appendix, p. 149

For a topological space $X$ and a sequence $X_0 \subset X_1 \subset X_2 \subset \cdots$ of subspaces, it is convenient to consider the infinite union $X_\Sigma = X_0 \times [0, 1] \cup X_1 \times [1, 2] \cup X_2 \times [2, 3] \cup \cdots$, "to be topologized as a subset of $X \times \mathbb R$". Definition: $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of the sequence $\{X_i\}$ if the projection map $p : X_\Sigma \to X$, $p(x, \tau) = x$, is a homotopy equivalence.

Proved in Lean

Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; for subsets $X_0, X_1, \dots$ of $X$, the telescope is $X_\Sigma = \bigcup_nX_n \times [n, n + 1] \subseteq X \times \mathbb R$, with the subspace topology; the $n$-th strip is the map $X_n \times [0, 1] \to X_\Sigma$, $(x, t) \mapsto (x, n + t)$; $p(x, \tau) = x$; and $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$ if $p$ is a homotopy equivalence. (T1) For a monotone sequence, $(x, \tau) \in X_\Sigma$ iff $x \in X_n$ for some integer $0 \le n \le \tau$; so raising $\tau$ stays in $X_\Sigma$.

Pasting maps along the strips (T3)

Milnor Appendix, pp. 151–153

The book has no such statement. Every map and homotopy on a telescope in the proof of Theorem A (pp. 151–153) is given strip by strip, by formulas in $(x, n + t)$, $0 \le t \le 1$, and its continuity is taken for granted.

Proved in Lean

Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; if every $X_n$ is closed in $X$, then for every space $P$ a function $F$ on $P \times X_\Sigma$ is continuous as soon as each $(p, x, t) \mapsto F(p, (x, n + t))$ is continuous on $P \times X_n \times [0, 1]$. Hence, for a monotone sequence of closed sets, maps $\Phi_n : P \times X_n \times [0, 1] \to Z$ with $\Phi_{n+1}(p, x, 0) = \Phi_n(p, x, 1)$ define a continuous map on $P \times X_\Sigma$; in particular maps on $X_\Sigma$, and homotopies between them, may be given strip by strip.

Milnor Appendix, p. 152

In Case 2, $X_\Sigma^n$ is the subset of $X_\Sigma$ of pairs $(x, \tau)$ with $\tau \le n$, i.e. $X_0 \times [0, 1] \cup \dots \cup X_{n-1} \times [n - 1, n] \cup X_n \times [n]$. Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; the truncation $X^n_\Sigma = \{(x, \tau) \in X_\Sigma : \tau \le n\}$ is closed in $X_\Sigma$, and $X^0_\Sigma \subseteq X^1_\Sigma \subseteq \cdots$, whatever the $X_i$. For a monotone sequence, $x \mapsto (x, n)$ is a homotopy equivalence $X_n \to X^n_\Sigma$ with homotopy inverse $(x, \tau) \mapsto x$, the homotopy raising $\tau$ to $n$; and a function on $X_\Sigma$ that sends the $n$-th strip to levels $\le n + 1$ and $X_n \times \{n\}$ to levels $\le n$ sends each $X^m_\Sigma$ to levels $\le m$.

Milnor Appendix, Example 1 · p. 149

Suppose that each point of $X$ lies in the interior of some $X_i$, and that $X$ is paracompact. Then using a partition of unity one can construct a map $f : X \to \mathbb R$ so that $f(x) \ge i + 1$ for $x \notin X_i$ and $f(x) \ge 0$ for all $x$; and $X$ is a homotopy direct limit.

Proved in Lean

Spaces are arbitrary topological spaces, with no separation axiom unless stated; (i) let $X$ be paracompact and Hausdorff, and $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ with every point of $X$ in the interior of some $X_i$; then $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{X_i\}$. (ii) Let $E : X \to \mathbb R$ be continuous, on any space $X$, and $a_0 \le a_1 \le \cdots$ with $a_i \to \infty$. Then $X$ is the homotopy direct limit of the sublevel sets $\{x : E(x) \le a_i\}$.

hypotheses explicit

Milnor Appendix, Case 1, pp. 151–152

Any map $h_1 : X_\Sigma \to X_\Sigma$ with $h_1(x, n + t) = (x, n + 2t)$ for $0 \le t \le \frac12$ and $h_1(x, n + t) \in X_{n+1} \times [n + 1]$ for $\frac12 \le t \le 1$ is a homotopy equivalence, with homotopy inverse $g(x, n + t) = (x, n + 2t)$ for $t \le \frac12$, $h_1(x, n + \frac32 - t)$ for $t \ge \frac12$, well defined since $h_1(x, n + \frac12) = h_1(x, n + 1) = (x, n + 1)$. $h_1g \simeq \mathrm{id}$ by a homotopy $H_u$, $0 \le u \le \frac12$, ending at $(x, n + \min(4t, 1))$, "clearly" homotopic to the identity; $gh_1 \simeq \mathrm{id}$ "by a completely analogous argument".

(i) For a map $\rho : I \to I$ with $\rho(0) = 0$, $\rho(1) = 1$, $(x, n + t) \mapsto (x, n + \rho(t))$ is homotopic to the identity of $X_\Sigma$. (ii) Let $\psi : X_\Sigma \to X_\Sigma$ be a map with $\psi(x, n + t) = (x, n + 2t)$ for $t \le \frac12$ and $\psi(x, n + t)$ at level $n + 1$ for $t \ge \frac12$. Then $\psi$ fixes the points at integer levels and is a homotopy equivalence, with homotopy inverse Milnor's $g$.

The mapping telescope

not in the book
pasting with no closednessstands for a union of complexes

Milnor Appendix, pp. 149–153

The book has no such construction. The Appendix works with the telescope $X_\Sigma$ of a sequence of subspaces of one space $X$, and the application to Theorem 17.3 with a union $K = \bigcup K_i$ of complexes $K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots$.

Proved in Lean

For a sequence of spaces and maps $K_0 \xrightarrow{c_0} K_1 \xrightarrow{c_1} \cdots$, the mapping telescope $T$ is the quotient of the disjoint union of the blocks $K_n \times [0, 1]$ by $(k, 1)_n \sim (c_n(k), 0)_{n+1}$; $(k, t)_n$ is at level $n + t$, a continuous function on $T$. Maps out of $T$, and out of $P \times T$ for locally compact $P$, may be given block by block, compatibly with the gluing, with no closedness condition. The truncations $T_n = \{\text{level} \le n\}$ are closed and increasing, $T$ is the homotopy direct limit of $\{T_n\}$, and $k \mapsto (k, 0)_n$ is an embedding $K_n \to T$ and a homotopy equivalence $K_n \to T_n$. For subsets $X_0 \subseteq X_1 \subseteq \cdots$ of $X$, the mapping telescope of the inclusions is homotopy equivalent to $X_\Sigma$ (homeomorphic when the $X_n$ are closed).

VA.18

Countable cell complexes

narrower
attaching maps need not be cellulara telescope stands for the union

Milnor Appendix, pp. 149–150

Each $\Omega^{a_i}$ has the homotopy type of "a certain CW-complex", and the union $\Omega$ should have the homotopy type of a CW-complex (p. 149); in the final step of Theorem 17.3 the complexes form a nested sequence $K_0 \subset K_1 \subset \cdots$ with union $K$ (p. 150).

Proved in Lean

A space $K$ is obtained from $L$ by attaching cells of dimensions $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ if it is obtained by attaching a $\lambda_1$-cell to $L$, then a $\lambda_2$-cell, and so on, each along an arbitrary map of its boundary sphere into the space built so far. A cell tower with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0, \mathrm{cells}_1, \dots$ (finite lists of dimensions) is a sequence $K_0 \to K_1 \to \cdots$ in which $K_0$ is an iterated adjunction space with cells $\mathrm{cells}_0$ and $K_{n+1}$ is obtained from $K_n$ by attaching the cells $\mathrm{cells}_{n+1}$. A space has the homotopy type of a countable cell complex with these cells if it is homotopy equivalent to the mapping telescope of such a tower; this is invariant under homotopy equivalence.

G.1

The torus: the intermediate sublevel sets and the cell attachments

not formalized

Milnor §1, pp. 1–3

For $f(p) < a < f(q)$, $f(q) < a < f(r)$ and $f(r) < a < f(s)$, $M^a$ is homeomorphic to a 2-cell, to a cylinder and to a compact genus-one surface bounded by a circle; up to homotopy type, passing $p$, $q$, $r$, $s$ attaches a 0-cell, a 1-cell, a 1-cell and a 2-cell (p. 2).

In the formalization

What is proved is the frame, not the pictures. The torus of revolution is a compact surface whose height function has exactly four critical points, non-degenerate, of indices $0, 1, 1, 2$ (V3.22, V3.23); $T^a$ is empty below $0$ and all of $T$ from $2R + 2\rho$ on, and between critical values Theorem 3.1 holds (V3.24). The homeomorphism types of (2)–(4) would need explicit homeomorphisms, and Theorem 3.2 on submanifolds (V2.8), which would give the cell attachments up to homotopy, has not been applied to the torus. Morse theory with the height function gives only $b_0 \le 1$, $b_1 \le 2$, $b_2 \le 1$ and $b_0 - b_1 + b_2 = 0$; the Betti numbers $1, 2, 1$ are not derived.

G.2

Regular sublevel sets are manifolds with boundary

not formalized

Milnor §2, p. 4

If $a$ is not a critical value of $f$, the implicit function theorem makes $M^a$ a smooth manifold-with-boundary, whose boundary $f^{-1}(a)$ is a smooth submanifold of $M$.

In the formalization

Not restated. It is the companion project's Lemma 3 (Milnor.isHalfSliceSubmanifold_of_regularValue) applied to $a - f$. Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 are stated here for sublevel sets as topological subspaces, without a structure of manifold with boundary.

G.3

The intrinsic Hessian

not formalized

Milnor §2, pp. 4–5

$f_{**}(v, w) = \tilde v_p(\tilde w(f))$ for vector fields $\tilde v$, $\tilde w$ extending $v$, $w$; it is symmetric because $[\tilde v, \tilde w]_p(f) = 0$ at a critical point, and therefore independent of both extensions.

In the formalization

The coordinate formula instead. The formal Hessian is the second derivative read in the preferred chart, Milnor's matrix of second partial derivatives (V1.4), and its independence of the extensions is replaced by its independence of the chart (V1.5).

not formalized

Milnor §2, pp. 8–9

(b) $F(x) = e^{-1/x^2}\sin^2(1/x)$ has a degenerate, non-isolated critical point at the origin; in (d) the critical set is a submanifold of $\mathbb R^2$, and in (e) it is not even a submanifold.

In the formalization

Not done. The smoothness of (b) at $0$ needs the flatness of $e^{-1/x^2}$ against the growth of the derivatives of $\sin^2(1/x)$. The critical sets of (d) and (e) are computed and shown to be degenerate (V1.12), but whether they are submanifolds is not formalized.

A smooth vector field on a manifold $M$ which vanishes outside a compact set generates a unique 1-parameter group of diffeomorphisms of $M$.

not formalized

Milnor §3, Theorem 3.1 · p. 12

For a smooth $f$ on any manifold $M$, with $f^{-1}[a, b]$ compact and free of critical points, $M^a$ is diffeomorphic to $M^b$ and is a deformation retract of it.

In the formalization

Three classes of spaces, not all manifolds. Proved on $\mathbb R^n$ (V2.2), on submanifolds of $\mathbb R^K$, closed or not (V2.3), and on compact Hausdorff manifolds through Mathlib's Whitney embedding (V2.4). A non-compact abstract manifold would need either a closed embedding into Euclidean space or flows of vector fields on manifolds, and Mathlib has neither.

G.8

Theorems 3.2 and 3.5, Remarks 3.3 and 3.4, on abstract manifolds

not formalized

Milnor §3, pp. 14–24

Each is stated for a function on an abstract manifold.

In the formalization

Not transferred. Theorem 3.1 is carried to compact abstract manifolds through the Whitney embedding (V2.4), but the cell-attaching statements are proved only on $\mathbb R^n$ (V2.6, V2.10) and for $f = F|N$ on submanifolds of a Euclidean space (V2.8, V2.9, V2.12, V2.15). The transfer, along the lines of V2.4 and V4.24, has not been made.

G.9

Remark 3.4 on submanifolds, and the Remark of p. 24 at a critical value

not formalized

Milnor §3, pp. 20 and 24

$M^c$ is a deformation retract of $M^{c+\epsilon}$, and $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup e^\lambda$ one of $M^c$; hence each $M^a$ has the homotopy type of a finite CW-complex with one cell for each critical point in $M^a$, even if $a$ is a critical value.

In the formalization

Only on $\mathbb R^n$, and at regular values. Remark 3.4 is proved on $\mathbb R^n$ (V2.10); on submanifolds it is not, so the Remark of p. 24 is proved only for $a$ not a critical value (V2.15).

G.10

The CW structure in Theorem 3.5

not formalized

Milnor §3, Theorem 3.5 · p. 20

$M$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex, the attaching maps being made cellular by cellular approximation (p. 23).

In the formalization

An iterated adjunction space instead. The formal Theorem 3.5 produces a space built from the empty space by attaching cells one at a time along arbitrary continuous maps, with exactly $C_\lambda$ cells of dimension $\lambda$ (V2.11, V2.12). Mathlib has no cellular approximation theorem, so the attaching maps are not made cellular and the result is not shown to be a CW-complex.

G.11

Theorem 3.5 for a non-compact manifold

not formalized

Milnor §3, proof of Theorem 3.5 · p. 23

If $M$ is not compact but all critical points lie in one compact $M^a$, then $M^a$ is a deformation retract of $M$; with infinitely many critical points, the union of the complexes $K_i$ with the direct limit topology and Whitehead's theorem give a homotopy equivalence $M \to K$ (pp. 23–24).

In the formalization

Compact submanifolds only. With finitely many critical points the non-compact case needs a deformation of $M$ onto some $M^a$ obtained by patching flows; with infinitely many it needs Whitehead's theorem and the fact that a manifold is dominated by a CW-complex, neither of which Mathlib provides.

G.12

Smale's handles

not formalized

Milnor §3, Remark, p. 17

In Smale's terminology $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup H$ is $M^{c-\epsilon}$ with a handle attached, and by Theorem 3.1 the manifold-with-boundary $M^{c-\epsilon} \cup H$ is diffeomorphic to $M^{c+\epsilon}$.

In the formalization

Not recorded. It is Theorem 3.1 applied to $F$, which the proof of Theorem 3.2 uses (Assertion 3, as a strong deformation retraction), but the diffeomorphism itself is not stated.

G.13

Reeb's theorem with degenerate critical points

not formalized

Milnor §4, Remark 1 · p. 25

The theorem remains true even if the critical points are degenerate, but the proof is more difficult; Milnor cites his own paper and one of R. Rosen.

In the formalization

Not formalized. A proof needs M. Brown's monotone union theorem, which is not in Mathlib; a proof by that route is written out in the exposition, Chapter 3, §1.

G.14

Exotic spheres

not formalized

Milnor §4, Remark 2 · p. 25

The theorem gives no diffeomorphism with the standard $S^n$, and none need exist: the 7-sphere with an exotic differentiable structure of Milnor's 1956 paper is shown to be homeomorphic to $S^7$ by means of a function with two non-degenerate critical points.

In the formalization

Out of scope. It needs characteristic classes and the signature theorem. The formal proof of Reeb's theorem shows where smoothness is lost: Alexander's cone is not differentiable at the centre (V3.5).

G.15

Manifolds with three critical points

not formalized

Milnor §4, p. 26

If an $n$-manifold carries a differentiable function with only three critical points, these have index $0$, $n$ and $n/2$ (by Poincaré duality), and the manifold has the homotopy type of an $n/2$-sphere with an $n$-cell attached; such functions exist on the real and complex projective planes.

In the formalization

Not formalized. Singular homology with its exact sequences is available (V3.26–V3.31), but Poincaré duality, needed mod 2 since $\mathbb RP^2$ is not orientable, is not; the homotopy type would also need Theorem 3.5 on abstract manifolds.

G.16

Complex projective space: what remains

not formalized

Milnor §4, pp. 26–27

On $\mathbb CP_n$ the function $f(z_0 : \dots : z_n) = \sum_j c_j|z_j|^2$, with distinct constants $c_j$, has $n + 1$ critical points, every even index between $0$ and $2n$ occurring exactly once; so $\mathbb CP_n$ has the homotopy type of $e^0 \cup e^2 \cup \dots \cup e^{2n}$, and $H_i(\mathbb CP_n; \mathbb Z)$ is $\mathbb Z$ for $i = 0, 2, \dots, 2n$ and $0$ otherwise.

In the formalization

Now proved for the submanifold of rank-one projections: the coordinates (V3.41), the critical points and indices of $f$ (V3.42), the cells and the Betti numbers over every field (V3.43). What remains: the CW-complex in the strict sense (cells are attached along arbitrary maps, V2.12) and the integral homology (next entry).

G.17

Integral homology

not formalized

Milnor §4, p. 27, and §5, p. 31

The homology groups of $\mathbb CP_n$ are given with integer coefficients, and Corollary 5.4 is said to find them without Theorem 3.5.

In the formalization

Fields only. §5 works over a field, and so do V3.32–V3.39. The integral groups, and more generally the exposition's Proposition G (in the lacunary case $H_\lambda(M; \mathbb Z)$ is free of rank $C_\lambda$), are not derived, although relative homology and the cell computations are available with integer coefficients (V3.26–V3.31).

G.18

Sard's theorem for $C^1$ maps

not formalized

Milnor §6, Theorem 6.1 · p. 33

For a $C^1$ map between manifolds of the same dimension with countable bases, the image of the set of critical points has measure $0$.

In the formalization

Smooth maps into a vector space. Sard's theorem is proved for smooth maps from a second countable manifold into a finite-dimensional vector space, in any dimensions (V4.3), which is every use Milnor makes of it; the Milnor project proves the Euclidean case for smooth maps only.

G.19

Corollary 6.7 for a non-compact abstract manifold

not formalized

Milnor §6, Corollary 6.7 · p. 36

On any manifold there is a function with no degenerate critical points all of whose sublevel sets are compact, by Whitney's embedding as a closed subset of $\mathbb R^{2n+1}$.

In the formalization

Closed submanifolds and compact manifolds. Proved for closed submanifolds of $\mathbb R^n$ (V4.13) and for compact Hausdorff manifolds (V4.17). Mathlib's Whitney embedding is for compact manifolds only, so a non-compact abstract manifold has no closed embedding into Euclidean space here; the abstract forms of Corollary 6.8 (V4.22) are limited in the same way.

G.20

Application 1: the homotopy type of a CW-complex

not formalized

Milnor §6, Application 1 · p. 36

A differentiable manifold has the homotopy type of a CW-complex, by Corollary 6.7 and Theorem 3.5.

In the formalization

Not formalized. Theorem 3.5 is proved only for compact submanifolds of Euclidean space and only as an iterated adjunction space, Mathlib having no cellular approximation (V2.11, V2.12); it has not been transferred to abstract manifolds, and the non-compact case needs Whitehead's theorem.

G.21

Application 2 as Milnor argues it

not formalized

Milnor §6, Application 2 · p. 36

On a compact manifold the index sum of $\mathrm{grad} f$ is $\chi(M)$, and the index sum of any vector field is $\chi(M)$ because it is a topological invariant (Steenrod, §39.7).

In the formalization

Run the other way, on an embedded copy. $\chi$ enters as the Poincaré–Hopf integer of the Milnor project (V3.17, V4.18) and is identified with $\sum_i (-1)^i \dim H_i(M; F)$ afterwards (V3.38). The topological invariance quoted from Steenrod is not formalized, and vector fields on an abstract manifold are not treated, only on an embedded copy (V4.19).

G.22

Independence of the principal curvatures

not formalized

Milnor §6, p. 34

The principal curvatures are the eigenvalues of $(\vec v \cdot \vec\ell_{ij})$ in coordinates with $(g_{ij})$ the identity at $q$, tacitly independent of the coordinates chosen.

In the formalization

Not proved, and not needed. The principal curvatures are the eigenvalues of the shape operator of the chosen slice chart (V4.6), and every statement that uses them is proved in that chart.

G.23

Theorem 7.2 for complex manifolds, and CW-complexes

not formalized

Milnor §7, Theorem 7.2 · p. 39

A complex manifold of complex dimension $k$, embedded bianalytically as a closed subset of $\mathbb C^n$, is homotopy equivalent to a CW-complex of dimension $k$.

In the formalization

Proved for closed submanifolds with complex tangent spaces (V5.15), as a countable cell complex with cells of dimension at most $k$. What remains: that a bianalytically embedded complex manifold is such a submanifold (holomorphic charts are not formalized as charts of the real submanifold), and a CW-complex in the strict sense, with cellular attaching maps.

G.24

Theorem 7.1 with integral coefficients

not formalized

Milnor §7, Theorem 7.1 · p. 39

A non-singular affine algebraic variety $M \subset \mathbb C^n$ of real dimension $2k$ has $H_i(M; \mathbb Z) = 0$ in every degree $i > k$.

In the formalization

Proved over every field (V5.16), for closed submanifolds with complex tangent spaces. What remains: integral coefficients, and that a non-singular affine algebraic variety is such a submanifold.

G.25

Assertion 2 for focal points, and the count of p. 41

not formalized

Milnor §7, pp. 40–41

The focal points of $(M, q)$ along a normal line occur in symmetric pairs about $q$; there are at most $2k$ of them on the line, hence at most $k$ between $p$ and $q$, which by Lemma 6.9 bounds the index of $L_p$.

In the formalization

Replaced. Assertion 2 is proved for Hessians in a holomorphic chart (V5.7), and the index bound by the Andreotti–Frankel identity (V5.8–V5.11), on the real submanifold in V5.13; these need neither focal points nor Lemma 6.9. The focal-point form is not formalized.

G.26

Corollary 7.3 with integral coefficients; Hypothesis (N)

not formalized

Milnor §7, Corollary 7.3 · p. 41

For an algebraic variety $V$ of complex dimension $k$ in $\mathbb CP_n$ and a hyperplane $P$ containing its singular points, the inclusion $V \cap P \to V$ induces isomorphisms of integral homology in dimensions less than $k - 1$, and a surjection in dimension $k - 1$.

In the formalization

Proved over every field (V5.17, V5.18), without Lefschetz duality, for a closed $V \subseteq \mathbb CP^n$ whose affine part is a complex submanifold, under Hypothesis (N). What remains: integral homology; algebraic varieties (that their affine parts satisfy the hypothesis); and Hypothesis (N) itself, the deformation of a neighbourhood of $V \cap P$ into it.

G.27

Theorem 7.4: triangulability

not formalized

Milnor §7, Theorem 7.4 · p. 41

Under the same hypotheses the relative homotopy groups $\pi_r(V, V \cap P)$ vanish for $r < k$.

In the formalization

Proved under Hypothesis (N) (V5.19), as the compression criterion for $\pi_r(V, V \cap P) = 0$. What remains: Hypothesis (N), which Milnor obtains from the triangulability of algebraic varieties (quoted), and relative homotopy groups as objects.

G.28

§§8–9 on an abstract Riemannian manifold

not formalized

Milnor §§8–9 · p. 43

Connections, Christoffel symbols, covariant derivatives along curves, parallel translation, the Levi-Civita connection and the curvature tensor are developed on an abstract Riemannian manifold, in local coordinates.

In the formalization

Embedded manifolds instead. The substance of §§8–9 is proved for submanifolds of a Euclidean space with the induced metric (V6.1–V6.21). On an abstract manifold only Milnor's rules for Mathlib's covariant derivatives, the definitions of compatibility and symmetry, the uniqueness half of Lemma 8.6, and the curvature formula with its sign (V6.3, V6.11, V6.13, V6.14, V6.16). Mathlib has no curvature, Christoffel symbols, covariant derivative along curves, parallel transport or Levi-Civita connection, and the embedded results reach an arbitrary Riemannian manifold only through Nash's embedding theorem, which is not proved. The induced connection is not constructed as a Mathlib covariant derivative, so the embedded existence and the abstract uniqueness are parallel results, not one theorem.

G.29

Symmetric Christoffel symbols, and the second covariant derivative

not formalized

Milnor §8, p. 48

If $\Gamma^k_{ij} = \Gamma^k_{ji}$ then the connection is symmetric throughout the coordinate neighbourhood; and, in a footnote, a connection is symmetric iff the covariant second derivative $X_p(Yf) - (X_p \vdash Y)f$ is symmetric in $X_p$ and $Y_p$.

In the formalization

Not formalized, there being no Christoffel symbols in either setting; the second covariant derivative of a function is not defined.

G.30

Parallel fields along a flat surface

not formalized

Milnor §9, pp. 52–53

If the curvature tensor vanishes, a vector field $P$ along a parametrized surface with $DP/\partial x = DP/\partial y = 0$ and a given value at the origin can be constructed.

In the formalization

Not formalized. Lemma 9.2, on which the construction rests, is proved for embedded manifolds (V6.19).

G.31

Geodesics and path spaces on an abstract Riemannian manifold

not formalized

Milnor §§10–19 · p. 55

Milnor's §§10–19 are written for an abstract Riemannian manifold $M$: the Levi-Civita connection of §8, geodesics and the exponential map, the distance and completeness, the path space $\Omega(M; p, q)$ with its energy, Jacobi fields, the index theorem, and the topology of $\Omega$.

In the formalization

Everything in Chapters 7–11 is proved for a submanifold $N$ of a Euclidean space $V$ with the induced metric (V7.1). Mathlib has no Levi-Civita connection, geodesics or exponential map on an abstract manifold, and the Christoffel-symbol form of the geodesic equation is not formalized (V7.3). Every Riemannian manifold is isometric to such an $N$ by Nash's embedding theorem, which is quoted in the Lean files but neither proved nor used, so the formal results reach an abstract manifold only through it. Within the setting, completeness is often obtained from closedness of $N$ in $V$, which implies it (V7.30, V10.22).

G.32

The remarks on minimal geodesics

not formalized

Milnor §10, p. 62

Theorem 10.4 asserts that any sufficiently small segment of a geodesic is minimal. On the other hand a long geodesic may not be minimal: a great circle arc on the unit sphere of length greater than $\pi$ is certainly not. In general minimal geodesics are not unique: two antipodal points of a unit sphere are joined by infinitely many.

In the formalization

Not stated as such. The short geodesics of Lemma 10.3 and Corollary 10.8 are shortest (V7.15, V7.20), from which the first remark follows for every geodesic, but the step is not written. For long arcs, every geodesic of $S^n$, $n \ge 2$, of length $> \pi$ is not minimal (V11.14, from Myers' theorem). The non-uniqueness of minimal geodesics between antipodal points is not formalized.

G.33

Geodesics of surfaces, and the footnote on $U(n)$

not formalized

Milnor §10, pp. 57 and 65–66

Among the familiar examples of p. 65: meridians of a surface of revolution are geodesics; the geodesics of a right circular cylinder are the generating lines, the circles cut by perpendicular planes, and the helices, so that two points of the cylinder are joined by infinitely many; antipodal points of $S^n$ are joined by a continuum of minimal geodesics. A footnote on p. 57 explains the name "exponential": on the group of unitary matrices, $\exp_I(A) = I + A + \frac1{2!}A^2 + \dots$.

In the formalization

The geodesics of $\mathbb R^n$ and of $S^n$ are V7.30′. Surfaces of revolution, the cylinder, the continuum of minimal geodesics between antipodal points, and the identification of the Riemannian exponential of $U(n)$ with the matrix exponential (which needs a bi-invariant metric) are not formalized.

G.34

Induced maps and Hessians of functions on $\Omega$

not formalized

Milnor §§11 and 13, pp. 68–69 and 74

To motivate the definitions, Milnor defines the induced map $F_* : T\Omega_\omega \to T\mathbb R_{F(\omega)}$ of a real function $F$ on $\Omega$ through variations, noting that without hypotheses on $F$ there is no guarantee that it exists or is independent of the variation; and he observes that if $F$ takes its minimum at $\omega_0$ and the derivatives $dF(\bar\alpha(u))/du$ are all defined, then $\omega_0$ is a critical path (p. 69). On p. 74 he recalls the Hessian $f_{**}$ of a function on a finite-dimensional manifold, defined through 2-parameter maps.

In the formalization

Not formalized: critical paths are defined only for the energy (V8.4), and the Hessian only for $E$ (V8.14), where Theorem 13.1 shows it to be well defined. The Hessian of a function on a finite-dimensional manifold is that of Part I.

G.35

Corollary 17.2 by Milnor's route

not formalized

Milnor §17, Corollary 17.2 · p. 95

The path space $\Omega$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex: by Theorem 17.1 it is homotopy equivalent to $\Omega^*$, which has the homotopy type of a CW-complex by Milnor's theorem (On spaces having the homotopy type of a CW-complex, 1959). It is used with Whitehead's theorem in the first proof of Theorem 17.3.

In the formalization

Proved for $N$ closed in $V$ (V10.29), by moving the end point to a non-conjugate one and Theorem 17.3, which gives a countable cell complex in the sense of VA.18. What remains: Milnor's theorem of 1959 and Whitehead's theorem, which are not in Mathlib, and the corollary for manifolds that are not complete. Theorem 17.3 does not use it (V10.22).

G.36

Corollary 17.5: infinitely many geodesics

not formalized

Milnor §17, Corollary 17.5 · p. 96

Let $M$ have the homotopy type of $S^n$, $n > 2$. Then any two non-conjugate points of $M$ are joined by infinitely many geodesics: the homotopy type of $\Omega^*(M)$, and hence of $\Omega(M)$, depends only on that of $M$, so there must be at least one geodesic of index $0$, at least one of index $n - 1$, $2(n - 1)$, and so on.

In the formalization

Not formalized. It needs the homotopy invariance of $\Omega^*$ (the path spaces of homotopy equivalent spaces are weakly equivalent, with the same homology) and the homology of the countable cell complex of Theorem 17.3 in each dimension. What is formalized is that the corollary as printed omits a hypothesis: $\mathbb R^{n+1} \setminus \{0\}$ has the homotopy type of $S^n$ and no conjugate points, yet two of its points are joined by a single geodesic (V10.27), so $M$ must be complete. For $M = S^n$ itself the geodesics and the homology of $\Omega(S^n; p, q)$ are computed (V10.23, V10.26).

G.37

Serre's remark, and the suspension theorem

not formalized

Milnor §17, Remark, p. 97

More generally, if $M$ is any complete manifold which is not contractible, then any two non-conjugate points of $M$ are joined by infinitely many geodesics (compare Serre, Homologie singulière des espaces fibrés, 1951). As another application of 17.4 one can give a proof of the Freudenthal suspension theorem (compare §22.3).

In the formalization

Not formalized: Serre's theorem on the homology of loop spaces (the spectral sequence of the path fibration) and the passage to the universal covering are not available. The suspension theorem belongs to §22, which is not formalized.

G.38

Corollary 19.3: no torsion in $\pi_1$

not formalized

Milnor §19, Corollary 19.3 · p. 103

If $M$ is complete with $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle \le 0$, then $\pi_1(M)$ contains no element of finite order other than the identity. Proof: the universal covering $\tilde M$ being contractible, $H^k(M)$ is the cohomology of the group $\pi_1(M)$ (Hu); a non-trivial finite cyclic subgroup $G$ would give a covering $\hat M$ with $H^k(G) = H^k(\hat M) = 0$ for $k > n$, while the cohomology groups of a finite cyclic group are non-trivial in arbitrarily high dimensions.

In the formalization

Not formalized: the cohomology of groups, of finite cyclic groups in particular, and the identification $H^k(M) \cong H^k(\pi_1(M))$ are not available. The first half of the corollary, $\pi_i(M) = 0$ for $i > 1$, is V11.21, where the universal covering is $\exp_p : T_pN \to N$ (V11.19).

G.39

Finiteness of $\pi_1$ in positive Ricci curvature

not formalized

Milnor §19, p. 105

Corollary 19.5 applies also to the universal covering space $\tilde M$ of $M$. Since $\tilde M$ is compact, the fundamental group $\pi_1(M)$ is finite.

In the formalization

Not formalized: universal coverings with a lifted metric are not formalized. In non-positive curvature the universal covering is $\exp_p$ itself (V11.19), but in positive Ricci curvature $\exp_p$ has critical points (Myers' theorem), so it is no covering. Corollary 19.5, compactness and the bound $\pi r$ on the diameter, is V11.13.

G.40

Sectional curvature as a Gaussian curvature

not formalized

Milnor §19, Remark, p. 100

If $A$ and $B$ are orthogonal unit vectors at $p$, the sectional curvature $\langle R(A, B)A, B\rangle$ is equal to the Gaussian curvature of the surface $(u_1, u_2) \mapsto \exp_p(u_1A + u_2B)$ spanned by the geodesics through $p$ with velocity vectors in the plane of $A$ and $B$ (Laugwitz).

In the formalization

Not formalized: the Gaussian curvature of this surface is not defined. The sectional curvature is that of Chapter 6, and the hypothesis of Lemma 19.1 is shown equivalent to all sectional curvatures being $\le 0$ (V11.7).

G.41

The optics of curvature, and examples of curvature $\le 0$

not formalized

Milnor §19, pp. 101–102

Intuitively, curvature can be described through "optics", geodesics being the paths of light rays: a short segment of length $L$ at $\exp_p(rU)$ in the direction $W$ appears to have length $L(1 + \frac{r^2}6\langle R(U, W)U, W\rangle + \dots)$, and a small object of volume $v$ appears to have volume $v(1 + \frac{r^2}6K(U, U) + \dots)$. Examples of complete manifolds of curvature $\le 0$: Euclidean space, the paraboloid $z = x^2 - y^2$, the hyperboloid of rotation $x^2 + y^2 - z^2 = 1$, the helicoid. The pseudo-sphere has constant curvature $-1$ and no conjugate points, but is not complete; by a theorem of Hilbert no complete surface of constant negative curvature can be imbedded in $\mathbb R^3$, although complete, even compact, ones exist, such as surfaces of genus $\ge 2$.

In the formalization

Not formalized; none of these statements is used later in the book.

G.42

The remarks after Theorem 19.6

not formalized

Milnor §19, pp. 106–107

Milnor does not know whether Theorem 19.6 remains true for $M$ complete but non-compact; the proof breaks down on the paraboloid $z = x^2 + y^2$, where $K(U, U)$ is not bounded away from $0$. The product $S^m \times S^k$, $m, k \ge 2$, has positive definite Ricci tensor while some sectional curvatures vanish; it is not known whether it can be remetrized with all sectional curvatures positive, and by a theorem of Synge such a metric could not be invariant under $(x, y) \mapsto (-x, -y)$.

In the formalization

Not formalized.

G.43

Example 2 of the Appendix: CW-complexes

not formalized

Milnor Appendix, Example 2 · p. 149

Let $X$ be a CW-complex and let the $X_i$ be subcomplexes with union $X$. Since $p : X_\Sigma \to X$ induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups in all dimensions, it follows from Whitehead's theorem that $X$ is a homotopy direct limit.

In the formalization

Not formalized: it needs Whitehead's theorem, the fact that a compact subset of a CW-complex lies in a finite subcomplex, and the CW topology of products, none of which is in Mathlib. Hence the mapping telescope of a cell tower is not compared with the union of its stages in the weak topology, and the "countable CW-complexes" of Theorems 17.3 and 19.6 are mapping telescopes of iterated adjunction spaces (VA.18). Example 1, the case used for the path space, is VA.7.

G.44

The Remark on Case 1 of Theorem A

not formalized

Milnor Appendix, Remark, p. 150

Under the conditions of Case 1 it would be natural to conjecture that $f_\Sigma$ must actually be homotopic to the identity; however counterexamples can be given.

In the formalization

Not formalized: the exposition's counterexample, a phantom map, needs cellular cohomology and $\mathbb{CP}^\infty$. Case 1 itself is VA.10.

G.45

Symmetric spaces: Lemma 20.1 and Corollaries 20.2–20.4

not formalized

Milnor §20, pp. 109–110

A symmetric space is a connected Riemannian manifold with, for each $p$, an isometry $I_p$ fixing $p$ and reversing geodesics through $p$. Lemma 20.1: $I_qI_p$ translates a geodesic through $p = \gamma(0)$ and $q = \gamma(c)$ along itself, $\gamma(t) \mapsto \gamma(t + 2c)$, and parallel fields likewise. Corollaries: 20.2, a symmetric space is complete; 20.3, $I_p$ is unique; 20.4, $R(U, V)W$ is parallel along $\gamma$ when $U, V, W$ are. Locally symmetric spaces; Cartan's theorem relating them.

In the formalization

Not formalized: isometries of an abstract Riemannian manifold and symmetric spaces are not defined. For matrix groups, completeness and the reflection are V12.15–V12.16, and the conclusion of 20.4 is used through the explicit frame of V12.18.

G.46

Theorem 20.5 for a general locally symmetric space

not formalized

Milnor §20, Theorem 20.5, p. 110

In a locally symmetric manifold the conjugate points along a geodesic and their multiplicities are given by the positive eigenvalues of $K_V$.

In the formalization

Proved only along one-parameter subgroups of matrix groups (the Jacobi equation, V12.18) and, with the multiplicities, for $SU(n)$ (V14.18).

G.47

The bi-invariant metric of a compact Lie group

not formalized

Milnor §21, p. 112

A compact Lie group has a bi-invariant metric, obtained by averaging any metric with the Haar measure; a left-invariant metric is bi-invariant iff it is invariant under $\operatorname{Ad}$.

In the formalization

Not formalized; the groups of §§23–24 are matrix groups with the induced metric, which is bi-invariant (V12.14).

G.48

Corollaries 21.5 and 21.6: the topology

not formalized

Milnor §21, pp. 115–116

21.5: trivial centre makes $G$ compact with finite $\pi_1$ (Myers). 21.6: a simply connected $G$ with a bi-invariant metric is $G' \times \mathbb R^k$ with $G'$ compact; conversely such products have bi-invariant metrics.

In the formalization

Only the Lie-algebra steps (V12.9, V12.10). Myers' theorem itself is V11.12–V11.13, but it is not applied to a Lie group; integrating an ideal decomposition to a product of groups is not formalized.

G.49

Theorem 21.7 (Bott): only even cells

not formalized

Milnor §21, Theorem 21.7, p. 116

If $G$ is compact and simply connected, $\Omega(G)$ has the homotopy type of a CW-complex with no odd-dimensional cells and only finitely many $\lambda$-cells for each even $\lambda$; so $H_\lambda(\Omega G; \mathbb Z)$ is $0$ for odd $\lambda$ and free of finite rank for even $\lambda$. Remarks: the complex is infinite-dimensional; the theorem extends to non-compact $G$ (Iwasawa).

In the formalization

Not formalized: only the algebra behind the evenness of the index (V12.11–V12.13). Theorem 17.3 (V10.22) and the Index Theorem (V9.24) are available, but Theorem 20.5 for a general compact group, the finiteness of §19.4 for it, and the passage to the loop space are not assembled.

G.50

Hanner's theorem, and Theorem 22.1 for a manifold $\Omega^d$

not formalized

Milnor §22, pp. 118, 121

Theorem 22.1 and Lemma 22.5 assume that $\Omega^d$ (resp. $M^0$) is a topological manifold; the proof uses Hanner's theorem: a manifold is a retract of a neighbourhood.

In the formalization

Not formalized. The formal Theorem 22.1 assumes the neighbourhood retraction (V13.2); for the sphere and for $SU(2m)$ it is constructed (V13.8, V14.21), so Corollary 22.3 and Theorem 23.3 are unconditional.

G.51

The homological form of Theorem 22.1

not formalized

Milnor §22, p. 118

By the relative Hurewicz theorem, $H_i(\Omega, \Omega^d) = 0$ for $i < \lambda_0$, so $H_i\Omega^d \cong H_i\Omega$ for $i \le \lambda_0 - 2$.

In the formalization

Not formalized (relative Hurewicz is not available).

G.52

$U(n)$: the distance from $I$ to $-I$ and the space of all subspaces

not formalized

Milnor §23, p. 127

In $U(n)$ the minimal geodesics from $I$ to $-I$ have length $\pi\sqrt n$ and correspond to all subspaces of $\mathbb C^n$, a space with components of varying dimensions; $\exp$ is onto.

In the formalization

Only $SU(2m)$ is treated (V14.15–V14.17); V14.12 records why $U(n)$ cannot be used.

G.53

$\pi_0$ in Lemma 23.4

not formalized

Milnor §23, Lemma 23.4, pp. 128–129

$\pi_0U(m) \cong \pi_0SU(m)$ (both groups are connected), and the case $i = 1$ of $\pi_iG_m(\mathbb C^{2m}) \cong \pi_{i-1}U(m)$ as groups.

In the formalization

For $i = 1$ the formal statement is a bijection of pointed sets (V14.26); the connectedness of $U(m)$ and $SU(m)$ is not formalized.

G.54

The limit spaces, and Theorem 24.5 as a homotopy equivalence

not formalized

Milnor §24, Theorem 24.5, p. 138; pp. 146, 148

$\Omega_k$ is the direct limit of the $\Omega_k(n)$ with the direct limit topology, and $O = \Omega_0$ the infinite orthogonal group. For each $k \ge 0$ the limit map $\Omega_{k+1} \to \Omega\Omega_k$ is a homotopy equivalence: it induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups in all dimensions, both spaces have the homotopy type of a CW-complex ("it can be shown"), and Whitehead's theorem applies.

In the formalization

Not formalized: no direct limits, no CW homotopy types, no Whitehead theorem. Theorem 24.5 is proved for each $n$, as bijections of homotopy groups in a range growing with $n$ (V15.31, V15.39, V15.40), for $k \le 7$; the compatibility with stabilization is V15.41, but the bijections are not shown natural.

G.55

Theorem 24.7 as $O \simeq \Omega^8O$, and the group structure

not formalized

Milnor §24, Theorem 24.7, p. 142

The infinite orthogonal group $O$ has the same homotopy type as its own 8-th loop space; $O$ has the homotopy type of $\Omega\Omega\Omega\Omega Sp$, and $Sp$ that of $\Omega\Omega\Omega\Omega O$.

In the formalization

Only $\pi_iO(n) \cong \pi_{i+8}O(n')$ in the stable range, as a bijection of sets (V15.45). The bijections along the chain are not shown to be homomorphisms, and nothing is proved about $Sp$.

G.56

The table of $\pi_iO$ and $\pi_iSp$

not formalized

Milnor §24, p. 142

$\pi_iO = \mathbb Z_2, \mathbb Z_2, 0, \mathbb Z, 0, 0, 0, \mathbb Z$ and $\pi_iSp = 0, 0, 0, \mathbb Z, \mathbb Z_2, \mathbb Z_2, 0, \mathbb Z$ for $i \equiv 0, \dots, 7 \pmod 8$; "the verification that these groups are correct will be left to the reader".

In the formalization

Not formalized.

G.57

Symmetric spaces, and $\Omega_1(n) \cong O(n)/U(n/2)$

not formalized

Milnor §24, pp. 133, 136

Each component of $\Omega_k(n)$ is a symmetric space. Remark: $\Omega_1(n)$ can be identified with the quotient space $O(n)/U(n/2)$.

In the formalization

Only the algebraic invariance of $\Omega_k(n)$ under the reflections (V15.5); the manifold structure is V15.23. The isotropy algebra of a point enters V15.28, but no quotient space is formed.

G.58

Lemma 24.6 (2)–(7): the spaces $\Omega_2, \dots, \Omega_7$

not formalized

Milnor §24, pp. 138–141

$\Omega_2(n) \cong U(n/2)/Sp(n/4)$; $\Omega_3(16r)$ the quaternionic Grassmann manifold; $\Omega_4(16r)$ diffeomorphic to $Sp(2r)$; $\Omega_5(16r) \cong Sp(2r)/U(2r)$; $\Omega_6(16r) \cong U(2r)/O(2r)$; the largest component of $\Omega_7(16r)$ diffeomorphic to the Grassmann manifold of $r$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb R^{2r}$; and, for $k > 8$, $\Omega_k(16r)$ diffeomorphic to $\Omega_{k-8}(r)$ (footnote, p. 142).

In the formalization

Only the bijections with involutions and the dimensions (V15.11, V15.12), and step (8) as a homeomorphism (V15.42). The periodicity theorem does not need the other identifications.

G.59

The curvature of $\Omega_k(n)$, and the exact index of a geodesic

not formalized

Milnor §24, pp. 135, 144–146

The index of a geodesic is computed from the eigenvalues of $K_A = -\tfrac14(\operatorname{Ad}A)^2$, by Theorem 20.5 and the index theorem; on $\Omega_k(n)$, $K_A$ is given by the same formula because $\Omega_k(n)$ is totally geodesic. For $O(2m)$: $\lambda = \sum_{i<j}(a_i + a_j - 2) + \sum_{a_i > a_j}(a_i - a_j - 2)$.

In the formalization

The lower bounds that Theorem 22.1 needs are proved for geodesics through Killing fields (V15.28, V15.30, V15.38). The exact formulas are obtained only as counts from Milnor's spectra (V15.3, V15.19, V15.20); the curvature of a totally geodesic submanifold and Theorem 20.5 for $\Omega_k(n)$ are not formalized.

G.60

Lemma 24.8 for $k = 3, 7$ and $k > 8$; isometries

not formalized

Milnor §24, p. 143

For $k = 3$ and $k = 7$ there are two non-isomorphic minimal spaces; for $k > 8$ "the situation repeats more or less periodically", and $m_k = 16m_{k-8}$; the isomorphisms of Lemma 24.8 are isometries.

In the formalization

For $k \le 8$: the dimension $m_k$ (V15.16) and, for $k \not\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, uniqueness up to a linear isomorphism (V15.17). For $k = 3, 7$ only that the central involution acts as $\pm1$; nothing for $k > 8$.

G.61

Hurwitz–Radon and Adams

not formalized

Milnor §24, Remark, p. 144

The vector fields obtained from Clifford modules are those of Hurwitz and Radon, and "J. F. Adams has recently proved that these estimates are best possible".

In the formalization

Only the $k$ orthonormal fields from $k$ anticommuting complex structures (V15.18); no count for general $n$, and no upper bound.
